summary:
This regulation establishes rules for railway undertakings, including information provision, transport contracts, ticketing, and liability, and applies to all rail journeys and services in the Community provided by licensed railway undertakings. It does not apply to unlicensed railway undertakings and services. The regulation applies to various parties, including railway undertakings licensed in accordance with Council Directive 95/18/EC, passengers using rail services, ticket vendors, tour operators, infrastructure managers, and station managers.

Railway undertakings have several obligations, including providing information to passengers, concluding transport contracts, issuing tickets, and implementing a Computerised Information and Reservation System for Rail Transport. They are also liable for passengers and their luggage. Passengers have the right to protection and assistance, particularly disabled persons and persons with reduced mobility. Railway undertakings must define and monitor service quality standards.

In terms of travel information, railway undertakings and ticket vendors must provide travel information to passengers upon request in the most appropriate format, considering the needs of people with auditory and/or visual impairment. Railway undertakings must also be adequately insured or make equivalent arrangements for cover of liabilities under this regulation. They must offer tickets, through tickets, and reservations where available, and distribute tickets via at least one of the following: ticket offices, selling machines, telephone, Internet, or on board trains.

Passengers have the right to be informed of delays and estimated departure/arrival times, and to free meals, refreshments, hotel accommodation, and transport in case of delays over 60 minutes. They also have the right to alternative transport services if the rail service cannot continue, and to certification of delay, missed connection, or cancellation on their ticket. Railway undertakings and station managers must provide assistance and information, with particular attention to the needs of disabled persons and persons with reduced mobility.

Railway undertakings, station managers, and tour operators must inform passengers of their rights and obligations under the regulation when selling tickets, and may use a summary of the provisions prepared by the Commission. The regulation also specifies conditions for the carriage of vehicles, including acceptance, registration, loading, carriage, unloading, and delivery, which are contained in the General Conditions of Carriage. Railway undertakings must issue a carriage voucher to the passenger, which must contain specific information, including the carrier, a statement that the carriage is subject to the Uniform Rules, and other details.

Overall, this regulation aims to protect the rights of passengers and ensure that railway undertakings provide adequate information, assistance, and services to passengers, while also establishing clear rules and obligations for the provision of rail services in the Community.

summary:
Regulation (EC) No 1371/2007 aims to safeguard users' rights for rail passengers and improve the quality and effectiveness of rail passenger services. This regulation applies to rail passengers' rights and obligations, and its scope extends to railway undertakings, ticket vendors, disabled persons and persons with reduced mobility, as well as Member States. Passengers have the right to receive information regarding the service before and during the journey, and railway undertakings and ticket vendors are required to provide such information in advance and as soon as possible. Additionally, disabled persons and persons with reduced mobility have the right to free movement, freedom of choice, and non-discrimination.

Railway undertakings are also required to be insured or make equivalent arrangements for their liability to rail passengers in the event of an accident. Furthermore, passengers have the right to submit a complaint to any railway undertaking involved regarding the rights and obligations conferred by this Regulation. Railway undertakings and ticket vendors shall provide travel information to passengers and distribute tickets via at least one point of sale. They shall also offer tickets for services under public service contracts and assist passengers claiming compensation for damage from third parties.

In the event of delays, passengers have the right to reimbursement or re-routing. Railway undertakings may offer contract conditions more favorable for passengers, and they are required to keep passengers informed of delays. Station managers must provide assistance free of charge to disabled persons and persons with reduced mobility. The regulation also governs liability of railway undertakings for passengers and their luggage, as well as delays, missed connections, and cancellations.

In terms of complaints, railway undertakings are required to set up a complaint handling mechanism, make contact details and working language(s) widely known to passengers, and respond to complaints within one month or inform the passenger of the expected response date within three months. Passengers may submit complaints to any railway undertaking involved. The regulation also provides for recourse claims among carriers, where a carrier has the right of recourse against other carriers and must present a claim in one proceeding against all non-settling carriers.

Member States are required to designate a body for the enforcement of this Regulation, which must ensure respect for passenger rights and be independent in organization, funding, and decision-making. The Commission shall submit a report on setting a minimum amount of insurance for railway undertakings. Overall, this regulation aims to protect the rights of rail passengers and ensure that railway undertakings and ticket vendors provide a high level of service and assistance to all passengers, including those with disabilities or reduced mobility.

summary:
Regulation (EC) No 1394/2007 regulates advanced therapy medicinal products intended for the market in Member States, prepared industrially or manufactured by an industrial process. This regulation applies to advanced therapy medicinal products containing medical devices, bio-materials, scaffolds, or matrices, and to Member States. However, it excludes products prepared on a non-routine basis according to specific quality standards, used within the same Member State in a hospital under a medical practitioner's responsibility. 

The regulation imposes certain obligations, including the requirement to include a description of physical characteristics, performance, and design methods in applications for authorisation of advanced therapy medicinal products containing devices. Additionally, there is a right to a single scientific evaluation of quality, safety, and efficacy of advanced therapy medicinal products by the European Medicines Agency. 

For combined advanced therapy medicinal products, the application for marketing authorisation must include evidence of conformity with essential requirements and the results of an assessment by a notified body, if available. The Agency may request information from the notified body or seek its opinion if the assessment results are not included. 

Holders of marketing authorisations for advanced therapy medicinal products, as well as hospitals, institutions, or private practices where these products are used, must establish and maintain systems for tracing individual products and materials, and for patient and product traceability. These systems must be compatible with relevant Directives. 

The Committee for Advanced Therapies plays a crucial role in the regulation of advanced therapy medicinal products, with tasks including formulating draft opinions on quality, safety, and efficacy, advising on data generated in development, and providing advice on whether a product falls within the definition of an advanced therapy medicinal product. The Committee also assists in the elaboration of documents related to the Regulation's objectives and provides scientific expertise and advice for Community initiatives. 

The Commission is obligated to publish a general report on the application of the Regulation, including comprehensive information on authorized advanced therapy medicinal products, and to assess the impact of technical progress on the Regulation's application. The report must also review the scope of the Regulation, including the regulatory framework for combined advanced therapy medicinal products. 

Manufacturing of advanced therapy medicinal products must be authorised by the competent authority of the Member State, and Member States must ensure that national traceability and pharmacovigilance requirements are equivalent to those at the Community level. Advanced therapy medicinal products must comply with the Regulation by a specified date, and marketing authorisation holders must provide specific information on the packaging and package leaflet. Furthermore, patients must be provided with certain information, although the specifics of this requirement are not detailed in the available information. 

Overall, the regulation aims to ensure the quality, safety, and efficacy of advanced therapy medicinal products, while also providing a framework for their development, authorisation, and post-marketing surveillance. It applies to various stakeholders, including medical practitioners, Member States, marketing authorisation holders, and manufacturers, and imposes certain rights and obligations on these parties to achieve its objectives.

summary:
This Regulation sets out specific rules for the authorisation, supervision, and pharmacovigilance of advanced therapy medicinal products, which include gene therapy medicinal products, somatic cell therapy medicinal products, and tissue engineered products. Advanced therapy medicinal products are defined as medicinal products for human use that have properties for, or are used in or administered to human beings with a view to regenerating, repairing, or replacing a human tissue. The Regulation applies to advanced therapy medicinal products intended to be placed on the market in Member States and either prepared industrially or manufactured by a method involving an industrial process. It also applies to products prepared on a non-routine basis according to specific quality standards, as well as to products used within the same Member State in a hospital under the exclusive professional responsibility of a medical practitioner.

The Regulation lays down requirements for the labelling of outer and immediate packaging of advanced therapy medicinal products, which must include particulars listed in Annex III to the Regulation. Combined advanced therapy medicinal products, which incorporate one or more medical devices and contain viable cells or tissues, or non-viable cells or tissues liable to act upon the human body, are subject to a final evaluation by the Agency and must comply with essential requirements. The application for marketing authorisation for combined advanced therapy medicinal products must include evidence of conformity with these requirements and the results of an assessment by a notified body, if available.

Holders of marketing authorisation for advanced therapy medicinal products, as well as hospitals, institutions, and private practices where these products are used, must establish and maintain systems for tracing individual products and starting materials, as well as for patient and product tracking. The Committee for Advanced Therapies plays a key role in the Regulation, with tasks including formulating draft opinions on the quality, safety, and efficacy of advanced therapy medicinal products, advising on data generated in their development, and providing advice on whether a product falls within the definition of an advanced therapy medicinal product.

The Commission is required to publish a general report on the application of the Regulation by 30 December 2012, which must include comprehensive information on authorized advanced therapy medicinal products and assess the impact of technical progress on the Regulation's application. The report must also review the scope of the Regulation, including the regulatory framework for combined advanced therapy medicinal products. The Regulation imposes various obligations on medical practitioners, Member States, marketing authorisation holders, and manufacturers, including the requirement for manufacturing authorisation, compliance with national traceability and pharmacovigilance requirements, and the provision of specific information on packaging and package leaflets. Additionally, patients must be provided with certain information, and no fee is payable to the Agency for certain applications. Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure the safe and effective use of advanced therapy medicinal products, while also promoting their development and availability.

summary:
The Regulation concerns the production and development of statistics on education and lifelong learning, applying to the production of statistics in three domains: education and training systems, participation of adults in lifelong learning, and other statistics on education and lifelong learning. Member States are responsible for the regular delivery of statistics on education and lifelong learning, while the Commission, specifically Eurostat, is responsible for implementing the statistical actions and ensuring international comparability of data. The Commission also has the right to seek cooperation with international organisations to ensure international comparability of data and has the obligation to institute pilot studies before any data collection if significant new data requirements or insufficient quality of data are identified.

Member States have the obligation to deliver statistics on education and lifelong learning within specified deadlines and to transmit micro-data on individuals for Community statistics production. They must also participate in pilot studies for new data requirements or insufficient data quality. The Commission, on the other hand, must implement statistical actions, ensure data quality, and cooperate with international organizations. Educational institutions and individuals are also affected, as they may be required to provide data. Available capacities within the Member States for data collection and processing shall be taken into account by the Commission, and special attention and consideration shall be given to various factors, including the potential burden on educational institutions and individuals, results of pilot studies, and agreements between international organizations.

In the domain of education and training systems, the aim is to provide comparable data on key aspects of education and training systems, covering all domestic educational activities, regardless of ownership or sponsorship, and all student types and age groups. The subjects covered include students' enrolment and characteristics, entrants, graduates and graduations, education expenditure, educational personnel, foreign languages learnt, and class sizes, with data and metadata to be supplied annually. In the domain of participation of adults in lifelong learning, the aim is to provide comparable data on participation and non-participation of adults in lifelong learning, covering the population age range of 25-64 years, with subjects including participation and non-participation in learning activities, characteristics of learning activities, self-reported skills, and socio-demographic information.

The Regulation also establishes a Committee, the Statistical Programme Committee, to assist the Commission, with a specific procedure to be followed. The Regulation enters into force on the 20th day following its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union and is binding and applicable in its entirety and directly in all Member States. Member States may be granted limited derogations and transition periods. Overall, the Regulation aims to provide a framework for the production of comparable and reliable statistics on education and lifelong learning, taking into account the needs of various stakeholders and the availability of resources.

summary:
The European Union has established a common framework for the systematic production of Community statistics in the field of education and lifelong learning. This framework applies to Member States, the Commission, particularly Eurostat, and national authorities. Its purpose is to produce and develop statistics on education and lifelong learning through individual statistical actions, ensuring international comparability of data. The Commission shall cooperate with international organizations to achieve this goal and may conduct pilot studies to assess the feasibility of data collection.

Member States are required to deliver statistics on education and lifelong learning within specified deadlines for certain domains, taking into account their available capacities for data collection and processing. The Commission shall implement measures for non-essential elements of the Regulation and ensure data quality. Member States shall also transmit micro-data on individuals for Community statistics production and participate in pilot studies. The Commission has the right to limited derogations and transition periods.

In producing these statistics, special attention shall be given to the regional dimension of the data collected where appropriate, and data shall be systematically broken down by gender where appropriate. The framework considers various factors, including the potential burden on educational institutions and individuals, results of pilot studies, and agreements between international organizations and the Commission.

The framework covers several domains, including education and training systems, and participation of adults in lifelong learning. For education and training systems, the aim is to provide comparable data on key aspects, such as students' enrolment, graduates, education expenditure, and educational personnel. Data and metadata are to be supplied annually. For participation of adults in lifelong learning, the aim is to provide comparable data on participation and non-participation, covering a population age range of 25-64 years, with subjects including participation in learning activities, characteristics of learning activities, and socio-demographic information.

A Committee, the Statistical Programme Committee, shall assist the Commission in implementing this framework, following specific procedures outlined in Decision 1999/468/EC. The framework shall enter into force on the 20th day following its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union and shall be binding and applicable in its entirety and directly in all Member States. Overall, the framework aims to provide a comprehensive and comparable set of statistics on education and lifelong learning across the European Union, facilitating informed decision-making and policy development in these areas.

summary:
The Regulation establishes a common legal framework for the systematic production of Community statistics on the aquaculture sector, applying to the submission by Member States of statistics on aquaculture. It covers various aspects of aquaculture, including input to capture-based aquaculture, production of hatcheries and nurseries, and data on the structure of the aquaculture sector, excluding aquarium and ornamental species. The Regulation applies to Member States, which are obliged to submit specific data to the Commission within 12 months of the end of the reference calendar year, starting from 2008. Member States must also provide a yearly report on data quality and a detailed methodological report at the time of data submission.

Member States shall submit to the Commission statistics on all aquaculture activities conducted in freshwater and saltwaters on their territory, using surveys or other statistically validated methods covering at least 90% of the total production by volume. However, a Member State having a total annual production of less than 1,000 tonnes may submit summary data estimating the total production. Additionally, a request for derogation may be submitted to estimate more than 10% of the total production, and the production of species that individually do not exceed 500 tonnes and do not represent more than 5% of the total production may be excluded.

The Commission shall be empowered to adopt technical changes to the Annexes to this Regulation and is responsible for examining the reports submitted by Member States and presenting conclusions to the relevant working group. Member States have the right to request a transitional period for implementing the Regulation, during which they may continue to apply the provisions of Regulation (EC) No 788/96. In cases where a Member State is granted a transitional period, they may be derogated from certain provisions, such as the second paragraph of Article 13.

The Regulation also provides for a committee procedure, where the Commission is assisted by the Standing Committee for Agricultural Statistics, and for the possibility of granting derogations to Member States that encounter difficulties in including certain aquaculture activities in statistics, provided that the request is made prior to the deadline for the first submission of data and is supported by a report on the problems encountered. Overall, the Regulation aims to establish a harmonized framework for the collection and submission of aquaculture statistics, while allowing for flexibility and exceptions in certain cases.

summary:
Regulation (EC) No 762/2008 establishes a common legal framework for the systematic production of Community statistics on the aquaculture sector, aiming to provide a wider range of data for the rational development and management of the aquaculture sector within the Common Fisheries Policy. The regulation applies to the collection and submission of statistical data for the sound management of the Common Fisheries Policy, and Member States are required to submit annual data on the volume of aquaculture production. The data to be submitted includes information on aquaculture production, input, hatcheries, nurseries, and the structure of the aquaculture sector.

Member States are obliged to use surveys or other statistically validated methods covering at least 90% of the total production by volume, and they must submit specific data to the Commission (Eurostat) within 12 months of the end of the reference calendar year. They are also required to provide a yearly report on data quality and a detailed methodological report at the time of data submission. The Commission (Eurostat) is responsible for examining the reports and presenting conclusions to the relevant working group. Member States have the right to request a transitional period for implementing the Regulation, which may be granted if they require major adaptations to their national statistical systems and are likely to cause significant practical problems by 31 December 2008.

In certain circumstances, Member States may submit a request for derogation under the conditions provided for in Article 8, which allows them to estimate more than 10% of the total production if they encounter difficulties in including certain aquaculture activities in statistics. The request must be made prior to the deadline for the first submission of data, and the Member State must support its request with a report on the problems encountered. The Commission is empowered to adopt technical changes to the Annexes to this Regulation, which include definitions for aquaculture data submission, input to capture-based aquaculture, production of hatcheries and nurseries, data on the structure of the aquaculture sector, and the format for methodological reports of national systems for aquaculture statistics.

The first reference calendar year for data submission is 2008, and Member States granted a transitional period under Article 7 may continue to apply Regulation (EC) No 788/96 for the duration of the transitional period. The Regulation also establishes a committee procedure, where the Commission is assisted by the Standing Committee for Agricultural Statistics, to assist the Commission in its tasks. Overall, the Regulation aims to provide a harmonized framework for the collection and submission of aquaculture data, ensuring the sound management of the Common Fisheries Policy and the rational development of the aquaculture sector.

summary:
Regulation (EC) No 762/2008 establishes a common legal framework for the systematic production of Community statistics on the aquaculture sector, aiming to provide a wider range of data for the rational development and management of the aquaculture sector within the Common Fisheries Policy. The regulation applies to the collection and submission of statistical data for the sound management of the Common Fisheries Policy, and Member States are required to submit annual data on the volume of aquaculture production. The data to be submitted includes information on aquaculture production, input, hatcheries, nurseries, and the structure of the aquaculture sector.

Member States are obliged to use surveys or other statistically validated methods covering at least 90% of the total production by volume, and they must submit specific data to the Commission (Eurostat) within 12 months of the end of the reference calendar year. They are also required to provide a yearly report on data quality and a detailed methodological report at the time of data submission. The Commission (Eurostat) is responsible for examining the reports and presenting conclusions to the relevant working group. Member States have the right to request a transitional period for implementing the Regulation, which may be granted if they require major adaptations to their national statistical systems and are likely to cause significant practical problems by 31 December 2008.

In certain circumstances, Member States may submit a request for derogation under the conditions provided for in Article 8, which allows them to estimate more than 10% of the total production if they encounter difficulties in including certain aquaculture activities in statistics. The request must be made prior to the deadline for the first submission of data, and the Member State must support its request with a report on the problems encountered. The Commission is empowered to adopt technical changes to the Annexes to this Regulation, which include definitions for aquaculture data submission, input to capture-based aquaculture, production of hatcheries and nurseries, data on the structure of the aquaculture sector, and the format for methodological reports of national systems for aquaculture statistics.

The first reference calendar year for data submission is 2008, and Member States granted a transitional period under Article 7 may continue to apply Regulation (EC) No 788/96 for the duration of the transitional period. The Regulation also establishes a committee procedure, where the Commission is assisted by the Standing Committee for Agricultural Statistics, to assist the Commission in its tasks. Overall, the Regulation aims to provide a harmonized framework for the collection and submission of aquaculture data, ensuring the sound management of the Common Fisheries Policy and the rational development of the aquaculture sector.

summary:
The Regulation establishes a common legal framework for the systematic production of Community statistics on the aquaculture sector, applying to the submission by Member States of statistics on aquaculture. It applies to all Member States, which are required to submit to the Commission statistics on all aquaculture activities conducted in freshwater and saltwaters on their territory. Member States must use surveys or other statistically validated methods covering at least 90% of the total production by volume. The Commission is empowered to adopt technical changes to the Annexes to this Regulation.

Member States are obliged to submit specific data to the Commission within 12 months of the end of the reference calendar year, along with a yearly report on data quality and a detailed methodological report. The Commission is responsible for examining these reports and presenting conclusions to the relevant working group. Member States have the right to request a transitional period for implementing the Regulation. The first reference calendar year for data submission is 2008.

Derogations may be granted to Member States that encounter difficulties in including certain aquaculture activities in statistics, provided that the difficulties are not commensurate with the importance of the sector and a request is made prior to the deadline for the first submission of data. In such cases, Member States may exclude data or use estimation methods for more than 10% of the total production. However, unforeseen difficulties after the deadline for the first submission of data are not eligible for derogation. Member States with a total annual production of less than 1,000 tonnes may submit summary data estimating the total production, and the production of species that individually do not exceed 500 tonnes and do not represent more than 5% of the total production may also be excluded.

The Regulation excludes aquarium and ornamental species, as well as plant species, from its scope. Annexes to the Regulation provide further details on the input to capture-based aquaculture, production of hatcheries and nurseries, data on the structure of the aquaculture sector, and the format for methodological reports. A Member State with a transitional period may continue to apply the repealed Regulation (EC) No 788/96 for the duration of the transitional period. The Commission is assisted by the Standing Committee for Agricultural Statistics in implementing the Regulation, and the committee procedure is established in accordance with Decision 1999/468/EC. Regulation (EC) No 788/96 is repealed, without prejudice to certain provisions.

summary:
The European Union has established common rules for the decennial provision of comprehensive data on population and housing, which applies to all Member States. The purpose of this regulation is to provide statistics based on different data sources, including a programme of statistical data and metadata to be transmitted, and the provision of final, validated, and aggregated data and metadata. Member States shall submit data on population and housing to the Commission, covering determined demographic, social, and economic characteristics of persons, families, and households, as well as on housing at national, regional, and local levels.

The Commission is empowered to establish conditions for the establishment of subsequent reference years and the adoption of the programme of statistical data and metadata. Member States may base statistics on various data sources, but shall meet data protection requirements and inform the Commission of revisions, corrections, and changes. The Commission shall adopt a programme of statistical data and metadata, and Member States shall provide the Commission with final, validated, and aggregated data and metadata. Each Member State shall determine a reference date, and the Commission shall establish subsequent reference years.

The quality of data transmitted by Member States is also a key aspect of this regulation, with quality assessment dimensions for data in place. Member States shall report on data quality, transmit validated data and metadata, and transmit modified data in case of revision or correction. The Commission shall provide methodological recommendations, adopt technical format for data transmission, adopt technical specifications of topics, and assess data quality.

In terms of implementation, the Commission is assisted by the Statistical Programme Committee, and certain measures are subject to a regulatory procedure with scrutiny. The regulation also applies to the transmission of data subject to statistical confidentiality, which is governed by Regulation (EC) No 322/97 and Council Regulation (Euratom, EEC) No 1588/90.

The regulation covers specific topics, including population and housing topics, which are obligatory and derived, and apply to geographical levels NUTS 3, LAU 2, national level, NUTS 1, and NUTS 2. The Commission shall be assisted by the committee, and certain procedures, such as the adoption of technical specifications, format, and quality report modalities, are subject to specific rules and timeframes. Overall, the regulation aims to provide a framework for the collection and transmission of high-quality data on population and housing, which is essential for informed decision-making at the European level.

summary:
The European Union has established common rules for the decennial provision of comprehensive data on population and housing, which applies to all Member States. The purpose of this regulation is to provide a framework for the collection and transmission of statistical data and metadata on population and housing censuses. Member States are required to submit data on population and housing to the Commission (Eurostat), covering determined demographic, social, and economic characteristics of persons, families, and households, as well as on housing at national, regional, and local levels.

The Commission is empowered to establish conditions for the establishment of subsequent reference years and the adoption of the programme of statistical data and metadata. The transmission of data subject to statistical confidentiality is governed by Regulation (EC) No 322/97 and Council Regulation (Euratom, EEC) No 1588/90. Member States may base their statistics on different data sources, but they must meet data protection requirements and inform the Commission of any revisions, corrections, and changes.

The Commission shall adopt a programme of statistical data and metadata, which shall be transmitted by Member States in electronic form. The programme will cover topics such as population, including place of usual residence, sex, age, and marital status, as well as housing, including type of living quarters, occupancy status, and number of occupants. The topics to be covered are listed in the annex and include obligatory and derived topics for different geographical levels.

Member States shall provide the Commission with final, validated, and aggregated data and metadata, and each Member State shall determine a reference date. The Commission shall establish subsequent reference years and provide methodological recommendations for data and metadata quality in cooperation with Member States. The Commission is assisted by the Statistical Programme Committee in accordance with Article 8, and the committee procedure applies Articles 5 and 7 of Decision 1999/468/EC.

The regulation also provides for the adoption of measures for implementing the Regulation, amending non-essential elements, via the regulatory procedure with scrutiny. This includes establishing reference years and adopting the statistical data and metadata programme. Member States must report to the Commission on data quality, covering the extent to which data sources and methodology meet essential features of population and housing censuses. Overall, the regulation aims to provide a harmonized framework for the collection and transmission of population and housing data, ensuring the quality and comparability of the data across the European Union.

summary:
The European Union has established common rules for the decennial provision of comprehensive data on population and housing, which applies to all Member States. The purpose of this regulation is to provide statistics based on different data sources, including a programme of statistical data and metadata to be transmitted, and the provision of final, validated, and aggregated data and metadata. Member States shall submit data on population and housing to the Commission, covering determined demographic, social, and economic characteristics of persons, families, and households, as well as on housing at national, regional, and local levels.

The Commission is empowered to establish conditions for the establishment of subsequent reference years and the adoption of the programme of statistical data and metadata. Member States may base statistics on various data sources, but shall meet data protection requirements and inform the Commission of revisions, corrections, and changes. The Commission shall adopt a programme of statistical data and metadata, and Member States shall provide the Commission with final, validated, and aggregated data and metadata. Each Member State shall determine a reference date, and the Commission shall establish subsequent reference years.

The quality of data transmitted by Member States is also a key aspect of this regulation, with quality assessment dimensions for data in place. Member States shall report on data quality, transmit validated data and metadata, and transmit modified data in case of revision or correction. The Commission shall provide methodological recommendations, adopt technical format for data transmission, adopt technical specifications of topics, and assess data quality.

In terms of implementation, the Commission is assisted by the Statistical Programme Committee, and certain measures are subject to a regulatory procedure with scrutiny. The regulation also applies to the transmission of data subject to statistical confidentiality, which is governed by Regulation (EC) No 322/97 and Council Regulation (Euratom, EEC) No 1588/90.

The regulation covers specific topics, including population and housing topics, which are obligatory and derived, and apply to geographical levels NUTS 3, LAU 2, national level, NUTS 1, and NUTS 2. The Commission shall be assisted by the committee, and certain procedures, such as the adoption of technical specifications, format, and quality report modalities, are subject to specific rules and timeframes. Overall, the regulation aims to provide a framework for the collection and transmission of high-quality data on population and housing, which is essential for informed decision-making at the European level.

summary:
This Regulation governs admission to, and the pursuit of, the occupation of road transport operator and applies to undertakings established in the Community engaged in or intending to engage in this occupation. However, exemptions are provided for undertakings using vehicles with a permissible laden mass not exceeding 3.5 tonnes, those engaged in road passenger transport services exclusively for non-commercial purposes, those using motor vehicles with a maximum authorised speed not exceeding 40 km/h, and road transport operators engaged exclusively in national transport operations with a minor impact on the transport market.

To be admitted to the occupation of road transport operator, undertakings must have an effective and stable establishment, be of good repute, have appropriate financial standing, and requisite professional competence. They must also satisfy conditions relating to establishment, including having premises. The concept of good repute is determined by the absence of compelling grounds for doubting it, and the undertaking must not have been convicted of or penalized for certain offenses.

Transport undertakings have the right to be authorised to engage in the road transport operator occupation if they meet the requirements, and they must submit an application and notify changes to their data within 28 days. The examination of applications must be completed within three months, although this time limit can be extended by one month in duly justified cases. Member States are responsible for designating competent authorities to examine applications, grant, suspend, or withdraw authorisations, declare transport managers unfit, and conduct checks to verify requirements.

Member States must also monitor undertakings' compliance with requirements, carry out checks, and extend risk classification systems where undertakings pose an increased risk. They are obliged to keep a national electronic register of road transport undertakings, process data, and ensure accessibility. In addition, Member States must verify if an undertaking meets the conditions for admission to the road transport operator occupation, and they must inform the Commission of the results and measures taken.

The regulation also establishes the knowledge required for official recognition of professional competence by Member States for road haulage and road passenger transport operators. Road haulage and road passenger transport operators, as well as Member States and their nationals, are subject to the regulation. They have the right to have their knowledge recognized for professional competence, but they must also comply with conditions for good repute, financial standing, and professional competence, and have a minimum level of knowledge, corresponding to level 3 of the training-level structure. Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure the correct implementation of its provisions and the proper functioning of the road transport market.

However, certain undertakings are exempt, such as those with vehicles not exceeding 3.5 tonnes, non-commercial passenger transport, and vehicles with a maximum speed not exceeding 40 km/h. Additionally, undertakings with a minor impact on the transport market due to the nature of goods carried or short distances involved may also be subject to this Regulation.

To be authorized to engage in the occupation of road transport operator, undertakings must have an effective and stable establishment, be of good repute, have appropriate financial standing, and requisite professional competence. They must also designate a transport manager who effectively and continuously manages transport activities and satisfies specific requirements. The transport manager must have the necessary knowledge in areas such as civil law, commercial law, social law, fiscal law, and business and financial management.

Member States are responsible for designating competent authorities to examine applications, grant, suspend, or withdraw authorizations, declare transport managers unfit, and conduct checks to verify requirements. These authorities must monitor undertakings that have been authorized to ensure they continue to fulfill the requirements, and may carry out targeted checks on undertakings that pose an increased risk. The Commission may also request individual checks to verify whether an undertaking meets the conditions governing admission to the occupation of road transport operator.

The examination of applications must be completed within three months, although this time limit may be extended by one month in duly justified cases. Member States must also draw up a report on the activities of competent authorities every two years and forward it to the Commission, which must submit a report to the European Parliament and the Council every two years on the pursuit of the occupation of road transport operator.

However, certain undertakings are exempt, such as those with vehicles not exceeding 3.5 tonnes, non-commercial road passenger transport, and vehicles with a maximum speed not exceeding 40 km/h. Additionally, undertakings with a minor impact on the transport market due to the nature of goods carried or short distances involved may also be exempt.

To be admitted to the occupation of road transport operator, undertakings must have an effective and stable establishment, be of good repute, have appropriate financial standing, and requisite professional competence. They must also designate a transport manager who satisfies specific requirements if the undertaking does not meet the professional competence requirement. The transport manager must have knowledge of various subjects, including civil law, commercial law, social law, fiscal law, and business and financial management of the undertaking. The minimum level of knowledge required is level 3 of the training-level structure laid down in the Annex to Council Decision 85/368/EEC.

Undertakings must demonstrate sufficient capital and reserves, with at least EUR 9,000 for one vehicle and EUR 5,000 for each additional vehicle. They must also submit annual accounts certified by an auditor or accredited person. Member States are responsible for designating competent authorities to examine applications, grant authorisations, suspend or withdraw authorisations, and declare transport managers unfit. These authorities have the power to carry out checks to ensure correct implementation of the Regulation.

Member States must carry out checks on undertakings at least every 5 years until 31 December 2014 to verify that they fulfil the requirements laid down in the Regulation. They must also keep a national electronic register of road transport undertakings, which must be interconnected and accessible throughout the Community by 31 December 2012. The register must include data such as the name of the person declared unfit to manage transport activities.

Applicants for admission to the occupation of road transport operator must provide proof of good repute, which can be demonstrated by producing an extract from a judicial record or an equivalent document. Member States must forward to the Commission a list of competent authorities and must accept as sufficient proof of good repute the production of an extract from a judicial record or an equivalent document. Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure that undertakings engaged in the occupation of road transport operator meet certain requirements and standards to guarantee safe and efficient transport services.

summary:
The European Union has established a regulatory framework for the approval of active substances in plant protection products, which includes conditions and restrictions for approval, as well as an application and approval procedure. Producers of active substances, Member States, associations of producers, and applicants are all subject to this framework. These entities have the right to submit an application for approval, but they are also obligated to provide a complete dossier and to assess confidentiality requests. In certain cases, they may request that certain information be kept confidential. Additionally, there is an obligation to set maximum residue levels for active substances.

The approval of active substances is subject to certain conditions, including the requirement that the substance meet specific criteria. There are also restrictions on the use of plant protection products, and derogations may be granted in cases where there is a serious danger to plant health. In such cases, a provisional authorization may be granted for a period of up to three years, provided that certain conditions are met, including the establishment of maximum residue levels in accordance with relevant regulations.

When authorizing plant protection products, Member States must define the plants or plant products and non-agricultural areas for use, set out requirements for placing on the market and use, and include classification for relevant directives. They must also include conditions of use to comply with the regulation approving the active substance, such as maximum dose per hectare, period between last application and harvest, and maximum number of applications per year.

In evaluating an application for authorization for a plant protection product containing an active substance approved as a candidate for substitution, Member States must perform a comparative assessment weighing up the risks and benefits. They must not authorize or restrict the use of the product if safer alternatives exist, and must consider economic and practical disadvantages of substitution, chemical diversity and resistance, and consequences on minor use authorisations. However, derogations from this requirement may be granted in exceptional cases, and authorization without comparative assessment may be granted for a period of up to five years for the purpose of acquiring experience.

To avoid duplicative testing, persons seeking authorization for plant protection products must consult information on existing authorizations and provide data on active substance identity and impurities. They must also submit evidence of intention to apply for authorization before carrying out tests or studies. Prospective applicants and holders of authorizations for plant protection products must reach agreement on sharing test and study reports involving vertebrate animals, and inform the competent authority if agreement cannot be reached.

In cases where there are serious risks to human or animal health or the environment, the Commission may take emergency measures, including examining evidence and requesting an opinion from the relevant authority. Overall, the regulatory framework is designed to ensure the safe and effective use of plant protection products, while also minimizing the risks associated with their use.

The Commission has the obligation to adopt regulations for approval, non-approval, or amendment of approval conditions. Active substances may be approved for a limited period, not exceeding 5 years, if necessary to control a serious danger to plant health.

In general, plant protection products must be authorized in the Member State concerned, in accordance with this Regulation, before being placed on the market or used. A comparative assessment shall be performed by Member States when evaluating an application for authorization for a plant protection product containing an active substance approved as a candidate for substitution, weighing up the risks and benefits, considering factors such as human or animal health, environment, and economic or practical disadvantages.

To avoid duplicative testing, persons seeking authorization for plant protection products must consult information on existing authorizations, provide data on active substance identity and impurities, and submit evidence of intention to apply for authorization, before carrying out tests or studies.

summary:
This Regulation applies to products consisting of or containing active substances, safeners, or synergists, intended for protecting plants or plant products, influencing plant life processes, preserving plant products, destroying undesired plants, or checking undesired plant growth. The Regulation lays down rules for the authorization of plant protection products in commercial form and for their placing on the market, use, and control within the Community. It applies to producers of active substances, Member States, and users of plant protection products, including professional and non-professional users.

Producers of active substances have the right to submit an application for approval, while Member States have the obligation to examine applications and assess confidentiality requests. Users of plant protection products have the obligation to follow conditions and restrictions on use. Approval may be subject to conditions, and applicants must submit required information, including evaluations of effects on human and animal health and the environment.

The Regulation also provides for mutual recognition of authorization for plant protection products, allowing holders of authorization to apply for authorization in another Member State under certain conditions. These conditions include authorization granted by a Member State in the same zone, or authorization granted for use in greenhouses, post-harvest treatment, and other specific uses.

In evaluating applications for plant protection product authorization, Member States must conduct a comparative assessment for products containing candidates for substitution, considering factors such as safer alternatives, economic and practical disadvantages, chemical diversity, and minor use authorizations. However, exceptions apply, including derogation from certain requirements for non-candidate substances with existing non-chemical controls, and no comparative assessment is required for acquiring experience for a limited period.

Member States authorizing plant protection products must keep and make available test and study reports, including data protection claims. The Regulation also regulates advertising of plant protection products, requiring that advertisements do not promote unauthorized products and include specific safety warnings. Additionally, it aims to avoid duplicative testing for plant protection product authorization by requiring persons seeking authorization to consult existing information and provide test and study reports to competent authorities.

In cases of disputes over sharing test and study reports, prospective applicants and holders of authorizations for plant protection products must inform the competent authority if an agreement cannot be reached. The Commission may also request an opinion or scientific and technical assistance from the Authority, which must provide its opinion or results within a specified timeframe. Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure the safe and effective use of plant protection products, while also promoting the development of safer alternatives and minimizing the risks associated with their use.

summary:
The European Union has established a common framework for Community statistics on pesticides, which applies to annual amounts of pesticides placed on the market and used, serving the purposes of Articles 4 and 15 of Directive 2009/128/EC. This framework is currently limited to pesticides that are plant protection products, but it is anticipated that it will be extended to biocidal products in the future. The framework applies to Member States at the Community level, and its primary goal is to provide harmonized statistics on the placing on the market of pesticides and their agricultural use.

Member States are obligated to collect data on the characteristics of pesticides, including those listed in Annex I on an annual basis and those listed in Annex II every five years. This data must be transmitted to the Commission, specifically to Eurostat, according to the schedules and periodicity outlined in the annexes. The data must be provided in electronic form and conform to the technical format adopted by the Commission. Member States can use various methods to collect this data, including surveys, information on the placing on the market and use of pesticides, administrative sources, or a combination of these methods. Confidential data will be aggregated by the Commission before publication to ensure statistical confidentiality.

The Commission is responsible for adopting the technical format for the transmission of data and for modifying requirements as necessary. The Commission will also submit a report to the European Parliament and the Council every five years, evaluating the quality of the data, the methods used for collection, the burden on businesses and administrations, and the usefulness of the statistics. This report will include proposals to improve data quality and collection methods, if appropriate, to enhance the coverage and comparability of the data and reduce the burden on businesses and administrations. The first report was due by 31 December 2016.

In terms of specifics, the data supplied by Member States must include information on the amount of pesticides placed on the market, expressed in kilograms of substances, and the areas treated, expressed in hectares. The reference period for pesticides placed on the market is the calendar year, while the reference period for agricultural use of pesticides is a maximum of 12 months. The first reference period for pesticides placed on the market began in the second calendar year following 30 December of the year the regulation came into effect.

The collection, transmission, and publication of data are subject to certain conditions and exceptions. The data must be collected and transmitted in accordance with the principles of professional independence, impartiality, objectivity, reliability, cost-effectiveness, and statistical confidentiality, as governed by Regulation (EC) No 223/2009. The publication and dissemination of the data are also subject to this regulation. Furthermore, the framework does not prejudice Directive 2003/4/EC and Regulation (EC) No 1367/2006. The European Union has established a common framework for Community statistics on pesticides, which applies to annual amounts of pesticides placed on the market and used. This framework serves the purposes of Articles 4 and 15 of Directive 2009/128/EC and is currently limited to pesticides that are plant protection products, although it is anticipated that it will be extended to biocidal products in the future. The framework applies to Member States at the Community level, and its primary purpose is to provide statistics on the placing on the market of pesticides and their agricultural use, as well as a harmonised classification of substances.

Member States are required to collect data on the characteristics listed in Annex I annually and Annex II every 5 years, and to transmit statistical results, including confidential data, to the Commission (Eurostat) according to the schedules and periodicity outlined in the annexes. The data transmission must be in electronic form, in a technical format adopted by the Commission (Eurostat), and confidential data must be aggregated by the Commission before publication, taking into account the protection of confidential data at the individual Member State level. Confidential data can only be used by national authorities and the Commission (Eurostat) for statistical purposes.

The collection and transmission of data are subject to certain standards, including professional independence, impartiality, objectivity, reliability, cost-effectiveness, and statistical confidentiality, as governed by Regulation (EC) No 223/2009. Member States must supply data on pesticides placed on the market and agricultural use of pesticides, publish data in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 223/2009, and provide a quality report to the Commission (Eurostat). The Commission (Eurostat) is responsible for receiving data and quality reports from Member States.

The data to be collected includes the amount of pesticides placed on the market, expressed in kilograms of substances, and the areas treated, expressed in hectares. The reference period for pesticides placed on the market is the calendar year, while the reference period for agricultural use of pesticides is a maximum of 12 months. The first reference period for pesticides placed on the market is the second calendar year following 30 December.

The Commission is required to submit a report on the implementation of the Regulation to the European Parliament and the Council every 5 years, evaluating data quality, collection methods, burden on businesses and administrations, and the usefulness of statistics. The report must contain proposals to improve data quality and collection methods, if appropriate, to improve coverage and comparability of data and reduce the burden on businesses and administrations. The Commission will be assisted by the European Statistical System Committee in its committee procedures, and will adapt the list of substances to be covered and their classification every 5 years. Without prejudice to Directive 2003/4/EC and Regulation (EC) No 1367/2006, the Regulation establishes a framework for the collection and use of data on pesticides, with the aim of providing reliable and comparable statistics at the Community level.

summary:
Regulation (EC) No 1185/2009 establishes a common framework for the systematic production of Community statistics on the placing on the market and use of pesticides, which are plant protection products. The statistics shall apply to the annual amounts of pesticides placed on the market and used, with the scope limited to pesticides which are plant protection products covered by Regulation (EC) No 1107/2009. The purpose of the Regulation is to reduce the risks and impacts of pesticide use on human health and the environment, and to encourage the development of sustainable agriculture. 

Active substances are defined as micro-organisms having general or specific action against harmful organisms or on plants, parts of plants or plant products, while substances are chemical elements and their compounds, as they occur naturally or by manufacture. Plant protection products are products, in the form in which they are supplied to the user, consisting of or containing active substances, safeners or synergists, and intended for one of the specified uses. A professional user is defined as anyone who uses pesticides in their professional activities, including operators, technicians, employers, and self-employed people.

Producers, suppliers, distributors, importers, and exporters of plant protection products must keep records for at least 5 years, while professional users must keep records for at least 3 years. Producers must undertake post-authorisation monitoring, and authorisation holders must provide sales data to competent authorities. Member States must collect data on pesticide characteristics annually and every 5 years using surveys, information on market placement and use, administrative sources, or a combination of these. The data shall be expressed in kilograms of substances, and areas treated shall be expressed in hectares, with reference periods for pesticides placed on the market and agricultural use of pesticides being the calendar year and a maximum of 12 months, respectively.

The Commission shall submit a report on the implementation of the Regulation to the European Parliament and the Council every 5 years, evaluating data quality, collection methods, burden on businesses and administrations, and usefulness of statistics. The report shall contain proposals to improve data quality and collection methods, if appropriate, to improve coverage and comparability of data and reduce burden on businesses and administrations. The Commission shall be assisted by the European Statistical System Committee for committee procedures, and shall adapt the list of substances to be covered and their classification every 5 years.

Member States shall supply data on pesticides placed on the market and agricultural use of pesticides, publish data in accordance with Regulation (EC) No 223/2009, and supply a quality report to the Commission. The Commission shall receive data and quality reports from Member States. The first reference period for pesticides placed on the market shall be the second calendar year following 30 December, and the first report on the implementation of the Regulation shall be submitted by 31 December 2016. Overall, the Regulation aims to provide a harmonised framework for the collection and analysis of data on pesticide use, in order to support the development of policies to reduce the risks associated with pesticide use and promote sustainable agriculture.

The Commission is responsible for adopting a technical format for the transmission of data and for modifying requirements as necessary. This report shall contain proposals to improve data quality and collection methods, if appropriate, to improve coverage and comparability of data and reduce burden on businesses and administrations. The Commission shall be assisted by the European Statistical System Committee for committee procedures, and shall adapt the list of substances to be covered and their classification every 5 years. 

The statistics shall cover substances listed in Annex III contained in pesticides, and Member States shall publish the data, in particular on the Internet, in accordance with the requirements regarding protection of statistical confidentiality. The framework is without prejudice to Directive 2003/4/EC and Regulation (EC) No 1367/2006, and its implementation is subject to the provisions of Decision 1999/468/EC regarding committee procedures. summary:
The EU Ecolabel scheme aims to promote products with reduced environmental impact and provide consumers with accurate information on environmental impact, as part of the sustainable consumption and production policy of the Community. The scheme applies to products on the Community market, with food and feed product groups subject to a study to ensure feasible criteria and added value. Unprocessed agricultural products within the scope of Council Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 may be eligible for the EU Ecolabel if certified as organic. 

Competent bodies must undertake verifications to ensure compliance with EU Ecolabel conditions, and Member States must lay down rules on penalties for infringements and ensure implementation. The Commission must coordinate the development and setting of EU Ecolabel criteria, which must be based on the best environmental performance achieved by products on the Community market. Operators who wish to use the EU Ecolabel must apply to competent bodies, which charge fees for application and use, and meet the costs of testing and assessment of conformity with EU Ecolabel criteria. 

The application must be complete and include all relevant documentation, and the competent body may reject the application if documentation is not complete within 6 months. The EU Ecolabel may only be used for products complying with EU Ecolabel criteria, which are established by Commission measures. Competent bodies verify compliance with EU Ecolabel criteria and assessment requirements, and must allow investigations and grant access to premises upon complaint or on a regular basis, including random spot-checks, and within a reasonable time, without notice.

The Commission must draw up a preliminary report and make it available for comment when developing and revising EU Ecolabel criteria. Holders of the EU Ecolabel must ensure the product complies with the terms of use and provisions, inform the competent body of modifications to the product, and not advertise or make misleading statements. The competent body may carry out verifications and investigations, suspend or withdraw authorization to use the EU Ecolabel, and may extend the contract to a wider range of products with agreement from the competent body. Overall, the EU Ecolabel scheme is designed to promote sustainable consumption and production, and ensure that products bearing the label meet rigorous environmental standards.

The EU Ecolabel scheme aims to promote products with reduced environmental impact and provide consumers with accurate information on environmental impact, as part of the sustainable consumption and production policy of the Community. The scheme applies to products on the Community market, with food and feed product groups subject to a study to ensure feasible criteria and added value. Unprocessed agricultural products within the scope of Council Regulation (EC) No 834/2007 may be eligible for the EU Ecolabel if certified as organic.

To use the EU Ecolabel, operators must apply to competent bodies, which must check documentation, verify compliance, and assign a registration number. Operators must meet the costs of testing and assessment, and competent bodies must conclude a contract with them. The application must be presented to the competent body in the specific Member State(s) depending on the product origin, and fees must be paid according to Annex III. The documentation must be complete and verified by the competent body.

Competent bodies must undertake verifications to ensure compliance with EU Ecolabel conditions, and Member States must lay down rules on penalties for infringements and ensure implementation. The Commission must coordinate the development and setting of EU Ecolabel criteria, which must be based on the best environmental performance achieved by products on the Community market. The Commission must also draw up a preliminary report and make it available for comment when developing and revising EU Ecolabel criteria.

Holders of the EU Ecolabel must ensure that their products comply with the terms of use and provisions, and inform the competent body of any modifications to the product. Competent bodies may carry out verifications and investigations, and may suspend or withdraw authorization to use the EU Ecolabel if necessary. Holders must not advertise or make misleading statements, and the contract may be extended to a wider range of products with agreement from the competent body.

Market surveillance and control of the use of the EU Ecolabel are also essential, with competent bodies responsible for verifying compliance, investigating complaints, and withholding the identity of complainants. Users of the EU Ecolabel must allow investigations and grant access to premises, which may be conducted on a regular basis, upon complaint, or through random spot-checks, and at reasonable times, without notice. Overall, the EU Ecolabel scheme is designed to promote sustainable consumption and production, and to provide consumers with accurate information about the environmental impact of products.

summary:
The EU Ecolabel scheme aims to promote products with reduced environmental impact and provide consumers with accurate information on environmental impact. The scheme applies to products, excluding medicinal products for human or veterinary use and medical devices. It is applicable to all relevant interested parties, including competent bodies, producers, manufacturers, importers, service providers, wholesalers, retailers, SMEs, environmental protection groups, and consumer organisations. Member States are responsible for laying down rules on penalties applicable to infringements of the Regulation.

The EU Ecolabel may not be awarded to goods containing toxic, hazardous, carcinogenic, mutagenic, or toxic for reproduction substances. The EU Ecolabel is awarded based on specific criteria and assessment requirements, and the scheme aims to promote environmental excellence. Any operator who wishes to use the EU Ecolabel can apply, and competent bodies in Member States, as well as the Commission, play a role in the scheme. Operators have the right to apply for the EU Ecolabel, but they are obliged to meet the costs of testing and assessment of conformity with EU Ecolabel criteria. Competent bodies are obliged to charge fees for the use of the EU Ecolabel and to undertake verifications and ensure compliance with the conditions for using the EU Ecolabel.

The European Union Ecolabelling Board has the right to contribute to the development and revision of EU Ecolabel criteria and to provide advice and assistance to the Commission. The Commission has the obligation to coordinate the development or revision of EU Ecolabel criteria and ensure the overall coherence of the scheme. The Commission also has the right to adopt measures to grant derogations from the rules on toxic substances. The promotion of the EU Ecolabel is done via the EU Ecolabel website, providing basic information, promotional materials, and information on where to purchase EU Ecolabel products in all Community languages. Market surveillance and control of EU Ecolabel use are also essential aspects of the scheme.

Competent bodies are responsible for awarding, monitoring, and controlling EU Ecolabel use, while operators must apply for the EU Ecolabel, meet the costs of testing and assessment, and comply with EU Ecolabel criteria. Member States and the Commission cooperate to promote EU Ecolabel use, and consumers, producers, manufacturers, wholesalers, service providers, and public purchasers are also involved in the scheme. The Commission is required to submit a report on the EU Ecolabel scheme implementation to the European Parliament and Council, identifying elements for possible review of the scheme. The scheme also involves the repeal of Regulation (EC) No 1980/2000 and establishes a procedure for developing and revising EU Ecolabel criteria, which includes requirements such as a preliminary report, proposal for draft criteria, and technical report. Overall, the EU Ecolabel scheme aims to promote environmental excellence and provide a reliable label for consumers to make informed choices.

summary:
The Regulation establishes rules for the creation and organization of international rail corridors for competitive rail freight, applying to the management and use of railway infrastructure included in these corridors. It applies to Member States with a rail border with another Member State, which are required to participate in the establishment of at least one freight corridor. These Member States must, upon request, also participate in the establishment of a freight corridor to allow a neighboring Member State to fulfill its obligation, unless they have a rail network with a specific condition that exempts them from this requirement. The establishment of a freight corridor is proposed by the concerned Member States, and the Commission examines these proposals and adopts a decision on compliance.

The management board of each freight corridor is responsible for drawing up and periodically reviewing an investment plan for infrastructure, implementing the freight corridor plan, and establishing a deployment plan for interoperable systems. The executive board defines the general objectives of the freight corridor and approves the investment plan. Infrastructure managers, allocation bodies, railway undertakings, managers and owners of terminals, and applicants likely to use the freight corridor are all subject to the provisions of the Regulation.

The Regulation aims to facilitate the allocation of infrastructure capacity, coordinate traffic management, and provide information on conditions of use for freight corridors. It introduces the concept of international pre-arranged train paths for freight trains and a one-stop shop for application for infrastructure capacity. Infrastructure managers are responsible for defining and organizing these train paths, facilitating journey times and frequencies, and publishing pre-arranged train paths. The management board evaluates the need for capacity, defines the framework for allocation of infrastructure capacity, and puts in place procedures for coordinating traffic management.

The Regulation promotes compatibility between performance schemes along the freight corridor and ensures non-discriminatory access to the corridor. Regulatory bodies monitor competition in the rail freight corridor, and the Regulation aims to foster free and fair competition on freight corridors. These bodies have the right to request information from infrastructure managers and other parties and are obliged to ensure non-discriminatory access to the corridor. The Commission, Member States, infrastructure managers, and market players are all involved in ensuring the proper functioning of the freight corridors, with the Commission having specific responsibilities in this regard. Overall, the Regulation seeks to create a framework for efficient and competitive rail freight transport in the European Union.

summary:
The Regulation establishes rules for the creation and organization of international rail corridors for competitive rail freight, applying to the management and use of railway infrastructure included in these corridors. It affects Member States with a rail border with another Member State, as well as those concerned by the freight corridors. Each Member State with a rail border must participate in the establishment of at least one freight corridor, and may be requested to participate in another to allow a neighboring Member State to fulfill its obligation. However, a Member State is not obliged to participate if it has a rail network with a different track gauge.

The Commission plays a crucial role in the establishment of freight corridors, adopting decisions on proposals and examining them for compliance. Once established, the management board of a freight corridor is responsible for various tasks, including drawing up and updating a document containing information on the network statement, terminals, procedures, and implementation plan. The management board must also promote compatibility between performance schemes, monitor the performance of rail freight services, and conduct satisfaction surveys of users.

In terms of infrastructure management, the management board must designate a joint body to handle requests for infrastructure capacity for freight trains crossing borders. It must also draw up an investment plan, including projects for infrastructure extension, renewal, or redeployment, as well as a plan for managing freight train capacity. The management board and infrastructure managers must evaluate the need for capacity allocation based on transport market studies and framework agreements, and define and organize international pre-arranged train paths for freight trains, taking into account the needs of other types of transport.

The Regulation aims to foster free and fair competition on freight corridors, with regulatory bodies monitoring competition and ensuring non-discriminatory access. These bodies have the right to request information from infrastructure managers and other parties, and are obliged to ensure that access to the corridor is not discriminatory. The management board, regulatory bodies, Member States, infrastructure managers, market players, and the Commission all have roles to play in the implementation and oversight of the Regulation. Ultimately, the goal is to create a more efficient and competitive rail freight system, with the management board and regulatory bodies working together to promote compatibility and fairness along the freight corridors.
