It affects Member States with a rail border with another Member State, as well as those concerned by the freight corridors. Each Member State with a rail border must participate in the establishment of at least one freight corridor, and may be requested to participate in another to allow a neighboring Member State to fulfill its obligation. However, a Member State is not obliged to participate if it has a rail network with a different track gauge.

The Commission plays a crucial role in the establishment of freight corridors, adopting decisions on proposals and examining them for compliance. Once established, the management board of a freight corridor is responsible for various tasks, including drawing up and updating a document containing information on the network statement, terminals, procedures, and implementation plan. The management board must also promote compatibility between performance schemes, monitor the performance of rail freight services, and conduct satisfaction surveys of users.

In terms of infrastructure management, the management board must designate a joint body to handle requests for infrastructure capacity for freight trains crossing borders. It must also draw up an investment plan, including projects for infrastructure extension, renewal, or redeployment, as well as a plan for managing freight train capacity. The management board and infrastructure managers must evaluate the need for capacity allocation based on transport market studies and framework agreements, and define and organize international pre-arranged train paths for freight trains, taking into account the needs of other types of transport.

The Regulation aims to foster free and fair competition on freight corridors, with regulatory bodies monitoring competition and ensuring non-discriminatory access. These bodies have the right to request information from infrastructure managers and other parties, and are obliged to ensure that access to the corridor is not discriminatory. The management board, regulatory bodies, Member States, infrastructure managers, market players, and the Commission all have roles to play in the implementation and oversight of the Regulation. Ultimately, the goal is to create a more efficient and competitive rail freight system, with the management board and regulatory bodies working together to promote compatibility and fairness along the freight corridors.

It affects Member States with a rail border with another Member State, which are required to participate in the establishment of at least one freight corridor. The establishment of a freight corridor is proposed by the concerned Member States, and the Commission examines these proposals and adopts a decision on compliance. Railway undertakings, shippers, freight forwarders, and combined transport operators are among those who can apply for infrastructure capacity. Regulatory bodies have obligations to monitor competition in the rail freight corridor, ensure non-discriminatory access, and exchange necessary information. They must also transfer relevant information to the responsible regulatory body for taking measures regarding parties concerned when a complaint is received or an investigation is initiated.

Furthermore, the management board of the freight corridor must promote compatibility between performance schemes along the corridor, and associated representatives of infrastructure managers must provide necessary information for handling complaints or investigations. summary:
The European Union has established a regulatory framework to govern the activities of its fishing vessels, as well as the inspection and surveillance of these vessels in the Regulatory Area. Member States are required to send a list of vessels flying their flag and registered in the Union to the Commission by 15 December each year, or 5 days before the vessel enters the Regulatory Area. This list must include vessels authorized to fish directly for one or more regulated resources, and any amendments to the list must be sent promptly. The format for transmission of this list will be determined in accordance with Article 50(2).

Masters of EU fishing vessels are obligated to record information in a bound paginated fishing logbook or by electronic means, including entry into and exit from the Regulatory Area, estimated cumulative catches retained on board, amount of fish discarded, date and time of transmission of reports, and fishing depth. These records must be made on a daily basis.

The Commission, Member States, and the body designated by the Commission are responsible for coordinating surveillance and inspection activities for the Union. The Commission or designated body must draw up a joint deployment plan and ensure the presence of inspection vessels in the Regulatory Area, while Member States must ensure that inspections are carried out in a non-discriminatory manner. This coordination is particularly important when there are more than 10 EU fishing vessels engaged in fishing activities in the Regulatory Area.

In the event of a serious infringement by an EU fishing vessel, the flag Member State and the vessel itself have certain obligations. The flag Member State must respond to notification without delay, inspect the vessel within 72 hours, and forward the results of the examination to the competent authority, the Commission, and the inspecting state. If evidence warrants, the flag Member State must require the vessel to proceed to port for a thorough inspection, and provide justification if the vessel is not called to port.

Inspectors have an obligation to notify the Commission, flag state, and NEAFC Secretary of any serious infringement, and transmit a copy of the notification to the NEAFC Secretary, if there are clear grounds for believing a serious infringement has occurred. The flag state of a fishing vessel must also confirm details of the vessel and its catch, including quota, reporting, authorization, and VMS data, when the vessel intends to land or tranship.

The purpose of these regulations is to regulate inspections, landings, and transhipments of non-Contracting Party vessels in EU ports, and to prevent illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing activities. The scope of these regulations includes reporting requirements, inspection procedures, and measures to prevent IUU activities, and applies to Member States, non-Contracting Party vessels, the Commission or the body designated by it, and the North-East Atlantic Fisheries Commission (NEAFC). Overall, these regulations aim to ensure the sustainable management of fish stocks and the enforcement of EU fisheries rules.

summary:
The Regulation establishes a control and enforcement scheme applicable to the area covered by the Convention on future multilateral cooperation in the North-East Atlantic fisheries. This scheme applies to fishing vessels operating in the Regulatory Area, including those flying the flag of Member States and non-Contracting Party vessels. The Regulation lays down specific obligations for masters of EU fishing vessels, such as recording cumulative production and stow catch in a specific way, as well as recording specific information in a logbook. Member States are also obligated to retrieve lost gears belonging to vessels flying their flag and to send a list of authorized vessels to the Commission.

The Regulation applies to all fish caught in the Convention Area, and requires labelling or stamping of frozen fish with species, production date, ICES sub-area and division, and vessel name at the time of stowage. This is intended to facilitate identification of frozen fish. In terms of inspection and surveillance, Member States and the Commission must coordinate their activities, draw up a joint deployment plan, and ensure inspections are carried out in a non-discriminatory manner. This applies when there are more than 10 EU fishing vessels engaged in fishing activities in the Regulatory Area, and when there is an inspection vessel from a Member State or an agreement with another Contracting Party.

Port inspections are also an important aspect of the Regulation, with Member States required to carry out inspections of at least 15% of landings or transhipments. These inspections must be carried out in a way that avoids delaying a vessel unduly, minimizes interference and inconvenience, and avoids degradation of fish quality. The Regulation also defines the scope of its provisions, which apply to EU fishing vessels and fishing vessels flying the flag of another Contracting Party.

In addition, the Regulation regulates inspections and monitoring of non-Contracting Party vessels, including inspections at sea and in ports, reporting requirements, and measures to prevent IUU activities. Member States, non-Contracting Party vessels, the Commission, and the North-East Atlantic Fisheries Commission are all subject to the provisions of the Regulation. Member States must report to the Commission by 15 February each year, and ensure inspections of non-Contracting Party vessels. Overall, the Regulation aims to establish a comprehensive system of control and enforcement to ensure the sustainable management of fisheries in the North-East Atlantic.

summary:
The Regulation establishes rules for bus and coach transport, covering non-discrimination, passenger rights in accidents, assistance for disabled persons, rights in cases of cancellation or delay, minimum information to be provided, handling of complaints, and enforcement. It applies to passengers travelling with regular services where the boarding or alighting point is in a Member State and the scheduled distance is 250 km or more, as well as to passengers travelling with occasional services where the initial boarding point or final alighting point is in a Member State, except for certain articles. The Regulation applies to various entities, including carriers, performing carriers, ticket vendors, travel agents, and tour operators, and grants rights to passengers, including the right to non-discrimination, assistance for disabled persons and persons with reduced mobility, and information in cases of cancellation or delay.

Passengers with disabilities or reduced mobility have the right to assistance, but carriers, travel agents, and tour operators may refuse to accept a reservation or issue a ticket due to safety requirements or health and safety concerns, or if it is physically impossible to take on board, alight, or carry the person in a safe and operationally feasible manner. In such cases, the carrier must inform the person concerned about alternative services, offer reimbursement or continuation of the journey, transport an accompanying person free of charge, and provide written reasons for the refusal within five working days. To receive assistance, disabled persons and persons with reduced mobility must notify the carrier, terminal managing body, travel agent, or tour operator at least 36 hours in advance and present themselves at a designated point at a stipulated time, although reasonable efforts will be made to provide assistance if no notification is made.

In cases of cancellation or delay, passengers have the right to free snacks, meals, or refreshments and hotel accommodation if the journey duration is more than three hours and the delay is more than 90 minutes, unless the cancellation or delay is due to severe weather conditions or major natural disasters. Carriers must offer assistance and pay attention to the needs of disabled persons and persons with reduced mobility, with a maximum of two nights' accommodation at a cost of up to EUR 80 per night. Carriers and terminal managing bodies must also provide information on passenger rights at terminals and on the Internet, and passengers have the right to request information in an accessible format. Additionally, carriers and terminal managing bodies must provide assistance to disabled persons and persons with reduced mobility at designated terminals and on board buses and coaches. Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure that passengers, particularly those with disabilities or reduced mobility, are treated fairly and have access to necessary assistance and information when travelling by bus or coach.

However, there are exceptions to the right to transport for persons with disabilities or reduced mobility, such as refusal to accept a reservation or issue a ticket due to safety requirements or health and safety concerns, or physical impossibility of taking on board, alighting, or carrying the person in a safe and operationally feasible manner. In such cases, the carrier must inform the person concerned about alternative services, offer reimbursement or continuation of the journey, transport an accompanying person free of charge, and inform the person of the reasons for refusal in writing within five working days.

To receive assistance, disabled persons and persons with reduced mobility must notify the carrier, terminal managing body, travel agent, or tour operator of their need for assistance at least 36 hours in advance and present themselves at a designated point at a stipulated time or agreed time. If no time is stipulated, they must present themselves no later than 30 minutes before departure. Carriers, terminal managing bodies, travel agents, and tour operators must facilitate the receipt of notifications and designate a point for announcing arrival and requesting assistance. If no notification is made, they must make reasonable efforts to provide assistance.

The Regulation also requires carriers to set up a complaint handling mechanism, offer assistance in case of cancelled or delayed departures, and provide passengers with information regarding their rights. Passengers have the right to submit complaints, and carriers and terminal managing bodies must provide them with information about their rights. The Regulation aims to ensure that passengers, including those with disabilities or reduced mobility, are treated fairly and have access to the information and assistance they need when travelling by bus or coach. Overall, the Regulation seeks to promote non-discrimination, accessibility, and passenger rights in the bus and coach transport sector.

summary:
The Regulation sets out rules for the use of textile fibre names, labelling, and marking of fibre composition of textile products made available on the Union market. It applies to products containing at least 80% by weight of textile fibres, but does not apply to textile products contracted out to persons working in their own homes or to independent firms, nor to customized textile products made up by self-employed tailors. A textile product is defined as a product exclusively composed of textile fibres, with a textile fibre being a unit of matter with flexibility, fineness, and a high ratio of length to maximum transverse dimension.

The Regulation requires the indication of textile fibre composition descriptions in catalogues, trade literature, packaging, labels, and markings, and the display of trade marks or name of undertaking separately from other information, using the official language or languages of the Member State where products are made available. However, there are exceptions, such as for bobbin, reels, skeins, balls, or other small quantities of sewing, mending, and embroidery yarn. Additionally, textile products listed in Annex V are exempt from labelling or marking requirements, while those listed in Annex VI may use inclusive labelling.

The Regulation also establishes tolerances for fibre composition, allowing for 2% of extraneous fibres that are technically unavoidable and not added as routine, 5% for extraneous fibres in carded textile products, and a 3% manufacturing tolerance between stated fibre composition and analysis results. These tolerances may be cumulative only if the extraneous fibres are of the same chemical type as the labelled fibres, and higher tolerances may be authorized by the Commission in exceptional cases.

Manufacturers must label products with fibre composition, and consumers have the right to know the fibre composition of products. However, labelling is not compulsory for components that make up less than 10% of the total weight of the product. Specific rules apply to certain textile products, such as corsetry, etch-printed textiles, and embroidered textiles. The Regulation also sets out surface area thresholds for table mats and mobile phone and media player covers, and lists textile products for which labelling or marking is not mandatory in Annex V.

In terms of derogations, the Regulation applies to textile products listed in Annex V and Annex VI, with exemptions from labelling or marking requirements and inclusive labelling allowed for certain products. The fibre composition must be made known to each purchaser in the supply chain, including the consumer, and the trade mark or name of undertaking containing textile fibre name must comply with certain articles of the Regulation. Overall, the Regulation aims to provide consumers with accurate information about the fibre composition of textile products, while allowing for certain exceptions and tolerances.

It applies to products containing at least 80% by weight of textile fibres, but does not apply to textile products contracted out to persons working in their own homes or to independent firms, nor to customized textile products made up by self-employed tailors. A textile product is defined as a product exclusively composed of textile fibres, with a textile fibre being a unit of matter with flexibility, fineness, and a high ratio of length to maximum transverse dimension.

The Regulation applies to manufacturers, importers, distributors who place products on the market under their name or trademark, economic operators within the supply chain, and contracting authorities. Manufacturers and importers must ensure the supply of labels or markings and the accuracy of the information contained therein, while distributors who place products on the market under their name or trademark have the same obligations as manufacturers. Textile products must be labelled or marked to give an indication of their fibre composition, with labels or markings being durable, easily legible, visible, and accessible. Accompanying commercial documents may replace or supplement labels or markings in certain cases.

The Regulation requires labelling or marking with the name and percentage by weight of all constituent fibres in descending order, with exceptions for fibres up to 5% of total weight or collectively up to 15% that may be designated as 'other fibres' if they cannot be easily stated at the time of manufacture. Fibres not listed in Annex I may also be designated as 'other fibres' with the total percentage by weight. A special case is provided for products with pure cotton warp and pure flax weft, with at least 40% flax, which may be labelled as 'cotton linen union'. Justification is required for any exceptions, which must be technically unavoidable in good manufacturing practice.

Tolerances are established for the fibre composition of textile products, with a 2% tolerance for extraneous fibres. The Regulation also provides specific rules for various textile products, such as corsetry, etch-printed textiles, and embroidered textiles. Labelling is not compulsory for components that make up less than 10% of the total weight of the product, and specific surface area thresholds apply to certain products, such as table mats and mobile phone and media player covers. A list of textile products for which labelling or marking is not mandatory is provided in Annex V, which includes products such as sleeve-supports. Overall, the Regulation aims to provide consumers with accurate information about the fibre composition of textile products, while also taking into account the technical and practical considerations of textile manufacturing.

summary:
Regulation (EU) No 1173/2011 sets out a system of sanctions to enhance the enforcement of the preventive and corrective parts of the Stability and Growth Pact in the euro area, applying to Member States whose currency is the euro. The preventive part of the Stability and Growth Pact refers to the multilateral surveillance system organised by Regulation (EC) No 1466/97, while the corrective part refers to the procedure for avoiding excessive deficits as regulated by Article 126 TFEU and Regulation (EC) No 1467/97. Exceptional economic circumstances, where an excess of a government deficit over the reference value is considered exceptional, are defined in accordance with Article 126(2) TFEU and Regulation (EC) No 1467/97.

The Regulation imposes sanctions on Member States that fail to take action in response to Council recommendations, including the requirement to lodge interest-bearing deposits with the Commission. Member States with excessive deficits, those that have lodged interest-bearing deposits, and those that have not taken effective action to correct excessive deficits are subject to these sanctions. The Commission has the right to recommend Council decisions, while the Council has the right to amend these recommendations. Member States are obligated to lodge non-interest-bearing deposits and pay fines, but may request a reduction or cancellation of these deposits or fines in exceptional economic circumstances or by submitting a reasoned request.

In cases of intentional or serious negligence in misrepresenting deficit and debt data, Member States may face fines that are effective, dissuasive, and proportionate to the nature, seriousness, and duration of the misrepresentation, not exceeding 0.2% of the Member State's GDP. Member States have the right to be heard and to defend themselves during investigations. The Commission is required to publish a review report every five years, starting from 14 December 2014, evaluating the effectiveness of the Regulation and progress in economic policy coordination, which may be accompanied by a proposal for amendments to the Regulation.

The Regulation also provides for the return of non-interest-bearing deposits to Member States under certain conditions. Delegated acts may be adopted, which enter into force after a two-month period, extendable by two months, during which the European Parliament or Council may object. Voting on measures in certain articles of the Regulation is limited to members representing eurozone countries, excluding the member representing the concerned state, and requires a qualified majority as defined in Article 238(3) TFEU point (b). Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure closer coordination of economic policies among euro area Member States and to prevent excessive deficits, with sanctions and incentives in place to promote compliance.

summary:
This EU legal act applies to commercial fishing and aquaculture activities in the General Fisheries Commission for the Mediterranean (GFCM) Agreement area, with the exception of fishing operations for scientific investigations that have obtained permission from the Member State and notified the Commission and relevant Member States. The act applies to EU fishing vessels and nationals of Member States operating in the GFCM Agreement area, as well as Member States conducting fishing operations for scientific investigations.

Member States are required to submit reports on fishing activities to the Commission and ensure that vessels are issued with a fishing authorization. They must also communicate their national legislation to the Commission and comply with the closed season for common dolphinfish fisheries using Fish Aggregating Devices (FADs), although exceptions are allowed in cases of bad weather conditions. Vessels that are unable to fish due to bad weather may carry over the lost days to a later period.

Member States must maintain a register of authorized vessels flying their flag and registered in their territory that are authorized to fish in the GFCM Agreement area. They must send an updated list of authorized vessels to the Commission by December 1 each year, and the Commission must forward this list to the Executive Secretary of the GFCM by January 1 each year. Vessels must be more than 15 meters in overall length to be included in this register.

Member States are also required to communicate to the Commission any information that suggests vessels over 15 meters in length that are not on the GFCM register are fishing or transhipping in the GFCM Agreement area. They must not allow third-country vessels to use their ports for landing, transhipping, or processing if the vessel does not comply with the Regulation, is on the IUU fishing list, or lacks valid authorization, except in cases of force majeure or distress situations.

In addition, Member States must carry out inspections in designated ports for at least 15% of landings and transhipment operations each year, and cooperate with the Commission to exchange information. Fishing vessels are required to use and keep on board only one of two types of nets, and must use a diamond-meshed net of 50 mm of an acknowledged size selectivity at the duly justified request of the ship owner.

The Commission must submit a report on the implementation of certain provisions to the European Parliament and the Council, and Member States must supply information to the Commission to facilitate this reporting. Inspection reports must include specific information, such as the name of the inspector, date and time of inspection, and vessel information, including the name of the vessel, type of vessel, and external identification number. Overall, this act aims to ensure the sustainable management of fisheries resources in the GFCM Agreement area and prevent illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing.

summary:
This Regulation sets out rules for the application of conservation, management, exploitation, monitoring, marketing, and enforcement measures for fishery and aquaculture products established by the General Fisheries Commission for the Mediterranean (GFCM). It applies to all commercial fishing and aquaculture activities conducted by EU fishing vessels and nationals of Member States in the GFCM Agreement area, with the exception of fishing operations conducted solely for scientific investigations with permission from the relevant Member State and notification to the Commission and other Member States.

The Regulation imposes various obligations on Member States, including ensuring the protection of deep-sea sensitive habitats, submitting reports on fishing activities to the Commission, and maintaining a register of authorised vessels flying the flag of a Member State and registered in its territory that are authorised to fish in the GFCM Agreement area. Vessels must be issued with a fishing authorization by their Member State to fish in certain areas, and must comply with GFCM conservation and management measures. Member States must also ensure that vessels comply with these measures and submit updated lists of authorised vessels to the Commission by 1 December each year.

In addition, the Regulation requires Member States to communicate to the Commission any information showing strong reasons for suspecting vessels over 15m in length not on the GFCM register are fishing or transhipping in the GFCM Agreement area, without delay. Member States must also not allow third-country vessels to use ports for landing, transhipping, or processing if the vessel does not comply with the Regulation, is on an IUU fishing list, or lacks valid authorization, except in cases of force majeure or distress situations. Furthermore, Member States must carry out inspections in designated ports for at least 15% of landings and transhipment operations each year.

The Regulation also imposes obligations on ship owners, fishing vessels, port inspectors, and vessel owners, operators, and beneficial owners, including the obligation to submit reports on implementation, verify documentation and authorisations, and keep accurate records. There are conditions and exceptions for using certain gear, such as diamond-meshed nets, and for vessel size and gear. The Regulation also defines various terms, including vessel types and gear, and depends on regional fisheries management organisations for certain aspects of its implementation.

Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure the sustainable management of fishery and aquaculture resources in the GFCM Agreement area, and to prevent illegal, unreported, and unregulated (IUU) fishing. It requires cooperation and exchange between the Commission and Member States, as well as between Member States and other stakeholders, to achieve these goals. The Regulation applies to a range of entities, including EU fishing vessels, nationals of Member States, and third-country vessels, and imposes various rights and obligations on these entities to ensure compliance with its provisions.

summary:
The purpose of this regulation is to compile statistics on the carriage of goods by road by means of goods road transport vehicles registered in each Member State, as well as on journeys made by such vehicles. This aims to ensure comparable, reliable, synchronised, regular, and comprehensive statistical data, including the regional origin and destination of transport within the Union, which is described on the same basis as national transport. The regulation applies to each Member State, except Malta, under certain conditions, specifically when the number of Maltese-registered goods road transport vehicles licensed to engage in international carriage of goods by road does not exceed 400 vehicles. In such cases, Malta shall submit annually to Eurostat the number of goods road transport vehicles licensed to engage in international carriage of goods by road.

Each Member State shall compile statistics for the Union on the carriage of goods by road, although they may exclude from the scope of this Regulation goods road transport vehicles whose load capacity or maximum permissible weight is lower than a certain limit. The regulation also requires the compilation of statistical data on vehicle, journey, and goods, with a focus on ensuring the precision of statistical results for comparable, reliable, synchronised, regular, and comprehensive data. Member States are responsible for compiling statistical data, ensuring the precision of statistical results, and transmitting statistical results to Eurostat. The Commission, on the other hand, is tasked with adopting detailed technical rules, arrangements for transmitting data, and delegated acts. Eurostat receives statistical results from Member States.

The transmission of data must be within a specified timeframe, and statistical results must be sufficiently precise. The regulation also outlines rules for the dissemination of statistical results, which must be done no later than 12 months after the end of the period to which the results relate. The Commission is responsible for adopting rules on the dissemination of statistical results by implementing acts, which must be adopted in accordance with the examination procedure. Furthermore, the Commission must submit a report on the implementation of the Regulation to the European Parliament and the Council by a specified deadline and every 3 years thereafter, evaluating the quality of statistical data, data collection methods, and administrative burdens, and proposing modifications to the list of variables if appropriate.

In terms of data collection, transport operators in Member States are required to provide data on the transport of goods, while National Statistical Offices are responsible for coding questionnaires and reconstituting data. Member States are required to provide data to the Commission, and the regulation allows for simplification of data collection when several basic transport operations are carried out in one laden journey. However, in cases where several types of goods are transported during a laden journey, the loss of information is accepted, and Member States carrying out simplification must make explicit mention of it to the Commission. Additionally, Member States are required to transmit verified individual data to Eurostat every quarter. Overall, the regulation aims to establish a harmonised system for collecting data on the transport of goods by road, ensuring the quality and comparability of statistical data across Member States.

summary:
The purpose of this Regulation is to compile statistics on the carriage of goods by road by means of goods road transport vehicles registered in each Member State, as well as on journeys made by such vehicles. This aims to ensure comparable, reliable, synchronised, regular, and comprehensive statistical data, including the regional origin and destination of transport within the Union, which is described on the same basis as national transport. The Regulation applies to each Member State, except Malta, under certain conditions, specifically when the number of Maltese-registered goods road transport vehicles licensed to engage in international carriage of goods by road does not exceed 400 vehicles.

Each Member State is required to compile statistics for the Union on the carriage of goods by road, although they may exclude from the scope of this Regulation goods road transport vehicles whose load capacity or maximum permissible weight is lower than a certain limit. Malta, in its exempted case, shall submit annually to Eurostat the number of goods road transport vehicles licensed to engage in international carriage of goods by road. The compilation of statistical data includes information on vehicle, journey, and goods, with the aim of ensuring precision of statistical results for comparable, reliable, synchronised, regular, and comprehensive data.

Member States are responsible for compiling statistical data, ensuring the precision of statistical results, and transmitting these results to Eurostat. The Commission, assisted by the European Statistical System Committee, adopts detailed technical rules, arrangements for transmitting data, and delegated acts. Eurostat receives statistical results from Member States. The transmission of data must be sufficiently precise and must be done within a specified timeframe, typically within 5 months of the end of the period to which the results relate.

The dissemination of statistical results in respect of the carriage of goods by road must be done no later than 12 months after the end of the period to which the results relate, following rules adopted by the Commission through implementing acts. These implementing acts are adopted in accordance with the examination procedure. The Commission is also obligated to submit a report on the implementation of the Regulation to the European Parliament and the Council by 31 December 2014 and every 3 years thereafter, evaluating the quality of statistical data, data collection methods, and administrative burdens, and proposing modifications to the list of variables if appropriate.

Member States are required to transmit verified individual data to Eurostat every quarter. National Statistical Offices (NSOs) in Member States must reconstitute data not explicitly required from transport operators, and Member States must make explicit mention of simplifications to the Commission. Transport operators are obligated to provide data on vehicle-related variables. Specific conditions apply when several basic transport operations are carried out in one laden journey, and when several different types of goods are transported during a laden journey, with the acceptance of potential loss of information in the latter case. Successive configurations of road transport vehicles must be recorded.

The Regulation repeals and replaces Regulation (EC) No 1172/98, indicating a shift in the legal framework governing the compilation and transmission of statistical data on the carriage of goods by road within the Union. Overall, the Regulation aims to establish a harmonized system for collecting and disseminating statistical data on road transport, ensuring that the data is accurate, reliable, and comparable across Member States, which is essential for policy-making and monitoring the performance of the transport sector within the European Union.

summary:
The Office for Harmonization in the Internal Market (Trade Marks and Designs) plays a crucial role in facilitating and supporting national authorities, the private sector, and Union institutions in their efforts to combat intellectual property rights infringements. The Office's tasks and activities are designed to improve understanding of intellectual property value, scope, and impact of infringements, as well as best practices and expertise in enforcement. However, it is important to note that the Office's tasks do not include participation in individual operations or investigations by competent authorities.

The Office works with a wide range of stakeholders, including national authorities, the private sector, Union institutions, Member States, and third countries. In particular, the Office shall carry out activities such as data collection, analysis, and dissemination, as well as providing assessments and reports. The Office also works with public administrations, bodies, and organisations in Member States dealing with intellectual property rights, private sector representatives, consumer organisations, small and medium-sized enterprises, authors, and other creators.

The Office is required to draw up an annual work programme prioritizing activities under the Regulation and to carry out tasks and activities in accordance with the Regulation and Title XII of Regulation (EC) No 207/2009. The Office shall also provide a management report, which shall contain information on its tasks and activities under the Regulation, as well as an overall assessment of the proper representation in the Observatory of all relevant actors. The management report shall also include observations on the enforcement of intellectual property rights and potential future policies and strategies, as well as an overview of the Office's future activities.

Member States and private-sector representatives are required to inform the Office of their policies and strategies on intellectual property rights. The Office shall invite representatives to meetings of the Observatory at least once per year. The President of the Office shall consult representatives on the relevant parts of the management report before submitting it to the European Parliament, Commission, and Administrative Board.

The Commission shall adopt a report evaluating the application of this Regulation, which shall assess the operation of the Regulation, particularly its impact on the enforcement of intellectual property rights in the internal market. The Commission shall consult the Office, Member States, and representatives of the Observatory when preparing the evaluation report and shall transmit the report to the European Parliament, Council, and European Economic and Social Committee, undertaking a broad consultation among stakeholders. The evaluation report is to be adopted by 6 June 2017. Overall, the Office's activities and tasks are designed to support the effective enforcement of intellectual property rights in the internal market, and its work is subject to regular evaluation and reporting requirements.

summary:
This regulation establishes an accelerated phasing-in scheme for double-hull or equivalent design requirements for single-hull oil tankers and bans the transport of heavy grade oil in single-hull oil tankers. The regulation applies to oil tankers of 5,000 tonnes deadweight and above flying the flag of a Member State or entering or leaving a port or offshore terminal under the jurisdiction of a Member State. However, it does not apply to warships, naval auxiliaries, or other ships used for government non-commercial service.

The regulation defines key terms, including "MARPOL 73/78", which refers to the International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships, 1973, as amended by the Protocol of 1978, and "oil tanker", which is defined in Regulation 1.5 of Annex I to MARPOL 73/78. The regulation also categorizes oil tankers into Category 1, 2, and 3 based on deadweight and compliance with specific regulations of MARPOL 73/78.

Oil tankers of Category 2 or Category 3 are subject to specific requirements, including the need to be double-hull to operate under the flag of a Member State or enter ports or offshore terminals. Additionally, oil tankers carrying heavy grade oil must be double-hull. However, there is an exemption for oil tankers operated exclusively in ports and inland navigation.

The regulation prohibits certain oil tankers from operating or entering ports or offshore terminals after a specific date, which is the anniversary of the date of delivery of the ship in 2015. Member States are required to inform the International Maritime Organization (IMO) of decisions to deny entry to oil tankers based on Regulation 20.8.2 of Annex I to MARPOL 73/78.

The regulation repeals Regulation (EC) No 417/2002 and amends several other regulations, including Regulation (EC) No 2099/2002, Regulation (EC) No 1726/2003, Commission Regulation (EC) No 2172/2004, Regulation (EC) No 457/2007, Regulation (EC) No 219/2009, and Commission Regulation (EC) No 1163/2009. References to the repealed Regulation shall be construed as references to this Regulation, and a correlation table is provided in Annex II.

The Commission is conferred the power to adopt delegated acts, subject to certain conditions, including the absence of objection from the European Parliament or Council within a specified period. The regulation aims to improve the safety and environmental standards of oil tankers operating in the European Union, and its provisions are designed to reduce the risk of oil spills and protect the marine environment.

summary:
This regulation establishes an accelerated phasing-in scheme for double-hull or equivalent design requirements for single-hull oil tankers and bans the transport of heavy grade oil in single-hull oil tankers. The regulation applies to oil tankers of 5,000 tonnes deadweight and above flying the flag of a Member State or entering or leaving a port or offshore terminal under the jurisdiction of a Member State. However, it does not apply to warships, naval auxiliaries, or other ships used for government non-commercial service.

The regulation defines key terms, including "MARPOL 73/78", which refers to the International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships, 1973, as amended by the Protocol of 1978, and "oil tanker", which is defined in Regulation 1.5 of Annex I to MARPOL 73/78. The regulation also categorizes oil tankers into Category 1, 2, and 3 based on deadweight and compliance with specific regulations of MARPOL 73/78.

Oil tankers of Category 2 or Category 3 are subject to specific requirements, including the need to be double-hull to operate under the flag of a Member State or enter ports or offshore terminals. Additionally, oil tankers carrying heavy grade oil must be double-hull. However, there is an exemption for oil tankers operated exclusively in ports and inland navigation.

The regulation prohibits certain oil tankers from operating or entering ports or offshore terminals after a specific date, which is the anniversary of the date of delivery of the ship in 2015. Member States are required to inform the International Maritime Organization (IMO) of decisions to deny entry to oil tankers based on Regulation 20.8.2 of Annex I to MARPOL 73/78.

The regulation repeals Regulation (EC) No 417/2002 and amends several other regulations, including Regulation (EC) No 2099/2002, Regulation (EC) No 1726/2003, Commission Regulation (EC) No 2172/2004, Regulation (EC) No 457/2007, Regulation (EC) No 219/2009, and Commission Regulation (EC) No 1163/2009. References to the repealed Regulation shall be construed as references to this Regulation, and a correlation table is provided in Annex II.

The Commission is conferred the power to adopt delegated acts, subject to certain conditions, including the absence of objection from the European Parliament or Council within a specified period. The regulation aims to improve the safety and environmental standards of oil tankers operating in the European Union, and its provisions are designed to reduce the risk of oil spills and protect the marine environment.

summary:
The European Union has established a regulatory framework for the protection of designations of origin and geographical indications. This framework applies to products with protected designations of origin and protected geographical indications, and requires a product specification that includes the name to be protected, a description of the product, a definition of the geographical area, evidence of origin, the method of obtaining the product, a link between the product and its geographical environment, authorities or bodies verifying compliance, and labelling rules. The Commission may adopt delegated acts to limit the information included in the specification. 

When applying for registration of a designation of origin or geographical indication, the application must include the name and address of the applicant group and authorities, the product specification, a single document summarizing the main points of the product specification and its link to the geographical environment, and proof of protection in the country of origin. The application process involves scrutiny by the Member State to check justification and compliance with scheme conditions, a national opposition procedure with publication and opportunity for opposition, and a decision by the Member State to lodge the application dossier with the Commission.

A transitional period of up to five years, extendable to 15 years in duly justified cases, is granted for products with designations that contravene certain provisions, provided that the registration of the name would jeopardize an entirely or partly identical name and the products have been legally marketed with that name in the territory concerned for at least five years. For a 15-year extension, the designation must have been in legal use consistently and fairly for at least 25 years, and its use must not have been intended to profit from the reputation of the registered name.

Verification of compliance with the regulatory framework is carried out by competent authorities, control bodies, or product certification bodies, and the costs are borne by operators or contributed by Member States. For products from third countries, verification is carried out by public authorities or product certification bodies. Groups entitled to ensure the quality, reputation, and authenticity of products may take action for legal protection, develop information and promotion activities, and ensure compliance with specifications. They may also take measures to enhance the product's value and prevent detrimental measures.

Operators complying with quality scheme rules are entitled to verification of compliance, and those preparing, storing, or marketing products under quality schemes are subject to controls. Member States must ensure non-discriminatory participation in quality schemes. Indications, abbreviations, and symbols may only be used for products that comply with the regulatory framework. The use of Union symbols is also established to provide a visual representation of the protected designations of origin and geographical indications. 

In the context of applications for registration, groups working with products with the name to be registered may apply, or a single natural or legal person may apply if certain conditions are met. The application process involves scrutiny, opposition, and a decision by the Member State, and any natural or legal person with a legitimate interest may oppose the application. The decision to register a name is made public, and the Commission may adopt measures to ensure the effective application of the regulatory framework.

summary:
The Regulation provides a framework for quality schemes for agricultural products and foodstuffs, with the aim of facilitating communication of their characteristics and value-adding features within the internal market. The scope of the Regulation is limited to agricultural products intended for human consumption listed in Annex I to the Treaty and products closely linked to agricultural production or the rural economy. It applies to producers of agricultural products and foodstuffs, as well as buyers and consumers of these products. Producers have the right to communicate the characteristics of their products under conditions of fair competition and to correctly identify their products on the marketplace, but they are also obliged to comply with the quality schemes.

The Regulation does not apply to existing Union legislation on wines, aromatised wines, spirit drinks, products of organic farming, or outermost regions. Additionally, the scope for designations of origin and geographical indications is limited to products with an intrinsic link between product characteristics and geographical origin. For products originating in the Union with protected designation of origin or protected geographical indication, the Union symbols and registered name must appear on labelling, provided that the products are registered in accordance with the Regulation.

In cases where products have designations that contravene certain provisions of the Regulation, they may be allowed to continue using the designation under which they were marketed, subject to certain conditions. For example, if an admissible statement of opposition is made or if the designation has been used for at least 5 years preceding publication, a transitional period of up to 5 years may be granted. In exceptional cases, this transitional period may be extended to 15 years if the designation has been in legal use for at least 25 years and its use was not intended to profit from the reputation of a registered name.

The Regulation also establishes a scheme for optional quality terms, which applies to protected designations of origin, protected geographical indications, traditional specialities guaranteed, and other quality schemes. This scheme is intended to facilitate communication of the value-adding characteristics of agricultural products and applies to producers, operators who prepare, store, and place products on the market, as well as Member States and control bodies. Member States must approve individual proposals for projects of common interest, and the decision-making body of each Group must adopt a regional list of proposed projects of common interest.

To be considered a project of common interest, a project must meet the criteria set out in Article 4, be necessary for at least one of the energy infrastructure priority corridors and areas, and have potential overall benefits that outweigh costs, including in the longer term. The Agency is responsible for evaluating the progress of projects of common interest and making recommendations to overcome delays and difficulties, and must submit a consolidated report to Groups within 3 months of receipt of annual reports. The Agency's evaluation must consider the consistent implementation of Union-wide network development plans.

Member States, national competent authorities, and project promoters have obligations related to the permit granting process for projects of common interest. Member States must designate a national competent authority by 16 November 2013, facilitate and coordinate the permit granting process, and issue a comprehensive decision within the time limit set out in Article 10. The national competent authority may delegate tasks to another authority, but must notify the Commission and publish the delegation. Project promoters must keep national regulatory authorities informed of project progress and costs at least once per year, and submit an investment request with a cost-benefit analysis, business plan, and proposal for cross-border cost allocation when the project has reached sufficient maturity.

The investment request must be submitted jointly if there are multiple project promoters, and the project must have received a cross-border cost allocation decision or aim to provide services across borders, bring technological innovation, and ensure safety of cross-border grid operation. Each Group must consult relevant stakeholders, including producers, distribution system operators, suppliers, consumers, and environmental protection organisations, and may organise hearings or consultations to accomplish its tasks. The Commission must publish internal rules, member organisations, progress updates, meeting agendas, and conclusions on a transparency platform.

Promoters of eligible projects must submit applications to the relevant Group, including assessments, analyses, and cost-benefit analyses, and recipients must preserve the confidentiality of commercially sensitive information. Proposed projects must be part of the latest 10-year network development plan, developed by ENTSO for Electricity or Gas, and the Commission must issue Guidelines on criteria for 10-year network development plans. A manual of procedures must be established, specifying relevant law, decisions, and opinions for projects of common interest, including environmental law, and outlining the work flow, including time frames and decision-making processes. The manual must provide information on the procedures for projects of common interest, ensuring transparency and consistency in the development and implementation of these projects.

summary:
The Regulation aims to establish guidelines for trans-European energy infrastructure, repealing Decision No 1364/2006/EC and amending Regulations (EC) No 713/2009, (EC) No 714/2009, and (EC) No 715/2009. It applies to the European Union and is intended to enhance the diversification of energy supply sources, routes, and counterparts. The Regulation is applicable to trans-European energy infrastructure priority corridors and areas, and its purpose is to establish a framework for the development of projects of common interest. The European Parliament and the Council of the European Union have adopted the Regulation, which empowers the Commission to adopt delegated acts to establish the Union list of projects of common interest. The Commission shall ensure the Union list is established every two years, with the first Union list to be adopted by 30 September 2013, and shall be subject to the second paragraph of Article 172 of the TFEU.

The Regulation applies to various entities, including Member States, promoters of projects potentially eligible for selection as projects of common interest, national regulatory authorities, and the Agency. The Commission has the right to make proposals for grants for works to enable the implementation of projects of common interest, while the Agency is responsible for requesting an exemption decision and for decisions on cross-border cost allocation. National regulatory authorities and the Agency shall participate in the Groups and ensure consistency between them, and the Groups shall consult with relevant stakeholders and publish certain information on the transparency platform.

In terms of project implementation, a European coordinator may be designated for a project of common interest encountering significant implementation difficulties, with the agreement of the Member States concerned, for a period of up to one year, renewable twice. The permit granting process for projects of common interest shall be organised by Member States, which shall designate a national competent authority, facilitate and coordinate the permit granting process, and establish time limits. Project promoters of projects of common interest shall keep national regulatory authorities informed of project progress and costs at least once per year and submit an investment request with a cost-benefit analysis, business plan, and proposal for cross-border cost allocation, provided the project has reached sufficient maturity.

The Regulation also requires the Agency to submit a consolidated report on projects of common interest within three months of receipt of annual reports, evaluating progress, making recommendations, and assessing the implementation of Union-wide network development plans. Furthermore, the project website shall make available certain information, including an information leaflet, a non-technical summary, project planning, and contact details. The Regulation aims to ensure equal opportunities for projects involving peripheral Member States, taking into account the number of Member States affected by each project. Overall, the Regulation provides a framework for the development of trans-European energy infrastructure, with the aim of enhancing the diversification of energy supply sources, routes, and counterparts, and ensuring the efficient and coordinated implementation of projects of common interest.

summary:
The European Union has established a regulatory framework governing the collection, storage, and comparison of fingerprint data for the purpose of managing asylum applications and facilitating law enforcement cooperation. This framework applies to Member States, which are obligated to update the Eurodac database when an applicant for international protection or another person arrives in or leaves the territory of the Member States. Specifically, Member States must update the database when a person arrives in the Member State responsible for examining their application, when a person leaves the territory of the Member States, and when a Member State becomes responsible for examining an application. 

The Central System, which is part of the Eurodac framework, is used to record and compare fingerprint data, as well as other relevant information such as the Member State of origin, place and date of application for international protection, sex, and reference number used by the Member State of origin. The data is recorded in the Central System, and the system informs all Member States of origin of any marking of data for beneficiaries of international protection. The marked data is stored in the Central System and is available for comparison for a period of three years after the grant of international protection, after which it is automatically blocked.

The regulatory framework also establishes rules for the protection of personal data, including the right of individuals to be informed about data processing, the right of access to data, and the right to correction or erasure of inaccurate data. Member States, the Agency, and authorities designated by each Member State have obligations to ensure lawful transmission and processing of data, adopt security measures for data protection, and regulate access to and correction of data. 

In addition, the framework requires Member States to prepare annual reports on the effectiveness of fingerprint data comparison for law enforcement purposes and to log and document data processing operations. It also establishes penalties for unauthorized data processing and provides for security incident notification and collaboration. The European Data Protection Supervisor has a role in overseeing the protection of personal data obtained from the Central System. 

The regulatory framework aims to ensure the secure and lawful transmission and processing of data, while also protecting the rights of individuals and promoting cooperation among Member States. It applies to persons covered by specific articles of the regulation, as well as to Member States, the Agency, and authorities designated by each Member State. Overall, the framework seeks to balance the need for effective asylum management and law enforcement cooperation with the need to protect individual rights and ensure the security and integrity of personal data.

summary:
This Regulation sets out the conditions for requesting comparisons of fingerprint data with those stored in the Central System for law enforcement purposes, applying to designated authorities of Member States and the European Police Office (Europol). Designated authorities are those responsible for the prevention, detection, or investigation of terrorist offences or other serious criminal offences, while Europol is a specialized unit with duly empowered officials acting as a verifying authority. Member States are responsible for designating authorities and ensuring that the conditions for requesting comparisons are fulfilled.

Designated authorities are authorized to request comparisons with Eurodac data, and the verifying authority ensures that the conditions for requesting comparisons are met. Member States must update data sets recorded in conformity with Article 11 when a person arrives or leaves the territory. Europol designates a specialized unit as a verifying authority. When a Member State becomes responsible for an applicant for international protection, it must update the data set recorded in conformity with Article 11 by adding the date when the decision to examine the application was taken.

Designated authorities may submit a request for comparison of fingerprint data if comparisons with national fingerprint databases, automated fingerprinting identification systems of other Member States, and the Visa Information System did not lead to the establishment of identity. The comparison must be necessary for the prevention, detection, or investigation of terrorist offences or serious criminal offences, and there must be reasonable grounds to consider that the comparison will substantially contribute to the prevention, detection, or investigation. However, if there are reasonable grounds to believe that a comparison with the automated fingerprinting identification systems of other Member States would not lead to the establishment of identity, this condition does not apply.

The Regulation also ensures that individuals are informed about data processing in Eurodac and that the transmission and processing of data are lawful. It adopts security measures for data protection, regulates access to and correction of data, and ensures the security of data before, during, and after transmission. Individuals have the right to be informed about data processing, access to data, and correction or erasure of inaccurate data. Member States, the Agency, and authorities designated by each Member State have obligations to ensure lawful data processing, protect personal data, and provide security measures.

The Regulation requires Member States to prepare annual reports on the effectiveness of fingerprint data comparison for law enforcement purposes and to log and document data processing operations. It also protects personal data obtained from the Central System, provides for security incident notification and collaboration, and establishes penalties for unauthorized data processing. Member States, Europol, the Agency, and the European Data Protection Supervisor have obligations to protect personal data, prepare reports, and collaborate in case of security incidents. The Regulation allows for the transfer of data to third countries under certain conditions and sets out the rules for its entry into force and applicability.

summary:
This Regulation sets out the conditions and procedures for customs authorities to act on goods suspected of infringing intellectual property rights within the EU customs territory. It applies to goods under customs supervision or control, including those declared for release, export, re-export, entering or leaving the EU, or in free zones or warehouses. The Regulation aims to prevent acts breaching intellectual property laws and cooperate with third countries on enforcement. However, it does not apply to goods released for free.

The Regulation applies to right-holders, intellectual property collective rights management bodies, professional defence bodies, and certain groups of producers, as well as persons or entities authorized by right-holders to initiate proceedings. Holders of exclusive licenses covering two or more Member States are also entitled to submit applications for customs action. Customs authorities are required to carry out adequate controls and take proportionate identification measures, while entitled persons and entities can submit applications for customs action and initiate proceedings.

To submit an application, applicants must provide details concerning themselves, their status, and documents to prove entitlement to submit the application. They must also provide information on the intellectual property right, specific and technical data on authentic goods, and information to enable customs authorities to identify the goods. Applicants must notify the competent customs department of any changes to the provided information and assume liability under the conditions laid down in Article 28. They must also bear the costs referred to in Article 29 and agree to the processing of their data by the Commission and Member States.

Once an application is granted, customs authorities may suspend the release or detain goods suspected of infringing intellectual property rights, except for perishable goods. They may request information from persons potentially entitled to submit an application and must notify the declarant or holder of the goods within one working day. The release or detention ends if no person entitled to submit an application is identified within one working day, or if no application is received or the application is rejected.

The Regulation also provides for the exchange of data between Member States and the Commission on decisions relating to applications and detentions. Competent customs departments must notify the Commission of decisions granting applications, extending periods, revoking decisions, and suspending decisions, and transmit relevant information on suspended or detained goods. The information must be stored in a central database, and access is restricted to customs authorities and the Commission.

In the event that the holder of the decision does not fulfill notification obligations, return samples, or initiate proceedings, the competent customs department may suspend customs authorities' actions. The decision to suspend actions has effect only in the Member State where the decision is taken in the case of a Union application. The holder of the decision must notify the competent customs department of any changes to intellectual property rights, entitlement to submit the application, or modifications to the provided information. Overall, the Regulation aims to provide a framework for customs authorities to effectively enforce intellectual property rights and prevent the entry of counterfeit goods into the EU market.

summary:
This Regulation sets out the conditions and procedures for action by the customs authorities in the European Union to enforce intellectual property rights. The customs territory of the Union is defined as the customs territory of the Community as outlined in Article 3 of Regulation (EEC) No 2913/92. Key terms used in the Regulation include "trade name", "geographical indication", and "trade mark", which are types of intellectual property rights protected by national or Union law. A trade mark can be a Community trade mark, a trade mark registered in a Member State, or a trade mark registered under international arrangements with effect in a Member State or the Union. An application to the customs authorities to take action with respect to goods suspected of infringing an intellectual property right must be made to the competent customs department and must include details about the applicant, the intellectual property right, and the goods in question.

The applicant must also provide specific and technical data on authentic goods and information to enable customs authorities to identify the goods. The applicant is required to notify the competent customs department of any changes to the provided information and assume liability under the conditions laid down in Article 28. The applicant must also bear the costs referred to in Article 29 and agree to the processing of their data by the Commission and Member States. The competent customs department may suspend customs authorities' actions if the holder of the decision does not fulfill notification obligations, return samples, or initiate proceedings. The decision to suspend actions has effect only in the Member State where the decision is taken in the case of a Union application.

Once an application is made, the customs authorities may inspect the goods suspected of infringing an intellectual property right. If the goods are found to infringe an intellectual property right, the holder of the decision must confirm the infringement in writing within a specified timeframe, usually 10 working days, or 3 days for perishable goods. The holder of the decision must also agree to the destruction of the goods in writing within the same timeframe. If the conditions for destruction are met, the goods will be destroyed under customs control, unless otherwise specified in national law. Samples may be taken for educational purposes. If the declarant or holder of the goods does not agree to destruction, the holder of the decision must initiate proceedings within the specified timeframe.

The Regulation also sets out rules on the exchange of data between Member States and the Commission, costs, including reimbursement and compensation, and liability of the customs authorities and the holder of the decision. The customs authorities and the holder of the decision must notify each other of certain information, including the destruction of goods. Personal data must be kept for six months after proceedings have determined whether an intellectual property right has been infringed. The Regulation applies to Member States, the Commission, customs authorities, and the holder of the decision, and sets out their respective obligations and responsibilities in enforcing intellectual property rights. Overall, the Regulation aims to provide a framework for the customs authorities to effectively enforce intellectual property rights and prevent the importation of counterfeit goods into the European Union.

summary:
The Regulation establishes a common legal framework for the systematic production of European demographic statistics in the Member States, aiming to provide comparable regional statistics using the NUTS classification for territorial units. This framework applies to all Member States, which are required to provide the Commission, specifically Eurostat, with data on their usually resident population and vital events. The data shall be provided based on the same concepts and refer to the same reference date or period, with the use of scientifically-based and well-documented statistical estimation methods encouraged. Member States shall also use the same population definition for national and regional levels.

The Commission has the right to adopt implementing acts laying down uniform conditions for the breakdown of data, deadlines, and revisions of data, which shall be adopted in accordance with the examination procedure. The Commission also has the obligation to submit reports to the European Parliament and the Council on the implementation of the Regulation, taking into account information provided by Member States. These reports shall evaluate specific aspects of the implementation, including data quality and comparability. The Commission may propose improvements to the common legal framework for European statistics and has the right to submit reports to the European Parliament, the Council, the Economic and Social Committee, and the Committee of the Regions.

Member States are responsible for ensuring the quality of transmitted data, reporting reference metadata, providing information for quality evaluation, ensuring data consistency, and making data and metadata available. They shall conduct feasibility studies on the 'usual residence' definition and may receive financial support from the Union for this purpose. The data quality criteria apply as per Regulation (EC) No 223/2009, and data sources shall be chosen according to national law. The right to respect for private and family life and to the protection of personal data is guaranteed.

The Regulation also provides that data on total population at the national level and data on vital events shall be provided to the Commission. The Commission may use this data for qualified majority voting in the Council. The Regulation refers to other EU laws and regulations, including Regulation (EU) No 182/2011. The Regulation shall enter into force on the twentieth day following its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union and shall cease to apply on 31 August 2028. Overall, the Regulation aims to establish a harmonized framework for the production of European demographic statistics, ensuring the quality, comparability, and reliability of the data provided by Member States.

summary:
The Regulation establishes a common legal framework for the systematic production of European demographic statistics in the Member States, aiming to provide comparable regional statistics using the NUTS classification for territorial units. This framework applies to all Member States, which are required to provide the Commission, specifically Eurostat, with data on their usually resident population and vital events, including live births and deaths. The data must be provided based on the same concepts and refer to the same reference date or period, and the use of scientifically-based and well-documented statistical estimation methods is encouraged.

Member States must also provide data on total population at the national level, as well as data on vital events, and use the same population definition for national and regional levels. The Commission has the right to adopt implementing acts laying down uniform conditions for the breakdown of data, deadlines, and revisions of data, which shall be adopted in accordance with the examination procedure. The Commission also has the right to submit reports to the European Parliament, the Council, the Economic and Social Committee, and the Committee of the Regions, and to propose improvements to the common legal framework for European statistics.

In terms of specific data requirements, Member States must provide data on population, including live births by sex, month, live birth-order, mother's age, and other characteristics, as well as deaths by age, sex, year of birth, and other characteristics. They must also provide data on population by age, sex, and region of residence, including persons having their usual residence in the Member State at the end of the reference period, disaggregated by groups of citizenship and country of birth.

Member States have obligations to ensure the quality of transmitted data, report reference metadata to the Commission, and keep the Commission informed of changes to data sources, definitions, and estimation methods. The Commission, in turn, has the obligation to submit reports on the implementation of the Regulation, evaluating specific aspects such as data quality and comparability, and taking into account information provided by Member States.

The Regulation guarantees the right to respect for private and family life and to the protection of personal data, and it refers to other EU laws and regulations, including Regulation (EU) No 182/2011. The Regulation shall enter into force on the twentieth day following its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union and shall cease to apply on 31 August 2028. Overall, the Regulation aims to establish a harmonized framework for the production of European demographic statistics, ensuring the availability of high-quality and comparable data for the Member States and the European Union as a whole.

summary:
The European Union's rural development policy aims to preserve and promote changes to agricultural practices that contribute to the environment and climate. To achieve this, Member States are required to make support available throughout their territories, in accordance with national, regional, or local needs and priorities, and include this support in their rural development programmes at the national and/or regional level. The policy defines key terms, such as "programming," "region," "measure," "support rate," "transaction cost," "agricultural area," "economic losses," "adverse climatic event," "animal diseases," and "environmental incident," to ensure clarity and consistency in its implementation.

The policy provides support for various initiatives, including farm and business development, such as business start-up aid for young farmers, non-agricultural activities, and small farms, as well as investments in non-agricultural activities and annual or one-off payments for small farmers scheme participants who transfer holdings. This support is available to young farmers, farmers or farm household members diversifying into non-agricultural activities, and micro- and small enterprises and natural persons in rural areas. Additionally, support is granted to newly formed clusters and networks, and those commencing new activities, to promote innovation and cooperation.

The policy also provides support to farmers who suffer economic losses caused by adverse climatic events, animal or plant diseases, pest infestation, or environmental incidents, including financial contributions to premiums for crop, animal, and plant insurance, financial contributions to mutual funds, and an income stabilisation tool for severe drops in income. Furthermore, the policy supports the development of rural areas through the provision of networking activities, training, and innovation support services, as well as the collection and dissemination of examples of projects and best practices.

The European Agricultural Fund for Rural Development (EAFRD) provides a total of EUR 84,936 million in support for rural development for the period 2014-2020, with 0.25% of resources allocated for technical assistance for the Commission. The funds are distributed among Member States, with an annual breakdown indexed at 2% per year, and the Commission is empowered to adopt delegated acts to review the ceilings. At least 30% of the total EAFRD contribution is reserved for certain measures, such as environment and climate-related initiatives, although there is an exception for outermost regions and overseas territories.

To ensure the effective implementation of the policy, beneficiaries are required to provide information for monitoring and evaluation, and Managing Authorities are responsible for collecting and managing this information. The Commission is also responsible for implementing acts for measures in this section, including procedures for selection. Overall, the policy aims to promote sustainable rural development, support farmers and rural communities, and contribute to the achievement of the Union's environmental and climate goals.
