The European Union's rural development policy aims to support the development of rural areas through various measures and initiatives. To achieve this goal, certain definitions are established, including "programming" as the process of organisation, decision making, and allocation of financial resources to implement joint action by the Union and Member States. A "region" is defined as a territorial unit corresponding to NUTS level 1 or 2, while a "measure" refers to a set of operations contributing to Union priorities for rural development. The "support rate" is the rate of public contribution to an operation, and "transaction cost" is the additional cost linked to fulfilling a commitment.

The policy also defines various terms related to agriculture, such as "agricultural area", "economic losses", "adverse climatic event", "animal diseases", and "environmental incident". These definitions provide a framework for understanding the types of support available to farmers and rural areas. For example, support may be provided for pilot projects, the development of new products, practices, processes, and technologies in the agriculture, food, and forestry sectors, as well as for measures aimed at preserving and promoting positive environmental and climate changes.

The policy also identifies areas facing natural and other specific constraints, including mountain areas, areas with significant natural constraints, and areas affected by specific constraints. Support may be granted to newly formed clusters and networks, and those commencing new activities, as well as to individual actors if provided for in the rural development programme. Additionally, support is available for farm and business development, including the creation of new products, practices, and technologies.

The European Network for Rural Development and the EIP Network play important roles in facilitating the exchange of expertise and good practices, establishing dialogue between farmers and the research community, and providing help desk functions and information to key actors. Support is also available for crop, animal, and plant insurance, including financial contributions to premiums, mutual funds, and income stabilisation tools, to help farmers mitigate economic losses caused by adverse climatic events, animal or plant diseases, pest infestation, or environmental incidents.

The policy also provides support for forestry measures, including afforestation, agroforestry systems, prevention and restoration of damage to forests, and investments improving forest ecosystem resilience and environmental value. Support is available per hectare of forest for public and private forest-holders, as well as for conservation and promotion of forest genetic resources. The total Union support for rural development is EUR 84,936 million (2011 prices) for 2014-2020, with at least 30% of the total EAFRD contribution reserved for specific measures, except in the case of outermost regions and overseas territories.

Overall, the policy aims to promote the development of rural areas, support farmers and rural communities, and protect the environment, while also providing a framework for the allocation of financial resources and the implementation of joint action by the Union and Member States. The various measures and initiatives available under the policy are designed to address the specific needs and challenges of rural areas, and to promote sustainable development and growth.

summary:
This Regulation sets out the general rules for Union support for rural development, which is financed by the European Agricultural Fund for Rural Development (EAFRD). The Regulation complements Regulation (EU) No 1303/2013 and lays down objectives, Union priorities, and measures for rural development policy. It applies to Member States and beneficiaries, as defined in Article 2 of Regulation (EU) No 1303/2013, who have the right to seek support from the EAFRD for achieving rural development objectives. The EAFRD shall contribute to sustainable rural development and a competitive agricultural sector, and Member States shall implement rural development programmes. 

Support from the EAFRD shall be sought for the achievement of Union priorities for rural development, and specific conditions for support include the implementation of a strategy to meet Union priorities through a set of measures. In certain areas, such as those affected by specific constraints, support may be provided for land management to conserve or improve the environment, maintain the countryside, preserve tourist potential, or protect the coastline, provided that the total extent of these areas does not exceed 10% of the Member State's area and at least 60% of the agricultural area meets certain criteria. However, Member States with entire territory considered as an area facing specific handicaps under certain regulations are exempt from these conditions.

The Regulation also provides for support to producer groups or organisations in the form of flat rate aid in annual instalments for up to 5 years, degressive, based on annual marketed production, provided that a business plan is implemented within 9 months of the aid decision. Additionally, the EAFRD may finance tasks referred to in Article 58 of Regulation (EU) No 1303/2013, up to 0.25% of the annual allocation. The Regulation also provides for grant support for co-operation projects, such as LEADER co-operation activities, and for insurance contracts to cover loss caused by adverse events.

Member States with more than one programme may designate a coordinating body for consistency in fund management, and beneficiaries of support under rural development measures and local action groups must provide information necessary for monitoring and evaluation. Managing Authorities are responsible for managing and implementing the programme efficiently and correctly and must ensure that beneficiaries are informed of their obligations and provide relevant data. At least 30% of the total EAFRD allocation must be used for certain purposes, although the specific details of this requirement are not fully outlined in the available information. Overall, the Regulation aims to support rural development and a competitive agricultural sector, while ensuring efficient and correct management of the EAFRD.

The Instrument provides financial support for police cooperation, preventing and combating crime, and crisis management, as part of the Internal Security Fund, which is established for the period from 1 January 2014 to 31 December 2020. The Instrument does not apply to matters covered by the Justice programme. It applies to Member States, law enforcement authorities, other national authorities, Europol or other relevant Union bodies, and third countries and international organisations. The Instrument contributes to operational objectives, including promoting measures to prevent crime and combat cross-border, serious and organised crime, and promotes administrative and operational coordination, cooperation, and exchange of information among law enforcement authorities.

The Instrument supports actions in Member States and third countries to achieve specific objectives, including police cooperation, networking, and exchange, training, and education of staff. The Commission, the European External Action Service, and the European Parliament and the Council are also involved in the implementation of the Instrument. The Commission and Member States shall ensure coordination for actions in and in relation to third countries, and Member States shall allocate amounts for national programmes as indicated in Annex III. The Commission shall assess explanations for departing from minimum percentages for national programmes.

The Instrument finances transnational actions or actions of particular interest to the Union, concerning general, specific, and operational objectives, which are consistent with priorities and initiatives identified at Union level, including those endorsed by the European Parliament and the Council. Eligible actions include preparatory, monitoring, administrative, and technical activities, transnational projects, analytical, monitoring, and evaluation activities, and projects promoting networking, public-private partnerships, and mutual confidence.

The strategic Union priorities include measures to prevent and combat crime, cybercrime, terrorism, and enhance security-related risks and crisis management, as well as measures to raise Member States' administrative and operational capability to protect critical infrastructure and increase the Union's resilience to crisis and disaster. Member States have the right to participate in joint investigation teams and European Multidisciplinary Platform against Criminal Threats operational projects, and the Union has the obligation to provide financial support for police cooperation, preventing and combating crime, and crisis management. However, the implementation of the strategic Union priorities is subject to the availability of funds and the approval of the Commission, and the support for third countries is subject to the conclusion of operational programmes of action. Critical infrastructure refers to infrastructure designated as European, and the Instrument's support is aimed at enhancing the security and resilience of such infrastructure. Overall, the Instrument aims to promote a high level of security within the Union, while respecting the principles of subsidiarity and proportionality.

summary:
The European Union's legal act establishes a framework for the implementation of national programmes by Member States. Each Member State is responsible for proposing a multiannual national programme based on the outcome of a policy dialogue, which must be submitted to the Commission within three months. The programme should include a baseline situation description, analysis of requirements and national objectives, strategy and targets, and a description of how the programme will cover the objectives of the Specific Regulations. The Commission will examine the proposed programme for consistency with the objectives and Union law, and may make observations. 

Member States are also required to implement their programmes, which must comply with the Regulation and Specific Regulations, and be proportionate, reducing administrative burden and facilitating efficient implementation. The Commission will adopt a model for national programmes and examine and approve proposed programmes. In addition, the Commission will assess Member States' management and control systems for compliance with the Regulation and ensure the effective functioning of these systems and the correctness of expenditure.

The Regulation also provides for technical assistance to support actions for the preparation, management, monitoring, evaluation, information, and communication of national programmes. Member States may support such actions, and the Commission may support actions to reduce administrative burden. The Commission will lay down arrangements for the annual clearance of accounts procedure and ensure the effective functioning of management and control systems.

Member States are obligated to submit implementation reports to the Commission, including annual reports until 2022 and a final report by 31 December 2023. The Commission will inform Member States of its observations on these reports within two months. Furthermore, both Member States and the Commission are required to submit evaluation reports, with Member States submitting interim and ex-post evaluation reports to the Commission, and the Commission submitting these reports to the European Parliament, Council, European Economic and Social Committee, and Committee of the Regions. These evaluation reports will be published in their entirety, except for confidential information.

The Regulation emphasizes the importance of proportionality, reducing administrative burden, and facilitating efficient implementation. It also highlights the need for effective management and control systems, as well as the importance of evaluation and reporting to ensure the successful implementation of national programmes. The Commission has the right to assess management and control systems, require actions for their effective functioning, and carry out on-the-spot audits or controls. Overall, the Regulation aims to establish a framework for the effective implementation of national programmes, while ensuring compliance with Union law and the principles of proportionality and efficiency.

summary:
The Regulation sets out general rules for the implementation of Specific Regulations, covering areas such as financing of expenditure, partnership, programming, reporting, monitoring, and evaluation, as well as management and control systems and clearance of accounts. It applies to the implementation of Specific Regulations, Union actions, emergency assistance, and technical assistance at the initiative of the Commission. The Commission has the right to implement these actions directly or indirectly, while Member States are obligated to establish a partnership with relevant authorities and bodies to develop and implement national programmes, ensuring no conflict of interest among partners. Member States are also responsible for setting up a monitoring committee and establishing practical arrangements for its operation.

The Commission is responsible for examining national programmes for consistency with objectives and approving or rejecting them. It must also regularly inform relevant parties and has the obligation to assess management and control systems. Technical assistance at the initiative of Member States is allowed, with the purpose of supporting actions for preparation, management, monitoring, evaluation, information, and communication. This assistance can cover various expenditures, including those related to programme preparation, audits, evaluations, and information dissemination. However, appropriations may only be used to support actions that reduce administrative burden, and actions may concern preceding and subsequent financial frameworks.

Systematic administrative control and on-the-spot controls are necessary to ensure a sufficient level of assurance for expenditure, and Responsible Authorities are tasked with carrying out these controls. Member States must submit documents for annual accounts, request payment of the final balance, and provide a final implementation report, as well as provide further information for the annual clearance of accounts. The Commission has the power to assess management and control systems, lay down arrangements for annual clearance of accounts, adopt implementing acts for rules on controls and reporting, and make financial corrections.

The Commission is also obligated to adopt implementing acts defining the technical characteristics of information and publicity measures, following an examination procedure. A committee is established to assist the Commission, and this committee operates within the meaning of Regulation (EU) No 182/2011. The Regulation also references other relevant regulations, including Regulation (EU) No 513/2014, which establishes an instrument for financial support for police cooperation, preventing and combating crime, and crisis management, and Council Regulation (EU, Euratom) No 1311/2013, which lays down the multiannual financial framework for 2014-2020. Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure effective management and control of Union funds, while also providing a framework for technical assistance and cooperation among Member States.

summary:
The Fund supports actions for third-country nationals, including those with refugee status, subsidiary protection status, or temporary protection, and those being resettled or transferred. It also supports integration-related measures and resettlement, transfer of applicants for, and beneficiaries of international protection. The Fund enhances solidarity and responsibility-sharing between Member States, particularly those affected by migration and asylum flows. It applies to third-country nationals with refugee status or subsidiary protection status, those who have applied for international protection and are waiting for a final decision, those with temporary protection, and those being or having been resettled in a Member State. The Fund also applies to Member States, particularly those most affected by migration and asylum flows.

The Fund shall support actions for third-country nationals, including reception conditions, asylum procedures, and integration-related measures. It shall also support resettlement, transfer of applicants for, and beneficiaries of international protection. summary:
The Asylum, Migration and Integration Fund (AMIF) is established to contribute to the development of the common Union policy on asylum and immigration, and to strengthen the area of freedom, security and justice. The Fund applies to Member States and third countries and their nationals. Member States are required to ensure that their national programmes include actions addressing specific objectives and allocate resources to meet general and specific objectives. The Commission is responsible for implementing the Fund in the most effective and user-friendly manner.

The Fund supports actions for the integration of third-country nationals residing legally in a Member State or acquiring legal residence, including setting up and developing integration strategies, providing advice and assistance, and introducing third-country nationals to the receiving society. It also supports education and training, self-empowerment, and promoting contact and dialogue between third-country nationals and the receiving society. Additionally, the Fund promotes equality of access and outcomes and capacity-building of beneficiaries.

The Fund also supports practical cooperation and capacity-building measures for Member States and third-country nationals. Furthermore, it provides for the allocation of additional amounts to Member States for specific actions, including the implementation of the Union Resettlement Programme. Member States shall pursue specific objectives under national programmes and receive additional amounts for resettling persons under the Union Resettlement Programme.

The Commission shall adopt delegated acts to revise Annex II and establish the timetable and implementation conditions for the Union Resettlement Programme. The Fund's support is subject to certain conditions, including that additional amounts shall only be used for specific actions listed in Annex II, and eligibility for funding under Union actions. The Fund also enhances solidarity and responsibility sharing between Member States.

The Regulation (EU) No 514/2014 applies to the Fund, which supports asylum, migration, and integration, as well as legal migration, integration of third-country nationals, and return strategies. The Fund applies to Member States, and the European Migration Network and National Contact Points are supported by the Fund. The Commission and Member States ensure actions are taken in synergy and coherence with other actions outside the Union. The Commission adopts the amount made available for the European Migration Network, and the Steering Board approves the work programme for the European Migration Network.

Certain costs, such as lump sums for resettlement and transfer of beneficiaries of international protection, are exempt from specific rules. The Fund's implementation is subject to detailed rules and conditions, including the requirement for Member States to provide detailed justifications for derogations from minimum percentages. Overall, the AMIF aims to promote a common European asylum system, support the integration of third-country nationals, and enhance solidarity and responsibility sharing between Member States.

summary:
The Regulation sets out specific requirements for the statutory audit of public-interest entities, aiming to ensure that such audits are of adequate quality and are carried out by statutory auditors and audit firms subject to stringent requirements. This Regulation applies to statutory auditors and audit firms carrying out statutory audits of public-interest entities, including credit institutions, insurance undertakings, issuers of securities admitted to trading on a regulated market, payment institutions, undertakings for collective investment in transferable securities (UCITS), electronic money institutions, and alternative investment funds. However, cooperatives, savings banks, and similar entities may be exempted by Member States under certain conditions.

Statutory auditors and audit firms have the obligation to assess and document certain requirements before accepting or continuing an engagement for a statutory audit of a public-interest entity and must comply with the requirements of the Regulation. They are also required to report any information concerning the public-interest entity that may bring about a material breach of laws, regulations, or administrative provisions, a material threat or doubt concerning the continuous functioning of the entity, or a refusal to issue an audit opinion to the competent authorities supervising the public-interest entity or the competent authority responsible for oversight of the statutory auditor or audit firm.

Competent authorities designated by Member States have a duty to forward information concerning the dismissal or resignation of statutory auditors or audit firms during engagement, along with an adequate explanation of the reasons for such dismissal or resignation. These authorities also have the power to access data related to statutory audits, obtain information related to statutory audits, carry out on-site inspections, refer matters for criminal prosecution, request experts to carry out verifications or investigations, and take administrative measures and impose sanctions, but only in relation to statutory auditors and audit firms carrying out statutory audits of public-interest entities and related parties.

Member States and competent authorities may delegate tasks to other authorities or bodies, and colleges established with participation of competent authorities may facilitate the exercise of tasks related to statutory audits of public-interest entities. Competent authorities are also required to cooperate with each other with regard to quality assurance reviews, investigations, and on-site inspections, and may request assistance from another competent authority and access information, except where this would breach national security rules or have an adverse effect on sovereignty, security, or public order. Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure effective financial market supervision and high-quality statutory audits of public-interest entities, while also providing for cooperation and coordination among competent authorities.

Regulation (EU) No 537/2014 applies to statutory audits of public-interest entities, aiming to ensure that these audits are of adequate quality and are carried out by statutory auditors and audit firms subject to stringent requirements. The regulation applies to statutory auditors and audit firms carrying out statutory audits of public-interest entities, although Member States may exempt cooperatives, savings banks, and similar entities, as well as their subsidiaries or legal successors, under certain conditions, provided that the principles of independence are complied with. 

Statutory auditors and audit firms are prohibited from providing non-audit services to the audited entity, its parent undertaking, or its controlled undertakings. Before accepting or continuing an engagement for a statutory audit, a statutory auditor or an audit firm must assess and document compliance with certain requirements. Additionally, statutory auditors or audit firms have a duty to report any information concerning the public-interest entity that may bring about a material breach of laws, regulations, or administrative provisions, a material threat or doubt concerning the continuous functioning of the entity, or a refusal to issue an audit opinion to the competent authorities supervising the public-interest entity or the competent authority responsible for oversight of the statutory auditor or audit firm.

Competent authorities designated by Member States have various responsibilities, including quality assurance, market monitoring, and transparency, as well as supervisory and investigatory powers necessary for the exercise of their functions under the Regulation. They must also forward information concerning the dismissal or resignation of statutory auditors or audit firms during engagement, along with an adequate explanation of the reasons. The regulation also facilitates cooperation between competent authorities, allowing them to request assistance from another competent authority and access information, except where this would breach national security rules or have an adverse effect on sovereignty, security, or public order.

The regulation applies to a wide range of entities and individuals, including statutory auditors and audit firms, competent authorities, persons involved in the activities of statutory auditors and audit firms, audited public-interest entities, their affiliates, and related third parties, as well as third parties to whom statutory auditors and audit firms have outsourced certain functions or activities. Colleges established with the participation of the competent authority of the home Member State and other competent authorities can also be formed to facilitate the exercise of tasks related to statutory audits of public-interest entities. Overall, the regulation aims to ensure the quality and independence of statutory audits, while also promoting cooperation and effective supervision among competent authorities.

The Regulation prohibits statutory auditors or audit firms from directly or indirectly providing prohibited non-audit services to the audited entity, its parent undertaking, or its controlled undertakings within the Union, as stated in Article 5.1 of Regulation 537/2014.

The Regulation requires the audit committee to submit a recommendation for the appointment of statutory auditors or audit firms, and competent authorities have supervisory and investigatory powers necessary for the exercise of their functions under the Regulation. summary:
This Regulation applies to statutory auditors and audit firms carrying out statutory audits of public-interest entities, as well as to public-interest entities themselves. It lays down requirements for the statutory audit of annual and consolidated financial statements of public-interest entities, rules on the organisation and selection of statutory auditors and audit firms, and rules on supervision. Statutory auditors and audit firms must assess and document compliance with certain requirements before accepting or continuing an engagement for a statutory audit of a public-interest entity. They must also inform the audited entity and invite it to investigate if they suspect irregularities, including fraud, and inform authorities if the entity does not investigate. Additionally, they have the right to request an exemption from certain requirements under specific conditions.

Statutory auditors and audit firms carrying out statutory audits of public-interest entities are required to make public an annual transparency report within four months after the end of each financial year. The report must be published on their website and kept available for at least five years, and they must communicate to competent authorities that the report has been published or updated. The report must include a description of the auditor's or firm's legal structure and ownership, network and members, governance structure, internal quality control system, quality assurance review information, list of public-interest entities audited, statement on independence practices, statement on continuing education policy, information on partners' remuneration, and policy on rotation of key audit partners and staff.

Competent authorities, on the other hand, have certain obligations, including publishing annual activity reports, work programmes, reports on quality assurance systems, and aggregated information on inspection findings. They also have the power to access data, obtain information, carry out on-site inspections, refer matters for prosecution, request experts, and impose sanctions. Member States are required to designate competent authorities and inform the Commission of the designation, with separate arrangements applicable to overseas countries and territories.

The Regulation also provides for cooperation between competent authorities at Union level for quality assurance reviews, investigations, and on-site inspections. The Committee of European Auditing Oversight Bodies (CEAOB) assumes existing and ongoing tasks of the European Group of Audit Oversight Bodies (EGAOB) and contributes to cooperation with third countries. Competent authorities must ensure effective cooperation at Union level and may request assistance from other competent authorities. The Commission shall review and report on the operation and effectiveness of the system of cooperation. Colleges may be established for specific statutory auditors or audit firms, and total fees for non-audit services provided by a statutory auditor or audit firm to an audited entity are subject to certain conditions. Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure the quality and independence of statutory audits of public-interest entities, and to promote cooperation and effective supervision among competent authorities.

summary:
The Regulation concerns the exercise of the Union's rights for the application and enforcement of international trade rules, particularly in cases following the adjudication of trade disputes under the WTO Dispute Settlement Understanding and other international trade agreements. It applies to the Union and its Member States, who should ensure the application of commercial policy measures within their territories. The Regulation also applies to third countries, economic operators within the Union, and contracting authorities or entities within the Union. The Commission has the right to adopt implementing acts determining commercial policy measures to safeguard the Union's interests, including the suspension of tariff concessions, imposition of customs duties, quantitative restrictions, and suspension of concessions regarding public procurement.

The Union has the right to suspend concessions or other obligations under international trade agreements in certain cases, such as when a WTO member modifies concessions without compensatory adjustments. The Commission must determine commercial policy measures based on criteria including effectiveness, potential relief, alternative sources, administrative complexity, and international trade agreements. The Commission must also include thresholds and determine sectors for measures, and Member States must submit lists of contracting authorities or entities. Measures must be based on specified criteria and avoid disproportionate administrative complexity and costs, with exceptions possible for specific sectors or categories of goods or services.

The Commission has obligations to repeal or suspend implementing acts in certain circumstances, such as when a third country brings itself into compliance or a mutually satisfactory solution is reached. The Commission may also introduce amendments to commercial policy measures subject to certain conditions and procedures. The Regulation is subject to review, particularly as regards commercial policy measures, with the aim of envisaging additional measures suspending concessions or other obligations in the field of trade in services. The Commission must undertake extensive consultations with private stakeholders and public authorities and report its findings to the European Parliament and the Council. The supplier of information has the right to request confidentiality, and the Commission is empowered to adopt implementing acts in certain specific situations. Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure the effective application and enforcement of international trade rules and the protection of the Union's interests.

The Regulation sets out rules and procedures to ensure the effective and timely exercise of the Union's rights to suspend or withdraw concessions or other obligations under international trade agreements, particularly in cases of trade disputes, rebalancing of concessions, and modification of concessions. This Regulation applies to the Union, its economic operators, third countries, and their measures. The Union has the right to suspend or withdraw concessions or other obligations under international trade agreements, with the aim of inducing compliance of third countries with international trade rules. The Commission is responsible for adopting implementing acts that determine the appropriate commercial policy measures, which may include suspension of tariff concessions, imposition of customs duties, quantitative restrictions, and suspension of concessions regarding public procurement. 

These measures are determined based on criteria such as effectiveness, potential relief, alternative sources, administrative complexity, and international trade agreements. The Regulation applies to third countries, economic operators within the Union, contracting authorities or entities within the Union, and Member States. The Commission, economic operators, and Member States have obligations to determine measures based on specified criteria, include thresholds, and determine sectors for measures. Member States are also required to submit lists of contracting authorities or entities. 

The Commission has the right to enact commercial policy measures, suspend the application of implementing acts, and introduce amendments to commercial policy measures under certain conditions. These conditions include that the third country accords adequate and proportionate compensation, or that the third country brings itself into compliance, a mutually satisfactory solution is reached, a safeguard measure is withdrawn or expires, or adequate and proportionate compensation is accorded to the Union. The Commission's actions are subject to examination procedures. 

The Regulation also provides for the Commission to review its scope, particularly with regards to commercial policy measures, and to envisage additional measures suspending concessions or other obligations in the field of trade in services. The Commission is empowered to adopt implementing acts in specific situations and shall report its findings to the European Parliament and the Council. The Commission shall undertake extensive consultations with private stakeholders and public authorities, and the supplier of information has the right to request confidentiality. 

Implementing acts must meet certain conditions, including not exceeding the level authorized by the WTO Dispute Settlement Body, and the Union's action shall be substantially equivalent to the level of concessions or other obligations affected. Measures must be based on specified criteria, avoid disproportionate administrative complexity and costs, and exceptions may be determined for specific sectors or categories of goods or services. Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure the effective enforcement of international trade rules and the protection of the Union's interests in trade disputes.

summary:
The European Union has established a framework for sea operations, which includes provisions for the interception of vessels suspected of carrying persons intending to circumvent checks or engaged in smuggling migrants by sea. This framework applies to host Member States, neighboring participating Member States, and participating units. When intercepting vessels in the territorial sea, participating units must have reasonable grounds to suspect that the vessel is carrying persons intending to circumvent checks or engaged in smuggling migrants by sea, and must ensure that any measures taken are proportionate and necessary to achieve the objectives of the operation. Evidence confirming the suspicion must be found in order to take further measures.

The framework also applies to situations where vessels are intercepted on the high seas, in which case participating units may take measures to intercept the vessel subject to the authorization of the flag State. The host Member State must instruct the participating unit through the International Coordination Centre, and participating units must take measures that are proportionate and necessary to achieve the objectives of the operation.

In the event of a search and rescue situation, the operational plan for the sea operation must contain provisions for dealing with vessels or persons in uncertainty, alert, or distress, as well as modalities for the disembarkation of intercepted or rescued persons. Participating units have a duty to transmit information to the Rescue Coordination Centre and place themselves at its disposal in search and rescue situations, and must also inform the International Coordination Centre of contact with the Rescue Coordination Centre and the course of action taken.

Member States have an obligation to render assistance to any vessel or person in distress at sea, and may request deployment of European Border Guard Teams, technical and operational assistance, or emergency assistance in situations of urgent and exceptional pressure at their external border. Similarly, Member States subject to strong migratory pressure may request deployment of an asylum support team or emergency assistance.

In certain circumstances, participating units may need to communicate with non-participating Member States, and must inform the International Coordination Centre of such communication and the subsequent course of action. If a non-participating Member State does not give authorization for measures to be taken in its contiguous zone, Article 7(14) may apply. The framework also defines key terms, such as "vessel" and "stateless vessel", and sets out dependencies on other EU regulations.

Overall, the framework aims to ensure that sea operations are conducted in a manner that is proportionate, necessary, and respectful of international law and human rights, while also providing support to Member States facing urgent and exceptional pressure at their external borders or strong migratory pressure.

summary:
The Regulation establishes rules for the surveillance of the external sea borders in the context of operational cooperation coordinated by the European Agency for the Management of Operational Cooperation at the External Borders of the Member States of the European Union. The scope of application is limited to border surveillance operations carried out by Member States at their external sea borders. Member States are responsible for the surveillance of their external sea borders, while the Agency is responsible for the coordination of operational cooperation between Member States in the field of management of the external borders, including border surveillance. Both the Agency and Member States must respect their respective obligations under international law during border surveillance operations at sea, including the principle of non-refoulement.

In cases where suspicion of smuggling of migrants is confirmed, participating units may take measures such as seizing vessels, apprehending persons, ordering vessels to alter course, and conducting vessels to a Member State. The Host Member State or participating Member State may authorise such measures, while the Flag State must be informed and authorise measures taken on the high seas. A Member State that is not participating in the sea operation must authorise measures taken in its contiguous zone.

The operational plan for a sea operation must contain provisions for search and rescue situations, including procedures for dealing with vessels or persons in uncertainty, alert, or distress, as well as modalities for the disembarkation of intercepted or rescued persons. Participating units in a sea operation have a duty to transmit information to the Rescue Coordination Centre and place themselves at its disposal in search and rescue situations. They must also inform the International Coordination Centre of contact with the Rescue Coordination Centre and the course of action taken. Member States must observe their obligation to render assistance to any vessel or person in distress at sea.

In situations of urgent and exceptional pressure at the external border, a Member State may request the deployment of European Border Guard Teams, technical and operational assistance, or emergency assistance. Similarly, a Member State subject to strong migratory pressure may request the deployment of an asylum support team or emergency assistance, provided that the pressure is placing urgent demands on reception facilities and asylum systems. Investigative and punitive measures are governed by national criminal law. Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure that border surveillance operations are carried out in a manner that respects international law and the rights of individuals, while also providing a framework for cooperation and assistance between Member States in managing their external sea borders.

summary:
The regulation applies to central securities depositories (CSDs) and their services, with definitions provided for terms used in the regulation. It applies to CSDs, third-country CSDs, competent authorities, and participants in securities settlement systems. A CSD must operate a securities settlement system and provide at least one other core service to be considered a CSD, while a third-country CSD must provide a similar service to a core service and perform at least one other core service.

When a CSD applies to provide services, the competent authority shall transmit information and consult with the authority referred to in Article 67 of Directive 2014/65/EU. CSDs have the right to establish CSD links with other CSDs. Third-country CSDs may be recognized to provide services in the EU if certain conditions are met, including a Commission decision, effective authorization, supervision, and oversight, cooperation arrangements between ESMA and responsible third-country authorities, and measures to comply with relevant national law.

CSDs must have publicly disclosed criteria for participation, and provide fair and open access, with transparent, objective, and non-discriminatory criteria. Participants have the right to complain to the competent authority, and the requesting participant has the right to a reasoned reply. CSDs must treat access requests promptly, and deny access only with written justification. The competent authority must examine complaints and provide a reasoned reply within a certain timeframe, such as one month for response to access requests.

Issuers of securities admitted to trading on regulated markets or MTFs or traded on trading venues have the right to arrange for securities to be recorded in any CSD established in any Member State, subject to certain conditions, including compliance with conditions referred to in Article 23. CSDs must treat requests promptly and non-discriminatorily, and provide full written reasons for refusal. The competent authority must examine complaints and provide a reasoned reply. However, a CSD may refuse to provide services based on a comprehensive risk assessment or non-provision of services.

CSDs that designate an authorised credit institution in accordance with Article 54 must ensure access to necessary information from the designated credit institution, and report infringements to the competent authority and other authorities, with the condition of protecting participants in securities settlement systems. Competent authorities must authorise and supervise designated credit institutions and CSDs, assess compliance with Article 59, and inform the CSD authority and other authorities of the results, with the condition of compliance with Regulation (EU) No 575/2013 and Directive 2013/36/EU. Overall, the regulation aims to establish a framework for the operation of CSDs and their services, with a focus on ensuring fair and open access, protecting participants, and promoting cooperation between authorities.

summary:
Directive 2014/65/EU applies to investment services and activities, and Article 17.5 specifically applies to applicant central securities depositories (CSDs) providing non-banking-type ancillary services and services referred to in point (2) of Article 4(1) of Directive 2014/65/EU. The directive applies to various entities, including applicant CSDs, CSDs, third-country CSDs, competent authorities, relevant authorities, and participants in securities settlement systems. 

Competent authorities have the obligation to transmit information and consult with the authority referred to in Article 67 of Directive 2014/65/EU. CSDs have the right to provide services and activities listed in Section A of Annex I, but they must comply with the requirements of Directive 2014/65/EU and Regulation (EU) No 600/2014. 

In the context of third-country CSDs, the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) may recognise a third-country CSD if certain conditions are met, including a Commission decision, effective authorisation, supervision, and oversight in the third country, cooperation arrangements between ESMA and responsible third-country authorities, and compliance with relevant national law of the Member State where services are provided. 

CSDs must comply with conditions for providing services, including authorisation that covers the services, a procedure for providing core services in another Member State, and conditions for starting services in the host Member State. Issuers of securities admitted to trading on regulated markets or multilateral trading facilities (MTFs) or traded on trading venues have the right to arrange for securities to be recorded in any CSD established in any Member State, and CSDs must treat such requests promptly and non-discriminatorily. 

However, a CSD may refuse to provide services based on a comprehensive risk assessment or non-provision of services. In such cases, the CSD must provide full written reasons for the refusal, and the competent authority must examine any complaint and provide a reasoned reply. 

Competent authorities, defined as public authorities or bodies recognised by national law and empowered to supervise institutions, have various responsibilities, including authorisation and supervision of CSDs, ensuring compliance with prudential requirements, and regular assessment and review of CSDs. CSDs, in turn, must ensure access to necessary information, report infringements to competent authorities, and comply with conditions for providing banking-type ancillary services. 

Regular review and evaluation by competent authorities, at least once a year, are required to ensure that CSDs comply with the relevant requirements. Overall, the directive and related regulations aim to establish a framework for the provision of investment services and activities, including the operation of CSDs, and to ensure that these entities comply with relevant requirements and conditions to maintain the stability and integrity of the financial system.

summary:
The Regulation aims to improve securities settlement in the European Union by establishing a set of common requirements for Central Securities Depositories (CSDs) operating securities settlement systems. It applies to CSDs and market participants in the European Union, including settlement internalisers, competent authorities, and ESMA. Settlement internalisers must report to competent authorities on a quarterly basis, while competent authorities must transmit information to ESMA and inform ESMA of potential risks. CSDs must operate securities settlement systems and comply with common requirements, and market participants must comply with uniform obligations regarding the settlement cycle and discipline.

CSDs are required to keep records and accounts to segregate securities of participants and their clients, and participants must offer clients a choice between omnibus client segregation and individual client segregation. CSDs must also provide individual client segregation for citizens and residents of, and legal persons established in, a Member State where required under national law, and publicly disclose levels of protection and costs associated with different levels of segregation. ESMA is responsible for maintaining a register of authorized CSDs, including services and financial instruments, and must conduct peer reviews of CSD supervision at least every three years.

The Regulation also establishes rules for the protection of securities of participants and their clients, including the requirement for CSDs to keep records and accounts to segregate securities. Issuers and CSDs have the freedom to issue in a CSD authorized in the Union, and CSDs must comply with organizational, conduct of business, and prudential requirements. Designated credit institutions must comply with specific prudential requirements, and CSDs must apply for authorizations and comply with the conditions for authorization.

Competent authorities are responsible for applying administrative sanctions and other measures to CSDs, designated credit institutions, and other responsible persons, and must transmit information to ESMA. The Regulation applies to CSDs, designated credit institutions, members of their management bodies, and other responsible persons, as well as MTFs that comply with certain criteria and third-country CSDs that intend to provide services on the basis of Article 25. The Commission is required to review the Regulation by 18 September 2019, and ESMA may develop draft regulatory technical standards and receive information from competent authorities. Overall, the Regulation aims to improve the safety and efficiency of securities settlement in the European Union by establishing common requirements and standards for CSDs and market participants.

summary:
This EU legal act applies to public collective proceedings, including interim proceedings, based on laws relating to insolvency for rescue, adjustment of debt, reorganisation, or liquidation. It includes proceedings where a debtor is divested of assets and an insolvency practitioner is appointed, assets and affairs are under court control, or a temporary stay of enforcement proceedings is granted. The act applies to debtors, including companies, legal persons, and individuals exercising independent business or professional activities, as well as other individuals, and to creditors, including those with claims arising from or in connection with the operation of an establishment. Insolvency practitioners appointed in insolvency proceedings and courts and authorities competent under national law are also subject to the act.

The courts of the Member State where the centre of the debtor's main interests is situated have the right to open insolvency proceedings. The courts of the Member State where secondary insolvency proceedings may be opened have the right to approve the termination or modification of contracts. To facilitate coordination of main, territorial, and secondary insolvency proceedings concerning the same debtor, courts are required to cooperate with each other, using any means considered appropriate, including coordination in the appointment of insolvency practitioners, communication of information, and coordination of administration and supervision of the debtor's assets and affairs. However, such cooperation shall not be incompatible with the rules applicable to each of the proceedings.

Insolvency practitioners appointed by a court with jurisdiction have the power to exercise all powers conferred by the law of the State of opening of proceedings in another Member State, as long as no other insolvency proceedings have been opened and no preservation measure to the contrary has been taken. However, these powers are subject to certain limitations. Insolvency practitioners are also required to communicate relevant information to each other.

In the context of group coordination proceedings, the court seised of a request to open such proceedings must give notice to insolvency practitioners of the request and the proposed coordinator, provided that the opening of proceedings is appropriate to facilitate effective administration of insolvency proceedings and no creditor is likely to be financially disadvantaged. Insolvency practitioners have the right to object to the inclusion of insolvency proceedings in group coordination proceedings and may request inclusion of proceedings in such proceedings under certain conditions.

Participating insolvency practitioners have the right to challenge decisions in group coordination proceedings, following the procedure under the law of the Member State where the group coordination proceedings were opened. Member States are required to provide information on their national legislation and procedures, within the framework of the European Judicial Network, for public availability. The act also provides for the application of its provisions to debtors in possession, with the same rights and obligations as other debtors.

The act includes a list of insolvency proceedings, which are defined as including bankruptcy, liquidation, and reorganization, among others. This list applies to various Member States and is subject to the definitions provided in the act. Overall, the act aims to facilitate the effective administration of insolvency proceedings and to provide a framework for cooperation and coordination among courts and insolvency practitioners in different Member States.

summary:
The Regulation aims to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of cross-border insolvency proceedings, applying to proceedings that meet the conditions set out in the Regulation, regardless of whether the debtor is a natural or legal person. It covers proceedings that promote the rescue of economically viable but distressed businesses and give a second chance to entrepreneurs, including those that provide for restructuring, debt discharge, or debt adjustment, and those that take place under court control or supervision. The Regulation also applies to procedures that grant a temporary stay on enforcement actions to facilitate restructuring negotiations, as well as collective proceedings that involve all or a significant part of the creditors, provided that the claims of non-involved creditors remain unaffected.

The Regulation applies to insolvency proceedings that meet the conditions set out in it, irrespective of whether the debtor is a natural person or a legal person, a trader or an individual. It applies to proceedings listed exhaustively in Annex A without further examination by the courts of another Member State. The law applicable to secondary insolvency proceedings is that of the Member State where the proceedings are opened. To facilitate the administration of insolvency proceedings, the Commission shall establish a decentralised system for interconnecting insolvency registers through implementing acts, which will include insolvency registers and the European e-Justice Portal, providing a search service in all official Union languages.

In main proceedings, an insolvency practitioner may give a unilateral undertaking regarding assets in another Member State to avoid secondary proceedings, which must specify factual assumptions, including asset value and realization options. A person honoring an obligation before publication of insolvency proceedings is presumed unaware of the proceedings, while a person honoring an obligation after publication is presumed aware of the proceedings. Courts with pending or opened insolvency proceedings shall cooperate to facilitate coordination, which may involve appointing an independent person or body, and cooperation methods include coordination in appointments.

The Regulation also provides for cooperation and communication between insolvency practitioners and courts in insolvency proceedings concerning members of a group of companies. Insolvency practitioners appointed in such proceedings have a duty to cooperate and communicate with courts and other insolvency practitioners, and may request information and assistance from courts. They must also consider coordinating administration and supervision of group members. summary:
This Regulation sets out the rules for the making available on the market and the free movement of subsystems and safety components for cableway installations, and contains rules on the design of these systems. It applies to cableway installations, subsystems, and safety components, as well as to Member States, economic operators, such as manufacturers, authorised representatives, importers, and distributors, and the person responsible for the cableway installation. 

Member States are required to determine procedures to ensure that cableway installations comply with the Regulation, while the person responsible for the cableway installation must submit a safety report, an EU declaration of conformity, and other documents. Manufacturers, on the other hand, must ensure that subsystems and safety components comply with the Regulation, and economic operators must comply with the Regulation. 

Subsystems and safety components can only be made available on the market if they comply with the Regulation. Manufacturers must design and manufacture these components in accordance with essential requirements and draw up technical documentation, carry out a conformity assessment procedure, and draw up an EU declaration of conformity, which must be accompanied by the CE marking. They must also keep the technical documentation and EU declaration of conformity for 30 years, ensure that series production remains in conformity with the Regulation, and carry out sample testing, investigate complaints, and keep a register of non-conforming subsystems or safety components. 

Manufacturers must also ensure that subsystems and safety components bear identification, such as a type, batch, or serial number, and provide instructions and safety information with the subsystem or safety component. If a subsystem or safety component is not in conformity, the manufacturer must take corrective measures and inform the competent national authorities of non-compliance and corrective measures. 

Conformity assessment bodies, which must be independent and impartial, carry out conformity assessments, while notified bodies inform the notifying authority of subcontracting and carry out conformity assessments. Economic operators must cooperate with market surveillance authorities, and manufacturers must take corrective measures if a subsystem or safety component presents a risk. 

In terms of procedures for conformity assessment, manufacturers of subsystems and safety components must lodge an application for unit verification with a notified body, operate an approved quality system, and draw up a written EU declaration of conformity. Notified bodies must examine technical documentation, carry out or have carried out appropriate examinations and tests, and issue a certificate of conformity. Economic operators must take measures to ensure that subsystems or safety components no longer present a risk. 

Overall, the Regulation aims to ensure the safety of cableway installations by setting out strict rules for the design, manufacture, and marketing of subsystems and safety components, and by requiring economic operators to comply with these rules and take corrective measures if necessary.

This regulation applies to new cableway installations, modifications requiring new authorisation, and subsystems or safety components for cableway installations, with certain exemptions, including historic, cultural, or heritage installations before 1 January 1986, agricultural or forestry purposes, mountain shelter or hut goods transport, leisure or amusement equipment, mining or industrial installations, and waterborne installations. The person responsible for a cableway installation, as determined by the Member State, must carry out a safety analysis, submit a safety report and documents, and ensure the installation complies with the conditions set out in the safety report. Member States are responsible for laying down authorisation procedures, ensuring subsystems and safety components comply with the regulation, and ensuring that a cableway installation remains in operation only if it complies with the conditions set out in the safety report.

Economic operators, including manufacturers, authorised representatives, importers, and distributors, must comply with the regulation, ensure subsystems and safety components meet essential requirements, and in the case of manufacturers, design and manufacture subsystems and safety components in accordance with essential requirements, draw up technical documentation, carry out conformity assessment procedures, and affix the CE marking. Manufacturers must also keep technical documentation and the EU declaration of conformity for 30 years and ensure series production remains in conformity. 

The regulation also establishes requirements for conformity assessment bodies, which must be established under national law of a Member State, independent and impartial, and not involved in the design, manufacture, construction, marketing, installation, use, or maintenance of subsystems or safety components. These bodies must ensure confidentiality, objectivity, and impartiality of conformity assessment activities, carry out conformity assessment activities with professional integrity and technical competence, and have the necessary personnel, procedures, and equipment.

Member States' national authorities are required to participate in the exchange of experience organised by the Commission, and the regulation lays down rules on penalties for infringements. The regulation applies to economic operators and Member States from 21 April 2018, with exceptions, and economic operators must comply with the regulation, while manufacturers, notified bodies, and authorised representatives have specific obligations, including lodging applications for unit verification, affixing CE marking and identification numbers, drawing up EU declarations of conformity, and keeping technical documentation and certificates of conformity. Notified bodies must examine technical documentation, carry out examinations and tests, and ensure that subsystems and safety components comply with the essential requirements.

summary:
The Regulation applies to the processing of personal data by public authorities and private bodies, but does not apply to processing activities for the purposes of prevention, investigation, detection, or prosecution of criminal offenses or execution of criminal penalties. Instead, Regulation (EC) No 45/2001 applies to the processing of personal data by the Union institutions, bodies, offices, and agencies. The Regulation also applies to controllers or processors not established in the Union, where processing activities are related to offering goods or services to data subjects in the Union, as well as to controllers or processors established in more than one Member State.

Member States may maintain or introduce more specific provisions to adapt the application of the rules of the Regulation. Controllers and processors have the obligation to implement technical and organisational measures to protect data subjects' rights, ensure data minimisation, and integrate necessary safeguards, taking into account the state of the art, cost of implementation, nature, scope, context, and purposes of processing, and the risks to the rights and freedoms of natural persons.

Controllers have the obligation to provide information to data subjects in a concise, transparent, intelligible, and easily accessible form, using clear and plain language. The Regulation also requires the designation of a data protection officer in certain circumstances, such as when the core activities of the controller or processor involve regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects on a large scale, or large-scale processing of special categories of data or personal data related to criminal convictions and offenses.

The transfer of personal data to third countries or international organizations is subject to certain conditions, including the need to protect the vital interests of the data subject or others when the data subject is incapable of giving consent. Appropriate safeguards must be in place for such transfers, which may include contractual clauses or provisions in administrative arrangements between public authorities or bodies, subject to authorization from the competent supervisory authority.

Supervisory authorities must act with complete independence in performing their tasks and exercising their powers. The Commission must assess the adequacy of the level of protection provided by third countries or international organizations, taking into account certain factors. In the context of processing for archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific or historical research purposes, or statistical purposes, technical and organisational measures must be in place to ensure respect for the principle of data minimisation, and derogations from certain rights may be provided by Union or Member State law under specific conditions.

Small enterprises or organisations with fewer than 250 persons may be exempt from record-keeping obligations, unless the processing is likely to result in a risk to data subjects' rights and freedoms, is not occasional, or includes special categories of data or personal data relating to criminal convictions and offences. Overall, the Regulation aims to protect the rights and freedoms of natural persons with regard to the processing of their personal data, while also providing for the free movement of personal data within the Union.

The European Union's legal act regarding Europol's processing of personal data aims to prevent and combat crimes while protecting the rights and freedoms of data subjects. Europol's objectives include ensuring operational effectiveness, and its activities are subject to parliamentary scrutiny by the European Parliament and national parliaments. The act applies to various entities, including Member States, Europol, national authorities, the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS), third countries and international organisations, and private parties. 

The EDPS is responsible for monitoring and ensuring the application of the provisions relating to the protection of fundamental rights and freedoms of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data by Europol. The EDPS has duties to hear and investigate complaints, conduct inquiries, and monitor and ensure the application of the Regulation. National supervisory authorities and Member States also play a role in ensuring the protection of personal data.

The processing of personal data by Europol is subject to certain conditions, including that it must be lawful and fair in relation to the data subjects. The right of access to data is restricted to those who need access to perform their tasks. Europol and Member States have an obligation to ensure data protection, and Europol must cooperate with the EDPS. 

In certain circumstances, personal data may be transferred to private parties not established in the Union or in a country with a cooperation agreement with Europol, provided that specific conditions are met, such as the protection of vital interests of the data subject or another person, or the prevention of an immediate and serious threat to public security. Europol's processing of personal data obtained from private parties is also subject to certain conditions, including that it must be received via a national unit in accordance with national law or via a contact point of a third country or international organisation with a cooperation agreement.

The European Parliament has the right to access sensitive non-classified information processed by Europol, and individuals whose data is processed by Europol have certain rights and protections. The act aims to balance the need to prevent and combat crimes with the need to protect the fundamental rights and freedoms of individuals, and its provisions are designed to ensure that the processing of personal data by Europol is lawful, fair, and transparent. Overall, the act provides a framework for the processing of personal data by Europol, while ensuring the protection of individual rights and freedoms.

This applies to Member States, Europol itself, national authorities, the European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS), third countries and international organisations, and private parties. The right of access to data is restricted to those who need it to perform their tasks, and the right to process personal data must be lawful and fair in relation to the data subjects. Europol and Member States have an obligation to ensure data protection, while Europol must also cooperate with the EDPS.

In terms of data transfer, an adequacy decision is a Commission decision that finds a third country or international organisation ensures an adequate level of protection. Such decisions are distinct from recommendations, proposals, and opinions. Transfers of personal data to third countries or international organisations may be allowed under certain conditions, such as when the transfer is in the interests of the data subject, with their consent or clear presumption of consent, or when it is absolutely necessary to prevent a crime, including terrorism. For private parties not established in the Union or in a country with a cooperation agreement or adequacy decision, transfers may be allowed if necessary to protect vital interests of the data subject or another person, to safeguard legitimate interests of the data subject, or to prevent an immediate and serious threat to public security.

The EDPS is responsible for hearing and investigating complaints, conducting inquiries, and monitoring the application of data protection rules. The EDPS must also keep national supervisory authorities fully informed and consult with them as necessary. summary:
Europol is established to support cooperation among law enforcement authorities in the Union, with tasks including supporting and strengthening action by the competent authorities of the Member States in preventing and combating serious crime, terrorism, and forms of crime affecting a common interest covered by a Union policy. Member States and Europol are required to cooperate with each other in the fulfilment of their respective tasks, with national units, competent authorities of the Member States, and Europol involved in the cooperation. 

Member States are responsible for the accuracy of data, keeping up to date the data they have transferred to Europol, and the legality of such data transfers, while Europol is responsible for the accuracy of data and for keeping up to date the data provided by other data suppliers or resulting from Europol's own analyses. Europol must ensure that data are processed fairly and lawfully, and are collected and processed for a specific purpose. 

In performing its tasks, Europol may process personal data obtained from private parties and may establish and maintain cooperative relations with Union bodies, third countries, international organisations, and private parties. Europol may exchange information with these entities, but shall ensure detailed records of personal data transfers and shall not process information obtained in violation of human rights. 

The European Data Protection Supervisor (EDPS) is responsible for monitoring and ensuring the application of the provisions of the Regulation relating to the protection of fundamental rights and freedoms of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data by Europol. The EDPS has duties to hear and investigate complaints, conduct inquiries, and monitor and ensure the application of the Regulation, and works with national supervisory authorities and Europol to protect the rights of data subjects. 

The Regulation applies to the processing of personal data by Europol and is binding in its entirety and directly applicable in Member States in accordance with the Treaties. It applies from 1 May 2017, with exceptions for certain articles that apply from 13 June 2016. The Regulation was adopted on 11 May 2016 and references several other EU acts, including Council Decisions and Regulations. Overall, the Regulation aims to support cooperation among law enforcement authorities while protecting the fundamental rights and freedoms of natural persons, particularly with regard to the processing of personal data.

summary:
The regulation applies to sales of vessels from non-market-economy countries, aiming to determine injury to the Union industry caused by injuriously priced vessels. It applies to the builder of any injuriously priced vessel, as well as buyers of vessels, including persons or companies that acquire an ownership interest in a vessel. The regulation also applies to natural or legal persons, associations, and the Union industry, including Member States, the Commission, and Contracting Parties. 

The parties to the investigation shall be informed of the market-economy third country envisaged and shall be given 10 days to comment. The buyer has the right to acquire an ownership interest in a vessel, including by way of lease or long-term bareboat charter. The normal value of a vessel shall be determined on the basis of the price or constructed value in a market-economy third country, or the price from such a third country to other countries, including the Union. However, the regulation does not apply to an ownership interest created or acquired solely for the purpose of providing security for a normal loan.

A complaint may be submitted to the Commission or a Member State, and the complainant has the obligation to provide evidence. The Commission has the right to examine the accuracy and adequacy of the evidence, and the complaint must be in writing and submitted within 6 or 9 months, depending on the circumstances. The Commission may initiate an investigation without a written complaint and has the right to request information and conduct investigations. Interested parties have the right to be heard, inspect information, and request disclosure of details underlying essential facts and considerations.

The investigation shall be conducted at the Union level, covering both injurious pricing and injury, and determinations must be checked against independent sources where practicable. The Commission shall give due regard to time limits of the investigation and ensure that final disclosure is given in writing, with due regard to protecting confidential information, at least 1 month before a definitive decision. Representations made after disclosure must be received within at least 10 days. The regulation also provides for special rules in agreements between the Union and third countries, which may take precedence over the general provisions of the regulation. Overall, the regulation aims to provide a framework for investigating and addressing injuriously priced vessels from non-market-economy countries, while also protecting the rights and interests of all parties involved.

summary:
The regulation aims to impose an injurious pricing charge on the builder of any injuriously priced vessel whose sale to a buyer other than a buyer of the country in which the vessel originates causes injury. This regulation applies to sales of vessels from non-market-economy countries and defines principles and definitions for injurious pricing. The regulation is intended to protect the Union industry from material injury caused by sales at less than normal value. 

The regulation applies to the builder of any injuriously priced vessel, as well as to sales from non-market-economy countries and the Union industry. Natural or legal persons, associations not having legal personality acting on behalf of the Union industry, Member States, the Commission, and Union producers capable of building the like vessel are all subject to the regulation. Authorities of a Contracting Party also have roles and obligations under the regulation.

Parties to an investigation have the right to be informed of the market-economy third country envisaged and to comment within 10 days. The buyer has the right to acquire an ownership interest in the vessel. The Union industry has the right to be protected from material injury caused by sales at less than normal value. Complainants have the right to submit a complaint to the Commission or a Member State, and the Commission has an obligation to send Member States a copy of any complaint it receives. Member States have an obligation to forward complaints to the Commission.

The Commission, acting in accordance with the examination procedure, may impose an injurious pricing charge if facts show injurious pricing and injury caused thereby. The amount of the charge is equal to the margin of injurious pricing established, and payment is due within 180 days of notification, with possible extension if payment within 180 days would render the shipbuilder insolvent or incompatible with judicially supervised reorganisation. 

The Commission may initiate an investigation without a written complaint if it decides, based on sufficient evidence of injurious pricing, injury, causal link, and Union industry criteria.
