summary:
The European Security and Defence College (ESDC) is established to provide training and education activities in the field of the Common Security and Defence Policy (CSDP) and the Common Foreign and Security Policy (CFSP). The ESDC has the necessary legal capacity to fulfill its tasks and meet its objectives, and its structure includes a Steering Committee, an Executive Academic Board, a Head, and a Secretariat. The Steering Committee, composed of one representative appointed by each Member State, has decision-making power and is responsible for overall coordination and direction of ESDC training and education activities. The Board, composed of senior representatives from civilian and military institutes and other actors identified by Member States, is responsible for ensuring the quality and coherence of ESDC training and education activities.

The ESDC shall organise and conduct training and education activities in the field of CSDP, support relations between institutes engaged in the network, and provide support to the management of training and education in the field of conflict prevention, civilian crisis management, and Security Sector Reform initiatives. The ESDC shall also maintain relationships with relevant actors in the field of Freedom, Security and Justice, Development and Cooperation, and International Organisations. The ESDC is open to participation by nationals of all Member States and acceding States, as well as nationals of countries that are candidates for accession to the Union and other third States and organisations. Participants include civilian, diplomatic, police, and military personnel, experts, and representatives of international organisations, non-governmental organisations, academic institutions, and the media.

The Head of the ESDC is the sole legal representative and is responsible for financial and administrative management, while the Secretariat assists the Head and provides support to the Steering Committee, Board, and institutes. The ESDC staff consist of seconded staff, national experts, and contracted staff, and are obligated to follow rules and regulations. The Steering Committee makes decisions on the number of ESDC staff and budget. The ESDC has the right to apply for research and other projects in the field of CFSP and has the right to receive an annual or multi-annual contribution from the general budget of the European Union. The ESDC is also obligated to report to the Steering Committee and to follow the rules and regulations applicable to it. The European Union Institute for Security Studies (EUISS) shall cooperate with the ESDC and provide expertise and knowledge-gathering capabilities for ESDC training activities. The establishment of the ESDC repeals Decision (CFSP) 2016/2382.

summary:
The European Year of Rail, designated as the year 2021, aims to promote and support efforts to increase the share of passengers and freight moving by rail. The general objective is to encourage and support these efforts, with specific objectives including promoting rail as a sustainable, innovative, interconnected, and intermodal mode of transport, highlighting its European and cross-border dimension, and enhancing its contribution to the Union's economy and society. Additionally, the European Year of Rail seeks to promote rail as an element in relations between the Union and its neighboring countries, build on rail's power to stimulate the collective imagination, promote the attractiveness of railway professions, and promote the key role of railways in international passenger transport and the development of a Union night train network.

The European Year of Rail will be promoted through various activities and initiatives, including promoting sustainable tourism, end-to-end mobility, and the single European railway area. These measures will apply at Union, national, regional, or local levels, involving partnerships or individual entities, and will engage citizens, businesses, public authorities, national, regional, and local authorities, civil society, businesses, and schools. The initiatives will promote public awareness of rail's potential in sustainable tourism, its key role in sustainable end-to-end mobility, and stimulate discussion on modernizing rolling stock and developing railway infrastructure, contributing to the implementation of the Fourth Railway Package.

The Commission will play a key role in the European Year of Rail, considering initiating studies, informing the European Parliament and the Council, convening meetings, and coordinating the European Year. Member States will be responsible for organizing participation at the national level, ensuring coordination of relevant activities, and appointing national contact persons. The Commission will also cooperate with international organizations and submit a report on the implementation and results of the European Year. Stakeholders, including youth organizations, communities, and organizations representing persons with disabilities and reduced mobility, will be involved in the European Year through regular stakeholder meetings and potential calls for proposals and projects, subject to budget availability.

The European Year of Rail will be coordinated at Union and national levels, creating synergies between Union programs and initiatives. The Commission will ensure that measures are closely coordinated with ongoing activities promoting rail. The European Year will promote awareness of the single European railway area and involve coordination at Union and national levels. Overall, the European Year of Rail aims to promote rail transport and achieve its objectives through a coordinated and inclusive approach, engaging various stakeholders and promoting the benefits of rail for the Union's economy, society, and environment.

summary:
The European Year of Rail, designated as the year 2021, aims to promote and support efforts to increase the share of passengers and freight moving by rail. The general objective is to encourage and support these efforts, with specific objectives including promoting rail as a sustainable, innovative, interconnected, and intermodal mode of transport, highlighting its European and cross-border dimension, and enhancing its contribution to the Union's economy and society. Additionally, the European Year of Rail seeks to promote rail as an element in relations between the Union and its neighboring countries, build on rail's power to stimulate the collective imagination, promote the attractiveness of railway professions, and promote the key role of railways in international passenger transport and the development of a Union night train network.

The European Year of Rail will be promoted through various activities and initiatives, including promoting sustainable tourism, end-to-end mobility, and the single European railway area. These measures will apply at Union, national, regional, or local levels, involving partnerships or individual entities, and will engage citizens, businesses, public authorities, national, regional, and local authorities, civil society, businesses, and schools. The initiatives will promote public awareness of rail's potential in sustainable tourism, its key role in sustainable end-to-end mobility, and stimulate discussion on modernizing rolling stock and developing railway infrastructure, contributing to the implementation of the Fourth Railway Package.

The Commission will play a key role in the European Year of Rail, considering initiating studies, informing the European Parliament and the Council, convening meetings, and coordinating the European Year. Member States will be responsible for organizing participation at the national level, ensuring coordination of relevant activities, and appointing national contact persons. The Commission will also cooperate with international organizations and submit a report on the implementation and results of the European Year. Stakeholders, including youth organizations, communities, and organizations representing persons with disabilities and reduced mobility, will be involved in the European Year through regular stakeholder meetings and potential calls for proposals and projects, subject to budget availability.

The European Year of Rail will be coordinated at Union and national levels, creating synergies between Union programs and initiatives. The Commission will ensure that measures are closely coordinated with ongoing activities promoting rail. The European Year will promote awareness of the single European railway area and involve coordination at Union and national levels. Overall, the European Year of Rail aims to promote rail transport and achieve its objectives through a coordinated and inclusive approach, engaging various stakeholders and promoting the benefits of rail for the Union's economy, society, and environment.

summary:
The Regulation establishes fishing opportunities in Union waters and for Union fishing vessels in non-Union waters, applying to Union fishing vessels, third-country vessels in Union waters, and recreational fisheries where expressly referred to. Member States have the right to fishing opportunities allocated to them and are obligated to ensure that fishing mortality does not exceed the FMSY point value. They must also record catches and fishing effort, notify data on exhaustion of fishing opportunities, and land all catches, including by-catches. 

Specific measures are in place for certain fisheries, such as European seabass fisheries, where Union fishing vessels and commercial fisheries from shore are subject to prohibitions on fishing in certain areas, with derogations for vessels with recorded catches of European seabass between 1 July 2015 and 30 September 2016. Catch limits for European seabass are not transferable between vessels or from one month to another, and Member States must report catches per type of gear to the Commission. Recreational fisheries for European seabass are limited to catch-and-release fishing in certain periods, with a limit of 2 specimens per fisherman per day in other periods.

In pelagic fisheries, Member States that actively exercised pelagic fisheries in the SPRFMO Convention Area in 2007, 2008, or 2009 may fish for pelagic stocks in accordance with total allowable catches set out in Annex IH, with a limit on the total gross tonnage of vessels. They must also send lists of vessels, records, and catch reports to the Commission. For tropical tunas and swordfish/albacore in the IOTC Area of Competence, Member States must limit the number of Union fishing vessels and capacity in gross tonnage, with conditions for reallocating vessels between fisheries.

Geographical zones are defined for specific fishing areas, with zone boundaries established by latitudes and the coasts of Ireland and the United Kingdom. Fishing quotas are allocated only to vessels participating in sentinel fishery for data collection, valid from 1 July 2020 to 30 June 2021, and are subject to amendment after scientific advice. Fishing is exclusively for by-catches, with no directed fisheries permitted, and special conditions apply to fishing in specific areas. Up to 5% or 10% of the quota may be fished in specific areas, and by-catches of certain species are counted against the quota. Overall, the Regulation aims to establish a framework for sustainable fishing practices, with specific rules and limitations to ensure the long-term conservation of fish stocks.

summary:
This Regulation establishes fishing opportunities for Union fishing vessels in Union waters and certain non-Union waters, applying to specific fish stocks and groups of fish stocks. It applies to Union fishing vessels and Member States, which have the right to fishing opportunities allocated to them. Member States must ensure that fishing mortality from their fleets and recreational fishermen does not exceed the FMSY point value, and Union fishing vessels must comply with Council Regulation (EC) No 1224/2009. Additionally, Member States have an obligation to land all catches, including by-catches, in mixed fisheries.

Fishing opportunities are fixed taking into account the change from fixing fishing opportunities that reflect landings to fixing fishing opportunities that reflect catches. The landing obligation applies fully from 1 January 2019. Specific conditions and exceptions apply to certain fisheries, such as the European seabass fishery, where fishing is prohibited in certain areas, except for Union fishing vessels with recorded catches of European seabass between 1 July 2015 and 30 September 2016, which are allowed to fish in certain areas with specific gear and limits. Catch limits for European seabass are not transferable between vessels or from one month to another, and Member States must report catches of European seabass per type of gear to the Commission.

In the context of pelagic fisheries, Member States that actively exercised pelagic fisheries in the SPRFMO Convention Area in 2007, 2008, or 2009 may fish for pelagic stocks in that area in accordance with TACs set out in Annex IH, subject to a limit on the total gross tonnage of vessels. They must also send lists of vessels, records, and catch reports to the Commission by the 5th day of the following month. Furthermore, Member States must limit the number of Union fishing vessels and capacity in gross tonnage for tropical tunas and swordfish/albacore in the IOTC Area of Competence, and may reallocate vessels between fisheries under certain conditions.

The Regulation also establishes conditions for fishing effort regimes, including the requirement that stocks of non-target species be within safe biological limits. Vessels may transit across a geographical area subject to a fishing effort regime if they have no fishing authorization to operate in that area or have notified competent authorities of their intention to transit. Additionally, vessels may choose not to count certain activities, such as non-fishing related activities or assisting another vessel in emergency, against the maximum allowable fishing effort. Zone boundaries are also defined, with reduced and increased zones bounded by specific geographical coordinates.

Recreational fisheries are also subject to specific rules, including catch-and-release fishing only in certain periods and a limit of 2 specimens per fisherman per day in certain periods. Overall, the Regulation aims to establish a framework for sustainable fishing practices, ensuring that fishing activities are managed in a way that prevents overfishing and promotes the long-term conservation of fish stocks. By setting out specific rules and conditions for different types of fisheries, the Regulation seeks to balance the needs of the fishing industry with the need to protect the marine environment and ensure the sustainability of fish stocks.

summary:
This legal act fixes fishing opportunities for certain fish stocks and groups of fish stocks in Union waters and non-Union waters for Union fishing vessels. It applies to fishing opportunities in Union waters and to Union fishing vessels in certain non-Union waters. The act is relevant to Union fishing vessels and Member States, which have the right to allocate fishing opportunities. However, they are also under an obligation to land all catches, including by-catches from certain stocks, and to take appropriate measures to ensure that fishing mortality from their fleets and recreational fishermen does not exceed the maximum sustainable yield.

In cases where fish stocks are below the biomass limit, such as cod and whiting in the Celtic Sea, remedial measures are to be taken. There are also exceptions to fishing effort limits, which apply from 1 February 2020, and specific dates of application for certain provisions concerning particular regions. Additionally, there are unallocated total allowable catches for certain species, such as the Southern Atlantic blue shark.

The act also prohibits European eel fisheries in Union waters of the ICES area and brackish waters, with Member States required to determine a 3-month period for prohibition between 1 August 2020 and 28 February 2021, and communicate this to the Commission by 1 June 2020. Furthermore, the act regulates quota transfers between Member States, allowing them to transfer quota and fishing authorisations, provided they notify the Commission and do not exceed the total fishing authorisations.

For pelagic fisheries, Member States that actively exercised these fisheries in the SPRFMO Convention Area in 2007, 2008, or 2009 may fish for pelagic stocks in this area in accordance with the total allowable catches set out in Annex IH, subject to a limit on the total gross tonnage of vessels and requirements to send lists of vessels, records, and catch reports to the Commission. The act also limits the fishing capacity for tropical tunas and swordfish/albacore in the IOTC Area of Competence, with conditions for reallocating vessels between fisheries.

The act sets out specific quotas for certain species, such as mackerel, with quotas allocated to Spain, France, Portugal, and the Union as a whole, and special conditions for catches in certain zones. For example, in zone 8c, 9, and 10, and Union waters of CECAF 34.1.1, the quotas are 34,708 for Spain, 230 for France, 7,174 for Portugal, and 42,112 for the Union. There are also quotas for mackerel in Norwegian waters of 2a and 4a, and for common sole in zone 3a and Union waters of Subdivisions 22-24, with quotas allocated to Denmark, Germany, the Netherlands, and Sweden. Overall, the act aims to regulate fishing activities in Union waters and non-Union waters to ensure the sustainable management of fish stocks.

summary:
The European instrument for temporary support to mitigate unemployment risks in an emergency, known as SURE, aims to address the impact of the COVID-19 outbreak and respond to its socio-economic consequences. The instrument provides financial assistance to Member States experiencing severe economic disturbance caused by the COVID-19 outbreak, with the primary goal of supporting short-time work schemes or similar measures, as well as some health-related measures. This assistance is available to all Member States of the European Union, excluding the United Kingdom due to the terms of the Withdrawal Agreement, and the UK is not liable for contingent financial liabilities arising from financial assistance under this Regulation.

Member States have the right to request financial assistance if their actual and possibly planned public expenditure has suddenly and severely increased due to national measures related to short-time work schemes and similar measures. The Union has the obligation to provide financial assistance in the form of loans to eligible Member States, and the Commission has the obligation to assess every six months whether exceptional circumstances causing severe economic disturbances still exist and report to the Council. Beneficiary Member States shall use financial assistance primarily in support of their national short-time work schemes or similar measures.

The financial assistance is conditional on a sudden and severe increase in actual and planned public expenditure intended to mitigate the direct economic, social, and health-related effects of the COVID-19 outbreak. The instrument becomes available after all Member States contribute at least 25% of the maximum amount, with contributions proportional to their gross national income. The availability period ends on 31 December 2022, but can be extended by six months if the severe economic disturbance continues, subject to a Council decision on a proposal from the Commission.

The Commission is responsible for administering the loans and concluding agreements with contributing Member States, who provide irrevocable, unconditional, and on-demand guarantees. The Commission also informs the Council when the instrument becomes available and forwards reports to the European Parliament, Council, Economic and Financial Committee, and Employment Committee every six months, including information on the use of financial assistance, outstanding amounts, and repayment schedule. Beneficiary Member States are required to inform the Commission about the implementation of planned public expenditure every six months, and loan agreements must contain necessary provisions regarding controls and audits. Overall, the SURE instrument provides a vital safety net for Member States to mitigate the impact of the COVID-19 outbreak on their economies and societies.

The European instrument for temporary support to mitigate unemployment risks in an emergency, known as SURE, has been established to address the impact of the COVID-19 outbreak and its socio-economic consequences. The instrument aims to provide financial assistance to Member States experiencing or threatened with severe economic disturbances caused by the pandemic. SURE applies to all Member States of the European Union, except the United Kingdom, which is not liable for contingent financial liabilities arising from financial assistance under this Regulation due to the terms of the Withdrawal Agreement.

The Union has the right to provide financial assistance in the form of loans to Member States, and Member States have the right to request such assistance. The Commission has the obligation to assess every six months whether the exceptional circumstances causing severe economic disturbances in Member States still exist. The Council, when deciding on the amount of a loan, must consider the existing and expected needs of the requesting Member State. The financial assistance provided by SURE is primarily intended for short-time work schemes or similar measures, and, as an ancillary, for some health-related measures.

Member States may request Union financial assistance under SURE if their actual and possibly planned public expenditure has suddenly and severely increased due to national measures related to short-time work schemes and similar measures. Beneficiary Member States are required to use the financial assistance primarily in support of their national short-time work schemes or similar measures. The Instrument becomes available after all Member States contribute at least 25% of the maximum amount, with contributions proportional to their gross national income. The availability period ends on 31 December 2022, but can be extended by six months if the severe economic disturbance continues.

The Commission is responsible for administering the loans and must conclude agreements with contributing Member States, who provide irrevocable, unconditional, and on-demand guarantees. The Commission may make additional calls on guarantees if a Member State fails to honour a call, and calls on guarantees are made pro rata to Member States' gross national income. The loan agreement must contain necessary provisions regarding controls and audits, and beneficiary Member States must inform the Commission about the implementation of planned public expenditure every six months.

The Commission is also obligated to forward a report to the European Parliament, Council, Economic and Financial Committee, and Employment Committee every six months, which includes the use of financial assistance, outstanding amounts, and repayment schedule. The report may also include a proposal for a Council implementing decision to extend the period of availability of the Instrument. The availability of the Instrument can be extended for an additional six months if the Commission concludes that the severe economic disturbance caused by the COVID-19 outbreak continues to exist, and the Council decides on a proposal from the Commission. Overall, SURE provides a vital safety net for Member States to mitigate the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on their economies and societies.

summary:
The European Union Recovery Instrument is designed to support recovery in the aftermath of the COVID-19 crisis, financing measures to tackle the adverse economic consequences of the crisis or the immediate funding needs to avoid a re-emergence of the crisis. This Instrument applies to all Member States, with a particular focus on supporting small and medium-sized enterprises. The Instrument provides support in the form of non-repayable support, loans, and provisioning for budgetary guarantees, with Member States having the right to receive support for specific measures and the Union having the obligation to provide support in accordance with its objectives.

The Instrument is financed up to EUR 750,000 million in 2018 prices, with the financing based on the empowerment provided for in Article 5 of the Own Resources Decision, and adjusted by a 2% per year deflator for implementation under specific Union programmes. The allocation of funds includes up to EUR 384,400 million for non-repayable and repayable support, up to EUR 360,000 million in loans to Member States, and up to EUR 5,600 million for provisioning for budgetary guarantees. Specific allocations are also made for structural and cohesion programmes, recovery and economic and social resilience, civil protection, research and innovation, and climate-neutral economy transitions.

The Union programmes referred to in the Instrument include those supporting investment operations in the field of Union internal policies, development in rural areas, and other specific areas. The Commission or its executive agencies shall enter into legal commitments for support, and decisions on granting loans shall be adopted by the Commission. The Union shall grant budgetary guarantees, with counterparts required to approve financial operations corresponding to at least 60% of the budgetary guarantees by 31 December 2022.

Support under the Instrument is subject to strict compliance with its objectives, and commitment appropriations resulting from external assigned revenue should not be automatically carried over beyond the end of the year. Commitment appropriations are made available automatically up to the respective amounts, and legal commitments for support must be entered into by 31 December 2023. The Union shall honour its obligations towards third parties, and the Commission shall submit a report on the progress achieved in the implementation of the Instrument. Payments related to legal commitments shall be made by 31 December 2026, with exceptions, and technical and administrative assistance costs shall be financed from the Union budget.

summary:
The European Institute of Innovation and Technology (EIT) is subject to a Decision that adopts a Strategic Innovation Agenda (SIA) for 2021-2027, which sets out priority fields, strategy, key actions, and assesses the EIT's social, economic, and environmental impact. This Decision applies to the EIT and its Knowledge and Innovation Communities (KICs) in compliance with Regulation (EU) 2021/695, as well as Higher Education Institutions (HEIs) and Small and Medium-sized Enterprises (SMEs). The EIT's strategy for 2021-2027 aims to support innovation ecosystems, tackle global and societal challenges, and promote entrepreneurship, in line with Horizon Europe and other Union programs. 

The EIT has the obligation to implement the SIA 2021-2027 in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2021/819, and the Decision repeals Decision No 1312/2013/EU with effect from 1 January 2021. The EIT shall support KICs, foster innovation and entrepreneurial skills, create new solutions, and ensure synergies within Horizon Europe. It shall also promote and support a new generation of entrepreneurs, contribute to closing the entrepreneurial gender gap, and stimulate the development of innovation ecosystems. The EIT is required to identify, codify, share, and disseminate learning and good practices from EIT-funded activities, and develop its role as an innovation institute to detect, analyze, codify, share, and ensure the take-up of innovative practices.

The EIT shall engage with Member State authorities, the Commission, and the European Parliament, and provide strengthened operational support to KICs. The EIT evaluations shall assess the effectiveness, efficiency, relevance, coherence, and Union added value of EIT activities, including those managed through KICs. These evaluations shall contribute to the development of framework conditions for transforming ideas into technological developments and social innovation. The Commission shall carry out periodic independent evaluations of EIT activities, while the EIT shall conduct interim reviews of KICs' performance and activities. The Governing Board shall decide on whether to extend the partnership agreement beyond the first seven years, and the EIT shall make the results of interim reviews and evaluations publicly available.

The Decision enters into force on the day of its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union. The EIT shall ensure the implementation of KICs in compliance with relevant requirements and develop international cooperation and global outreach activities. Stakeholders, including those in areas where women are underrepresented, such as information and communications technologies, science, technology, engineering, and mathematics, shall be supported by the EIT. Overall, the Decision aims to support the EIT in achieving its objectives and contributing to the development of innovation ecosystems in the European Union.

summary:
The European Institute of Innovation and Technology (EIT) is adopting a Strategic Innovation Agenda (SIA) for 2021-2027, which sets out priority fields, strategy, key actions, and assesses the EIT's social, economic, and environmental impact. This Decision applies to the EIT and its Knowledge and Innovation Communities (KICs) in compliance with Regulation (EU) 2021/695. The EIT has the obligation to implement the SIA 2021-2027 in accordance with Regulation (EU) 2021/819, and the Decision repeals Decision No 1312/2013/EU with effect from 1 January 2021.

The EIT shall promote collaboration between KICs and smart specialisation platforms to facilitate synergies between EIT resources, Cohesion Policy Funds, and other Union, national, and regional programmes. It shall also contribute to the necessary innovation efforts by providing a coherent response to the COVID-19 crisis and improve its monitoring system by introducing a reporting and monitoring framework. KICs shall seek collaboration with the InvestEU Advisory Hub, contribute to the InvestEU Portal, and cooperate with the Enterprise Europe Network (EEN) and its Sector Groups. The EIT and its KICs shall work with various Union initiatives and partnerships and involve microenterprises, SMEs, start-ups, students, researchers, entrepreneurs, and employees in their activities.

Two new KICs are proposed: Cultural and Creative Sectors and Industries (CCSI) and Water, Marine and Maritime Sectors and Ecosystems (WMM). The CCSI KIC is to be launched in 2022 or 2023, with a call for proposals in 2021 if feasible, while the WMM KIC is to be launched in 2026, with a call for proposals in 2025 and an ex-ante analysis by 2024. Other new KICs may be selected if additional budget allocations become available. The EIT is also to design and launch a pilot initiative to support innovation and entrepreneurial capacities of higher education institutions (HEIs) through KICs, starting in 2021, with activities including the exchange of best practices, development of action plans, and implementation of innovation capacity development plans.

The KIC on CCSI aims to empower network opportunities, collaboration, co-creation, and know-how transfer between education, research, business, public, and third-sector organisations within the cultural and creative sectors and with other sectors of society and the economy. The KIC on WMM will help address challenges in the water, marine, and maritime sectors with a holistic and integrated approach. These KICs will apply to relevant sectors, including education, research, business, public, and third-sector organisations, as well as research organisations, enterprises, and public authorities.

The Decision enters into force on the day of its publication in the Official Journal of the European Union. KICs have the right to seek technical support and assistance from the InvestEU Advisory Hub. Eligibility criteria for the pilot higher education initiative will ensure that the majority of funding goes to HEIs outside of KICs. Overall, the EIT's Strategic Innovation Agenda for 2021-2027 aims to promote innovation, entrepreneurship, and collaboration across various sectors, with a focus on addressing societal challenges and supporting economic growth.

summary:
The Agreement establishes a framework for a coordinated approach to transparent and ethical interest representation at the Union level, setting a high standard for activities carried out by interest representatives to influence policy or legislation, or decision-making processes of Union institutions. The scope of the Agreement includes activities of interest representatives, but excludes activities of public authorities of Member States, as well as certain activities and bodies, including intergovernmental organisations and churches. The Agreement applies to interest representatives, including natural or legal persons, formal or informal groups, associations, or networks, as well as signatory institutions, including the European Parliament, the Council of the European Union, and the European Commission. Other Union institutions, bodies, offices, and agencies, as well as Member States' permanent representations, may also apply the operating principles voluntarily.

Interest representatives have the right to engage in covered activities, but may be subject to conditionality, which requires registration in the register. Registrants have the right to be entered in the register if they meet the requirements and must operate in line with the Code of Conduct, which sets out rules and principles for registrants in their relations with Union institutions. The Code of Conduct applies to registrants operating in the EU and requires them to identify themselves, declare the interests and objectives they promote, and not obtain or try to obtain information or decisions dishonestly. Registrants must also cooperate sincerely and constructively with the Secretariat, which is responsible for monitoring registrations and evaluating registrants' ongoing eligibility.

The Secretariat has various obligations, including reporting, establishing guidelines, deciding on eligibility, providing support, and carrying out investigations. The Management Board, consisting of the Secretaries-General of the signatory institutions, has obligations including overseeing implementation, issuing instructions, determining priorities, and adopting the annual report. The Agreement aims to achieve an optimal level of data quality in the register, and the Secretariat and Management Board carry out tasks assigned to them by the Agreement. The signatory institutions have the obligation to implement the coordinated approach and set out covered activities, and the Agreement applies to applicants and registrants who carry out covered activities and observe the code of conduct. Overall, the Agreement provides a framework for transparent and ethical interest representation, ensuring that interest representatives operate in a responsible and accountable manner.

The Agreement establishes a framework for a coordinated approach to transparent and ethical interest representation, covering activities carried out by interest representatives to influence policy or legislation, or decision-making processes of Union institutions. The scope of the Agreement includes activities of interest representatives, but excludes activities of public authorities of Member States, associations and networks of public authorities, intergovernmental organisations, public authorities of third countries, and political parties, with certain exceptions applying to churches and religious associations or communities. The Agreement applies to interest representatives, including natural or legal persons, formal or informal groups, associations, or networks, as well as to the signatory institutions, including the European Parliament, the Council of the European Union, and the European Commission, and other Union institutions, bodies, offices, and agencies that voluntarily wish to apply the operating principles.

Interest representatives have the right to engage in covered activities, but may be subject to conditionality, which requires registration in the register. To register, applicants must carry out covered activities, observe the code of conduct, and provide information listed in Annex II, which will be published. Applicants may be requested to substantiate their eligibility and the accuracy of submitted information. Once an applicant's registration is activated, they become a registrant and must cooperate with the Secretariat during monitoring or investigations. Registrants must operate in line with the code of conduct, provide complete, up-to-date, accurate, and not misleading information, and respect the rules and standards of behavior applicable to them.

The Secretariat is set up to manage the functioning of the register, with the aim of achieving an optimal level of data quality. The Secretariat has various obligations, including reporting, establishing guidelines, deciding on eligibility, providing support, and carrying out investigations. The Management Board oversees the implementation of the Agreement, issues instructions, determines priorities, and adopts the annual report. The Agreement also provides that registrants have the right to be heard before any decision establishing ineligibility is taken and the right to request that an investigation be reopened. Overall, the Agreement aims to provide transparency and ensure that registrants behave ethically, and its provisions apply to registrants, signatory institutions, Union institutions, bodies, offices, and agencies, as well as members and former members of the European Parliament, the Commission, and the staff of the Union institutions.

summary:
The European Union has established a framework for transparent and ethical interest representation, which applies to the European Parliament, Council of the European Union, and European Commission. The objective of this framework is to promote interest representation that is transparent and ethical, and it sets a high standard for such representation at the Union level. This framework applies to various entities, including interest representatives, applicants, registrants, clients, intermediaries, and staff subject to the Staff Regulations of Officials of the European Union. Interest representatives have the right to engage in covered activities, while signatory institutions have the obligation to implement a coordinated approach on transparent and ethical interest representation.

The framework does not cover certain activities and bodies, such as public authorities, intergovernmental organisations, and churches. To be part of this framework, applicants and registrants must carry out covered activities and observe a code of conduct. Signatory institutions commit to the principle of conditionality, and the Management Board, consisting of the Secretaries-General of the signatory institutions, oversees the overall implementation of the Agreement. The Secretariat is responsible for monitoring registrations and evaluating registrants' ongoing eligibility.

Registrants have the right to be entered in the register if they meet the requirements, and they have the obligation to cooperate sincerely and constructively with the Secretariat. The Secretariat has various obligations, including reporting, establishing guidelines, deciding on eligibility, providing support, and carrying out investigations. The Management Board also has obligations, including overseeing implementation, issuing instructions, determining priorities, and adopting the annual report.

The framework also allows for the voluntary involvement of Member States' permanent representations, enabling them to notify the Management Board of measures taken to make certain activities targeting their permanent representations conditional upon registration in the register. These measures must be taken in accordance with national law. Additionally, registrants must provide specific information, including details about the person legally responsible for the entity, annual estimates of full-time equivalents for persons involved in covered activities, goals, remit, fields of interest, and geographical level of engagement.

The Secretariat is set up to manage the functioning of the register, with the aim of achieving an optimal level of data quality. The Management Board and Secretariat carry out tasks assigned to them by the Agreement, and the signatory institutions, as well as Union institutions, bodies, offices, and agencies, are also involved in the implementation of the framework. Overall, this framework establishes a coordinated approach to transparent and ethical interest representation, with clear rights and obligations for registrants, the Secretariat, and the Management Board, and allows for the involvement of Member States' permanent representations on a voluntary basis.

summary:
The Technical Support Instrument is designed to assist Member States in designing, developing, and implementing reforms in key economic and societal areas, including policy areas related to cohesion, competitiveness, education, productivity, research, and innovation. The instrument provides technical support for the implementation of reforms, preparation for euro area membership, and recovery and resilience plans, and establishes a framework for technical support, management modes, funding forms, and work programmes. The Technical Support Instrument applies to Member States, and national authorities, including public authorities at regional and local levels, and Member State organisations, are eligible for technical support.

Member States have the right to request technical support, and the Commission is obligated to provide technical support upon request. Member States are required to submit requests for technical support by 31 October, unless otherwise specified. Relevant stakeholders may be consulted by Member States before requesting technical support, and requests for technical support must identify policy areas and priorities. The Commission may provide guidance on the main elements to be included in the request and is obligated to provide guidance on requests for technical support.

The Commission implements the instrument in accordance with the Financial Regulation, and measures may be implemented directly or indirectly by the Commission or by persons or entities. Grants may be awarded to national authorities, European Investment Bank group, international organisations, public or private bodies and entities, with a co-financing rate for grants of up to 100% of eligible costs. Technical support may be provided with the cooperation of other Member State entities and international organisations, and special measures may be adopted in the event of unforeseen and duly justified grounds of urgency.

Work programmes set out the allocation, measures, and selection and award criteria for grants, with a limited part of the work programme, up to 30% of the yearly allocation, reserved for special measures. Resources allocated to Member States under shared management may be transferred to the instrument for technical support. The Commission is required to report on the implementation of the Regulation, with annual reports submitted to the European Parliament and Council, including information on requests for support from Member States, analysis of application of criteria for support, cooperation and support plans, special measures adopted, implementation of support measures, and communication activities carried out by the Commission.

In addition to annual reports, the Commission must submit a mid-term evaluation report by 20 February 2025, assessing the achievement of general and specific objectives, adequacy and efficiency of resources, and European added value, to the European Parliament, Council, European Economic and Social Committee, and Committee of the Regions. An ex post evaluation report is also required by 31 December 2030, providing a global assessment of Regulation implementation and long-term impact, to the same recipients. Overall, the Technical Support Instrument aims to support Member States in implementing reforms and achieving their objectives, with a focus on cohesion, competitiveness, and innovation, and is subject to regular reporting and evaluation to ensure its effectiveness.

summary:
The Technical Support Instrument aims to promote the Union's economic, social, and territorial cohesion by supporting Member States' efforts to implement reforms, contributing to the implementation of the European Green Deal, mainstreaming of climate actions, and achievement of climate and biodiversity objectives. The instrument establishes a framework with general and specific objectives, budget, forms of Union funding, and rules for providing funding for the period from 1 January 2021 to 31 December 2027. The specific objectives of the instrument include preparing, amending, implementing, and revising recovery and resilience plans, and its scope includes policy areas related to cohesion, competitiveness, education, productivity, research, and innovation.

The instrument applies to Member States, which may request technical support upon which the Commission provides support in various policy domains. Member States have the right to request technical support, and they shall pay for the expenses pertaining to additional technical support. The Commission may provide guidance on the main elements to be included in the request for technical support. Requests for technical support shall be submitted by 31 October unless otherwise specified, and Member States may consult relevant stakeholders before requesting technical support. The Commission organizes additional dedicated calls for requests in response to specific emerging needs of Member States.

The instrument also applies to Member States that receive Union financial assistance, and national authorities, the European Investment Bank group, international organisations, public or private bodies and entities, and European Free Trade Association countries may be involved in its implementation. The Commission shall implement the instrument, adopt work programmes, and provide technical support to Member States. The Commission also has the responsibility to report on the implementation of the Regulation through annual reports, which shall include information on requests for support from Member States, analysis of application of criteria for support, cooperation and support plans, special measures adopted, implementation of support measures, and communication activities carried out by the Commission. These reports shall be submitted to the European Parliament and the Council.

In addition to the annual reports, the Commission shall also submit a mid-term evaluation report by 20 February 2025, assessing the achievement of the general and specific objectives, the adequacy and efficiency of resources, and the European added value. This report shall be submitted to the European Parliament, the Council, the European Economic and Social Committee, and the Committee of the Regions. An ex-post evaluation report shall also be submitted by 31 December 2030, providing a global assessment of the Regulation's implementation and its long-term impact, to the same recipients. Overall, the Technical Support Instrument provides a framework for the Commission to support Member States in their efforts to implement reforms and achieve the Union's objectives, while ensuring transparency and accountability through regular reporting and evaluation.

summary:
The EU4Health Programme, which runs from 2021 to 2027, aims to promote Union action in the field of health by emphasizing collaboration and cooperation at the Union level. The Programme focuses on areas with Union added value, including cross-border health threats, internal market issues, and innovation in health, and supports coordinated public health measures at the Union level to address cross-border threats to health. It applies to all Member States, with country-specific assistance provided to those with the greatest needs. Member States and participating countries have designated National Focal Points to assist the Commission, and competent authorities of Member States are considered identified beneficiaries for grants under the Programme. Additionally, persons and entities established in Overseas Countries and Territories are eligible for funding under the Programme.

The Programme has a financial envelope of EUR 2,446,000,000 in current prices for 2021-2027, with an additional allocation of EUR 2,900,000,000 in 2018 prices. The funds will be used for technical and administrative assistance, as well as the implementation of the Programme, with a minimum of 20% allocated to health promotion and disease prevention, and maximum allocations for procurement of crisis-relevant products, global commitments and health initiatives, and administrative expenses. The Programme's objectives include improving human health and ensuring a high level of protection of human health, and its general objectives include improving and fostering health.

The Programme supports the transfer, adaptation, and roll-out of best practices and innovative solutions between Member States, as well as cross-border collaboration and partnerships. It also strengthens cross-sectoral collaboration and coordination, and supports the functioning of European Reference Networks and the establishment of new transnational networks. The Programme provides support for the implementation of European Reference Networks in Member States, the creation of new networks for rare, complex, and low prevalence diseases, and collaboration among networks. Furthermore, it supports the improvement and development of network registries, stakeholder consultation activities, and actions contributing to World Health Organization objectives.

In terms of governance, the EU4Health Steering Group ensures consistency and complementarity between Member States' health policies and Union policies, and meets at least three times a year. The Programme also allows for joint procurement, procurement by the Commission on behalf of Member States, and procurement by the Commission as wholesaler in cases where a serious cross-border threat to health has been notified or a public health emergency has been recognized. Eligible costs under the Programme include costs incurred prior to the date of submission of the grant application, subject to certain conditions, and costs incurred by entities in non-associated countries may be eligible in exceptional cases during a health crisis. The Programme's budgetary commitments may be broken down over several years, and activities may be considered eligible as of January 1, 2021, if implemented before grant application submission. Overall, the EU4Health Programme aims to improve human health and ensure a high level of protection of human health, while promoting collaboration and cooperation among Member States and supporting the development of innovative solutions and best practices in the field of health.

It applies to all Member States, with country-specific assistance provided to those with the greatest needs. Member States and participating countries have designated National Focal Points to assist the Commission, and competent authorities of Member States are considered identified beneficiaries for grants under the Programme. A serious cross-border threat to health is defined as a life-threatening or otherwise serious hazard to health of biological, chemical, environmental, or unknown origin that spreads or entails a significant risk of spreading across national borders of Member States, and may necessitate coordination at the Union level.

summary:
The EU4Health Programme, established for the period 2021-2027, aims to promote the well-being of the Union's peoples and ensure a high level of human health protection in all Union policies and activities. The programme supports actions with Union added value, particularly in areas where collaboration at Union level can bring advantages and efficiency gains. It applies to Member States, participating countries, national focal points, competent authorities, international organisations, and persons and entities established in Overseas Countries and Territories, as well as European Reference Networks.

The programme has several objectives, including improving human health, reducing the burden of diseases, protecting people from cross-border threats, improving the availability of medicinal products, and strengthening health systems. It adopts a One Health approach, recognizing the connection between human health, animal health, and the environment. To achieve these objectives, the programme supports the transfer of best practices, cross-border collaboration, and cross-sectoral collaboration, as well as the functioning of European Reference Networks and the establishment of new transnational networks.

The programme has a financial envelope of EUR 2,446,000,000 in current prices and EUR 2,900,000,000 in 2018 prices for its implementation. Grants paid by the Union can cover up to 60% of eligible costs, and up to 80% in cases of exceptional utility, which includes situations where at least 30% of the budget is allocated to Member States with a GNI per inhabitant below 90% of the Union average, or where bodies from at least 14 Member States participate. The distribution of funds is subject to certain limits, with a minimum of 20% allocated to health promotion and disease prevention, and maximum allocations for procurement, global commitments, and administrative expenses.

The programme is implemented through a range of actions, including grants, procurement, and information and communication actions. The Commission is assisted by a EU4Health Programme Committee and has the power to adopt delegated acts. Eligible actions are those that implement the objectives listed in the programme, and eligible costs include those incurred prior to grant application submission, provided they are directly linked to the implementation of supported actions and activities.

The programme also supports stakeholder consultation activities, collaboration with third countries and international organizations, and actions contributing to the objectives of the World Health Organization. The InvestEU Fund is established to provide an EU guarantee for financing and investment operations, along with an advisory support mechanism, known as the InvestEU Advisory Hub, for project development and access to financing, and a database, known as the InvestEU Portal, for project visibility and investment opportunities. The InvestEU Programme encompasses the InvestEU Fund, InvestEU Advisory Hub, InvestEU Portal, and blending operations, which combine non-repayable and/or repayable forms of support from the Union budget with repayable forms of support from other institutions or investors. The EU guarantee is an overall irrevocable, unconditional, and on-demand budgetary guarantee provided by the Union budget, and it is divided into compartments defined by the origin of the resources backing it. The EIB Group, which includes the EIB, its subsidiaries, and other entities established in accordance with the EIB Statute, plays a key role in implementing the InvestEU Programme.

The InvestEU Fund provides strategic and operational guidance for implementing partners, and the EU guarantee covers financing and investment operations that meet specific criteria and requirements. Implementing partners are responsible for ensuring that these operations comply with the Regulation and investment guidelines, and the Investment Committee checks compliance with relevant requirements. The InvestEU Advisory Hub supports public authorities and project promoters, and the Commission has the right to decide on the use of the EU guarantee. Implementing partners have the right to use the EU guarantee for financing and investment operations, but they are obligated to ensure compliance with the Regulation and investment guidelines.

The EU guarantee is subject to certain conditions and exceptions, including the requirement that support be provided through equity, quasi-equity, or debt with conditions not available on the market, or to operations with a higher risk profile than standard activities. Additionally, the EU guarantee is not granted for refinancing operations, except in exceptional circumstances. The InvestEU Programme also excludes certain activities, such as those that limit individual rights and freedoms, violate human rights, or involve prohibited products or technologies. Other excluded activities include tobacco-related products and activities, research on human cloning, genetic heritage modification, and human embryo creation, gambling, sex trade and related activities, and activities involving live animals for experimental purposes without compliance with the European Convention.

The EIB Group shall implement a portion of the EU guarantee and support the implementation of the EU compartment of the InvestEU Fund and the Member State compartment. The EIB Group shall also provide various services, including investment guidelines, risk methodology, technical advice, and financial reports. The Commission shall engage with implementing partners based on the EIB Group's opinion, and the EIB Group's tasks shall be conducted independently from its role as advisory partner. The InvestEU Programme aims to foster consistency, inclusivity, additionality, and efficient deployment, and it has a budget of EUR 300 000 000 for advisory initiatives and operational tasks. Overall, the InvestEU Programme is designed to support the implementation of the InvestEU Fund and to provide strategic and operational guidance for implementing partners, while ensuring that the EU guarantee is used in a way that is consistent with the programme's objectives and requirements.

summary:
The InvestEU Fund provides an EU guarantee to support financing and investment operations, contributing to the objectives of the Union's internal policies. The Fund is part of the InvestEU Programme, which also includes the InvestEU Advisory Hub, InvestEU Portal, and blending operations. The EU guarantee is an overall irrevocable, unconditional, and on-demand budgetary guarantee provided by the Union budget, and it is divided into compartments defined in terms of the origin of the resources backing it. A blending operation, supported by the Union budget, combines non-repayable and/or repayable forms of support. The EIB Group, comprising the EIB, its subsidiaries, and other entities, plays a crucial role in the implementation of the InvestEU Programme.

The InvestEU Programme has a central point of entry, managed and hosted by the Commission, to support capacity building actions, which involve developing organisational capacities, skills, and processes. The Commission and the EIB Group have an agreement in relation to the InvestEU Advisory Hub, with the objective of supporting the implementation of the InvestEU Programme, fostering consistency, inclusivity, additionality, and efficient deployment. The EIB Group is obligated to implement a portion of the EU guarantee, support the implementation of the EU compartment of the InvestEU Fund and the Member State compartment, contribute to investment guidelines, and define risk methodology and risk mapping systems.

Financing and investment operations supported by the InvestEU Fund must comply with certain conditions, including contributing to Union policy objectives, falling within the scope of eligible areas, and not supporting excluded activities. Excluded activities include those that limit individual rights and freedoms, violate human rights, involve defence activities, or relate to tobacco, gambling, or live animals for experimental purposes. The Fund may support projects involving entities in one or more Member States extending to one or more third countries, including acceding countries, candidate countries, and countries under the European Neighbourhood Policy.

The InvestEU Fund's support is subject to a policy check, which involves confirming that financing and investment operations comply with Union law and policies. Additionality is also verified, particularly for SME support, and exists when the InvestEU Fund supports a financial intermediary in setting up a new portfolio with a higher level of risk or increasing the volume of activities that are already highly risky. A Scoreboard is used to assess proposed financing and investment operations, taking into account elements such as contribution to EU policy objectives, additionality, market failure, and financial profile.

The InvestEU Fund's operations are guided by investment guidelines, and the EIB Group is responsible for assessing the systems of potential implementing partners and providing technical advice. The Fund's activities are also subject to a fee arrangement, with conditions applicable to any amount due to the Union. Overall, the InvestEU Fund aims to support financing and investment operations that contribute to the Union's internal policies, while ensuring that its activities are consistent with Union law and policies, and that they do not support excluded activities.

summary:
The InvestEU Programme aims to support Union policy objectives through financing and investment operations, contributing to areas such as competitiveness, growth, employment, sustainability, social resilience, and economic cohesion. The programme applies to the EU and its Member States, as well as third countries and their entities, with specific conditions and limitations. The EU provides a guarantee for the InvestEU Programme, with a specified amount and provisioning rate, and Member States may provide additional guarantees or cash for the programme. Implementing partners have obligations, including providing information for climate, environmental, and social sustainability proofing, while the Investment Committee and the Steering Board have roles in setting requirements and guidelines.

The programme sets out conditions for financing and investment operations, including compliance with the Financial Regulation, contribution to Union policy objectives, and consistency with investment guidelines. Eligible projects and operations include those situated in the Union or in an overseas country or territory linked to a Member State, as well as projects involving entities located or established in one or more Member States that extend to third countries. Legal entities established in Member States, overseas countries or territories, or third countries associated with the InvestEU Programme are eligible as final recipients.

The InvestEU Programme also establishes policy windows, which define the scope of the programme's support. Additionally, the programme provides for an InvestEU Advisory Hub, which offers advisory support for investment projects and enhances the capacity of project promoters and financial intermediaries. The Commission is responsible for establishing and allocating requests for advisory support, while the EIB Group and other advisory partners provide the support.

To ensure compliance with Union law and policies, a policy check is conducted by the Commission for implementing partners other than the EIB. The Commission also assesses requests for EU guarantee using a scoreboard. Implementing partners must comply with Union law and policies, and the EIB's financing and investment operations are not covered by the EU guarantee if the Commission delivers an unfavourable opinion.

The Commission is required to report on the implementation of the InvestEU Programme, providing information on the level of implementation with respect to its objectives and performance indicators. Implementing partners must provide necessary information for the Commission's reporting obligations. An independent final evaluation report on the InvestEU Programme will be submitted by the Commission by 31 December 2031.

Implementing partners and advisory partners have various responsibilities, including proposing InvestEU Advisory Hub support to project promoters, informing project promoters of the possibility of listing their projects on the InvestEU Portal, and acknowledging the origin and ensuring the visibility of Union funding. Overall, the InvestEU Programme aims to support sustainable and inclusive growth, while ensuring transparency, accountability, and compliance with Union law and policies.

The programme also covers the management of expenditure in the area of plants, animals, food, and feed, and the programming and financing framework for European statistics. summary:
The Single Market Programme aims to establish a programme for the internal market, competitiveness of enterprises, including small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), the area of plants, animals, food and feed, and European statistics. The programme's purpose is to improve the functioning of the internal market, the competitiveness and sustainability of enterprises, especially SMEs, standardisation, market surveillance, and consumer protection. It also supports the design, implementation, and enforcement of Union legislation underpinning the proper functioning of the internal market. The programme applies to all citizens and businesses, notably micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), as well as consumers, employees, representatives of civil society, and public authorities.

The programme empowers all actors of the internal market, including businesses, citizens, and public authorities, by raising awareness of their rights and providing them with tools, information, and assistance. It also supports the enforcement of consumer protection and safety rules. To achieve its objectives, the programme finances actions implementing specific objectives, including those related to market surveillance authorities and Union testing facilities, which may be financed up to 100% of eligible costs. Actions constituting activities in Article 36 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1020 and implementing specific objectives are also eligible for funding.

Eligible entities for funding include legal entities in a Member State, overseas country or territory, or third country associated to the Programme, as well as legal entities created under Union law or international organisations. Exceptionally, legal entities in a third country not associated to the Programme may be eligible if their participation contributes to Programme objectives. The Commission, Member States, consumers, citizens, businesses, especially SMEs, and public administrations are all involved in the programme. The European Parliament, the Council, the European Economic and Social Committee, and the Committee of the Regions also play a role, as do the European Statistical System Committee and the European Statistical Advisory Committee.

The Commission is responsible for adopting work programmes, implementing information and communication actions, and submitting interim and final evaluation reports. The Commission must also consult the European Statistical System Committee and the European Statistical Advisory Committee. In terms of rights and obligations, eligible actions are entitled to funding, and there is an obligation to implement veterinary and phytosanitary emergency measures and to comply with relevant Union law. In case of official confirmation of animal diseases or plant pests, measures must be implemented immediately, and the application of measures must comply with relevant Union law. The establishment of stocks of biological products is subject to Commission approval. Overall, the programme aims to support the proper functioning of the internal market and promote the competitiveness and sustainability of enterprises, while ensuring consumer protection and safety.

The Programme aims to support and accelerate the digital transformation of the European economy, industry, and society, with a focus on bridging the digital divide, enhancing cybersecurity and trust, and implementing the European strategy on High Performance Computing and Artificial Intelligence. The Programme applies to the public sector, areas of public interest, businesses, and citizens across the Union, with specific support for small and medium-sized enterprises, mid-caps, scale-up companies, and public administrations. Associated countries and international organisations of European interest are also relevant. 

The Programme supports the integration and use of trans-European digital service infrastructures, facilitates the development, update, and use of solutions and frameworks by public administrations, businesses, and citizens, and ensures the continuous capacity at Union level to lead digital development and share best practices. It also aims to benefit the Union industry, particularly SMEs and mid-caps, as well as the public sector, through European Digital Innovation Hubs, which must perform activities such as raising awareness, providing digital transformation expertise, and facilitating the transfer of expertise.

Eligible participants include legal entities established in a Member State, an overseas country or territory linked to a Member State, or a third country associated to the Programme, as well as entities created under Union law and international organisations of European interest. Legal entities from non-associated third countries can participate in specific actions if necessary for the Programme's objectives, but they typically bear their own costs. Beneficiaries have the right to receive funding under the Programme, which shall be in the form of grants, procurement, or prizes, and the Programme shall be implemented under direct or indirect management.

The Commission shall implement information and communication actions relating to the Programme, ensure that integrated information is provided and reaches potential applicants to Union funding in the digital sector, and establish a network of European Digital Innovation Hubs through an open and competitive process based on specified criteria. Member States shall participate in the joint procurement framework for the acquisition of HPC and post-exascale supercomputing infrastructure. The Programme shall be implemented in accordance with the technical description set out in Annex I, and departure from participation and dissemination rules is only allowed in specified cases. Grants may be awarded only to beneficiaries that are contracting authorities or entities, and the Programme's general objectives are laid down in Article 3(1), with specific objectives set out in Articles 4 to 8.

The Programme aims to support and accelerate the digital transformation of the European economy, industry, and society, with a focus on bridging the digital divide and enhancing cybersecurity and trust. It applies to the public sector, areas of public interest, businesses, and citizens across the Union, with specific support for small and medium-sized enterprises, mid-caps, scale-up companies, and public administrations. Associated countries and international organisations of European interest are also relevant. The Programme's general objectives are to support the integration and use of trans-European digital service infrastructures, facilitate the development and use of solutions and frameworks by public administrations, businesses, and citizens, and ensure the continuous capacity at Union level to lead digital development and share best practices.

The Programme has five interrelated specific objectives: High Performance Computing, Artificial Intelligence, Cybersecurity and Trust, Advanced Digital Skills, and Deployment and Best Use of Digital Capacity and Interoperability. It will support the implementation of the European strategy on High Performance Computing and build up and strengthen core Artificial Intelligence capacities in Europe. The Programme will also support the deployment and best use of digital capacities and interoperability, and will benefit the Union industry, particularly SMEs and mid-caps, as well as the public sector, through European Digital Innovation Hubs.

Eligible participants include legal entities established in a Member State, an overseas country or territory linked to a Member State, or a third country associated to the Programme, as well as entities created under Union law and international organisations of European interest. Legal entities from non-associated third countries can participate in specific actions if necessary for the Programme's objectives, but they typically bear their own costs. European Digital Innovation Hubs must perform activities such as raising awareness, providing digital transformation expertise, and facilitating the transfer of expertise. Beneficiaries have the right to receive funding under the Programme, which shall be in the form of grants.

The Commission shall implement information and communication actions relating to the Programme and ensure that integrated information is provided and reaches potential applicants to Union funding in the digital sector. Member States shall participate in the joint procurement framework for the acquisition of HPC and post-exascale supercomputing infrastructure. The Programme shall be implemented in accordance with the technical description set out in Annex I. Each Member State is required to designate candidate entities for the initial network of European Digital Innovation Hubs through an open and competitive process, based on criteria such as appropriate competences and management capacity. The Programme may also receive complementary funding from Union programmes where management arrangements allow it. Overall, the Programme aims to create a comprehensive and integrated approach to digital transformation, supporting the development of a strong and competitive digital economy in the European Union.

summary:
The Digital Europe Programme is established for the period 2021-2027 to support the digitisation of European economies and address the skills gap. The Programme applies to the European Union and its Member States, and persons and entities established in overseas countries and territories are eligible for funding subject to the rules and objectives of the Programme. The Programme aims to support cooperation for a European ecosystem for trusted data sharing and digital infrastructures, as well as the uptake of advanced digital technologies by the public sector and industry, including small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) and start-ups.

The Programme provides grants to support digital transformation and is implemented through work programmes with specific objectives. These objectives include supporting the development, update, and use of solutions and frameworks by public administrations, businesses, and citizens, as well as ensuring continuous capacity at Union level to lead digital development. The Programme also focuses on advanced digital skills, aiming to support persons, especially those in SMEs, in acquiring these skills through training, and on the deployment and best use of digital capacity and interoperability, encouraging the use of digital public services and alignment with the European Interoperability Framework.

Any person or entity receiving Union funds must fully cooperate in the protection of the financial interests of the Union, and the European Anti-Fraud Office (OLAF) has the power to carry out administrative investigations. The European Public Prosecutor’s Office (EPPO) is empowered to investigate and prosecute criminal offences affecting the financial interests of the Union. Beneficiaries of grants must comply with the conditions of the grant, including reporting requirements, and may be subject to obligations such as raising awareness, providing access to digital transformation expertise, and facilitating the transfer of expertise.

Grants may be awarded for actions that have already begun, provided that the applicant can demonstrate the need for starting the action prior to the signature of the grant agreement. The designation of candidate entities for the network shall be through an open and competitive process. The Commission has the power to adopt delegated acts to amend certain annexes and shall adopt decisions on the selection of entities forming the initial network. Member States shall designate candidate entities for the network, and beneficiaries of grants must be contracting authorities or contracting entities. Legal entities established in a third country not associated to the Programme may participate in specific actions if necessary to achieve the Programme's objectives. Overall, the Digital Europe Programme aims to facilitate the digital transformation of European economies and societies, supporting cooperation, innovation, and the development of advanced digital skills.
